Agents act in worlds, learn from experience and reuse verified skills. Hylo connects those capabilities through a measured improvement loop.

docs.title: Physical RSI
docs.text:
Physical RSI connects the capabilities below: run a task, propose a change, evaluate it and carry an adopted version into later runs. People define the goals, evaluation conditions and boundaries. For hardware use, configure manual campaign approval and validate the target deployment.

Concept What it provides Worlds scenes, robots, observations and physical goal checks Agents policies, programs or model tool calls that decide actions Memory observations and experience that inform later decisions Skills reusable implementations with applicability and verification evidence

Concepts explains their relationship. Research publishes measured outcomes and analysis. A simulation result applies to its stated task and observation conditions; it does not establish readiness on hardware.

docs.title: Physical RSI
docs.text:
Use task outcomes to propose changes, compare them with the current agent and carry adopted versions into later runs. Hylo connects worlds, agents, memory and skills through this improvement loop.

People define the tasks, success checks and operating boundaries. Campaign promotion defaults to auto; configure approval: manual for anything that will run on hardware and validate the target deployment.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Running a robot autonomously does not make its improvement autonomous. Someone still has to inspect failures, choose a change, compare it with the current version and decide whether to keep it. Physical RSI connects those steps so an adopted improvement becomes the starting point for the next round.

The change can be a controller setting, a recovery rule, a prompt, a program, a memory bank or learned weights. This lets a system improve a useful part of its behaviour without requiring a new model-training run every time. Which changes are available depends on the agent and its compatible generators or learners.

docs.title: Physical feedback
docs.text:
The proposal and its evaluation have different roles. A model may suggest a better grasp or write a sorting program, but its explanation is not evidence that the task succeeded. Task checks measure what happened: whether an object was lifted, where it ended up, whether a controller reached its target, and which interventions occurred. In simulation, scoring can use privileged state while the agent receives only its permitted observations.

This separation matters because an optimiser can improve a score by exploiting its definition. Success conditions must be fixed outside the candidate, and evaluation must cover the claim being made. Passing one scene's check establishes that result; improvement across a task family requires a comparison on a declared set of tasks.

docs.title: Improvement loop
docs.text:
Step Capability Guide Build Create scenes, robots and task conditions Worlds Run Execute an agent and record actions and outcomes Experiments Improve Produce candidate settings, programs or learned artifacts Campaigns, Learning Verify Compare frozen candidates under declared conditions Benchmarking Deploy Activate a version for later execution and retain rollback Deployment

Each round starts from the version the previous round adopted. A rejected candidate stays in the archive; it does not replace the active version. Task checks provide feedback independently of an agent's own summary.

docs.title: Campaigns
docs.text: A campaign diagnoses failures, asks a generator for changes, screens candidates and applies a paired promotion gate. It records the evidence and version history. Generators may propose settings, steering rules, programs or learner artifacts. They cannot change the protected safety, scoring or benchmark settings.

docs.title: Selection and confirmation
docs.text:
Development runs expose failures; a separate screening split helps choose among candidates. The gate then compares a selected candidate with its parent on matched initial states. Pairing reduces differences caused by which scenes happened to be easy. Regression and safety checks can veto a candidate even when its average success rate improves. Matching seeds also requires a consistent model runtime and batching protocol when controlling policy randomness.

The held-out report is separate from candidate selection. These roles reduce selection bias, but the current campaign can reuse gate states across cycles and expose previous outcomes through its archive. They are not an unlimited supply of fresh tests; the split access rules describe that limit.

docs.title: Versioned progress
docs.text:
A candidate names a configuration change and any sealed artifacts it needs. Their provenance records the data and settings used to produce them. Promotion records the parent, candidate and evidence; a rejected candidate remains in the archive without replacing the active version. Retaining failures helps later proposals avoid repeating them, while retaining versions makes rollback possible.

Behaviour changes, measurement tools and proposal advice need different evidence. An agent change goes through the campaign gate; a learned judge needs calibration against known outcomes; a lesson earns credit through the outcomes of candidates that used it. A persuasive lesson or a calibrated judge does not by itself prove an agent has improved.

Start with First improvement for a complete CPU example, then use Campaigns to configure your own loop.

docs.title: Reusable outputs
docs.text:
• Agent versions retain adopted configuration changes and rollback history.
  • Artifacts retain weights, critics, world models, judges or memory banks with their provenance.
  • Skills retain reusable programs or procedures with applicability and verification evidence.

Each output has its own validation path. A calibrated judge is an instrument; it does not become a promoted agent. A verified program skill is available for reuse; it does not deploy itself onto a robot.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Bring a task and its success conditions, a simulation or robot interface, and a starting agent. Existing models, programs, demonstrations and recorded runs can supply that starting point. Follow Agents to choose the execution mode and Learning to ingest external data.

docs.title: Operation
docs.text:
Serve runs agents through policy servers and workcells. Studio shows runs and campaigns and provides operator controls. Every executed action passes the safety shield. Rollback changes the active version; it does not undo physical actions.

Keep development and evaluation data separate, retain observation conditions with results, and revalidate when the task or robot changes. Simulation evidence supports its stated conditions; hardware needs target validation.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
Find Python contracts and implementation APIs here. Core contracts define the boundary between Hylo plugins; the package index provides the complete module inventory.

You need Start here Environment, agent, policy, reasoner, benchmark or learning contracts Core contracts Episode execution, events and traces Episode loop Experiment models, execution profiles and plugin registration Configuration API Artifacts, store IDs, scorecards and active versions Artifacts and store Memory records, queries and store protocol Core memory module Any other package or module Package index

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Data contracts such as EnvSpec, Observation, ActionChunk and ExperimentConfig are frozen pydantic models. Build them with keyword arguments, copy them with model_copy(update=...), and obtain a JSON Schema with model_json_schema(). Behavioural contracts such as Environment, Agent, ChunkPolicy and Guard are typing.Protocols: a plugin implements their methods without inheriting from them.

The core pages and module pages render docstrings and type annotations from the checked-out code. A module covered by a core page links back to that page from the package index, so its API has one definition. Names starting with an underscore are omitted. Inclusion in the package index is not a stability guarantee; plugins should depend on the core contracts at their integration boundary.

docs.title: Artifacts and store
docs.text: What Hylo learns is saved as an artifact: a directory with a content digest and a record of what it was built from, sealed unless marked mutable. Configs can refer to runs and artifacts by store id instead of path. Scorecards and active versions are the formats bench and serve exchange. User guides: learning, the store, benchmarking, deployment.

docs.title: artifact
docs.text:
Derived artifacts (RFC-0004): everything the system learns is a versioned, digest-pinned directory with provenance.

The trace store is the single source of truth. Action memories, critics, value models, fine-tuned weights, datasets, judges are all derived from traces (or from external data sources) by a builder, and each one carries an artifact.json manifest: what it is, which role it plays, a content digest, and which runs / splits it was built from. Three roles, three trust paths:

  • behaviour changes what the robot does (memory, critic, noise policy, weights): only the RSI gate activates it;
  • instrument measures or labels (success judge, progress model, world model): trusted only after calibration against ground truth, never the gate's verdict;
  • proposal only changes what gets proposed (lessons, skill index); curated by outcome votes.

One split guard for every builder: development splits (search, search_val) and calibrated external sources may be read; gate and held-out data never. The gate re-checks the provenance of every artifact a candidate references, so a leak is caught even if a builder forgot the guard.

docs.title: store
docs.text:
Run and artifact store (hylo.store/v0.1): global ids, references instead of paths, deletion protection, sync.

A store is a directory tree on one machine (this machine's profile says where: hylo store init PATH, else $HYLO_STORE, else ./runs). Runs (directories with an evallog.json) and sealed artifacts (an artifact.json) anywhere under it get an id:

run:<run_id>                       run ids are unique (they end in a random suffix)
artifact:<name>@<digest>           name from the manifest, digest = content digest (a prefix of >= 8 hex works)
artifact:<name>                    allowed when exactly one artifact has that name; the run manifest pins it

Configs reference artifacts by id (critic: {path: artifact:l10-v1@3d8d6096f7111acc}); the registry resolves ids to this machine's paths when it builds a component, after the experiment digest is taken, so the same config means the same content on every machine. Learner job inputs accept run and artifact ids too.

The index (/.hylo-store/index.json) is a cache, rebuilt by walking the tree when an id is not found. It also records who refers to what: an artifact's provenance (the runs and artifacts it was built from) and a campaign's archive and promotion ledger. hylo store rm refuses to delete anything still referred to unless forced, and a forced or plain removal leaves a tombstone, so a dangling reference says what happened instead of "not found".

hylo store push|pull HOST:PATH [ID ...] copies runs and artifacts between machines with rsync (runs from the robot computer to the workstation, artifacts the other way). Sealed artifacts are never overwritten: the same path holding a different digest on the other side is a conflict and nothing is copied.

docs.title: scorecard
docs.text:
Scorecards (hylo.scorecard/v0.1): the result of running one policy under one benchmark protocol.

Written by hylo-bench (hylo bench run), read by leaderboards, the catalog, the playground and the project site, so the format lives here. A scorecard is self-contained: the protocol and policy it measured, the headline metrics with a 95% interval on success, per-task success, and the per-episode outcomes (episodes, keyed "task#seed") that let two scorecards of the same protocol be compared pairwise.

{"schema_version": "hylo.scorecard/v0.1", "protocol": "libero-10", "protocol_version": "1",
 "protocol_digest": "...", "policy": "smolvla", "agent": {"type": ..., "params": ...},
 "metrics": {"success_mean": 0.54, "steps_mean": 312.0, ...}, "success_ci95": [0.40, 0.67],
 "per_task": {"libero_10/0": {"success": 0.6, "n": 5}, ...}, "episodes": {"libero_10/0#30000": 1.0, ...},
 "run_dir": "runs/...", "config_digest": "...", "created_at": ...}

docs.title: wilson_interval
docs.text:
wilson_interval(successes: float, n: int, z: float = 1.96) -> tuple[float, float] | None

95% Wilson score interval for a success rate (well behaved at 0 and 1, unlike the normal approximation).

docs.title: deployment
docs.text:
The active version of an improvement campaign, as a file (hylo.active/v0.1).

The campaign (hylo-evolve) writes <campaign>/active.json whenever its active version changes: at start, on a promotion, on an approval, on a rollback. Anything that deploys the campaign's current behaviour (the policy server in hylo-serve) reads only this file, so the deploying side needs neither the improvement code nor the candidate registry, and the file can be copied to another machine.

{"schema_version": "hylo.active/v0.1", "campaign": "libero10-steering", "version": "cand-1a2b3c4d5e",
 "agent": {"type": "lerobot.steered", "params": {...}}, "patch": {"agent.params.kp": 2.0},
 "lineage": ["cand-1a2b3c4d5e"], "updated_at": 1793400000.0}

version is None while the base configuration is active. agent is the fully resolved agent spec (base config with the lineage's patches applied), so a reader builds it with the registry and nothing else.

Atomic write (temp file + rename): a reader never sees a half-written file.

docs.title: profile
docs.text:
Execution profiles (hylo.profile/v0.1): where components run on this machine, kept out of experiment configs.

An experiment says what is measured. Where an interpreter lives, which rendering library to load, where the model cache is, differ per machine and must not change an experiment's identity. Configs name a runtime instead:

env:   {type: libero, remote: {runtime: libero}}
agent: {type: remote, params: {ref: lerobot.steered, runtime: libero, params: {...}}}

and each machine's profile says what that runtime is:

schema_version: hylo.profile/v0.1
runtimes:
  libero:
    python: /home/me/hylo/bench/envs/libero/.venv/bin/python
    env: {MUJOCO_GL: osmesa, LIBERO_CONFIG_PATH: /home/me/hylo/bench/envs/libero/config, HF_HOME: ...}

The profile is found at $HYLO_PROFILE, else ~/.config/hylo/profile.yaml. hylo profile shows and edits it; bench's envs/libero/setup.sh registers the runtime it builds. Explicit python / env in a config still work and take precedence over the runtime's (for a one-off); neither enters the experiment digest. The profile also says where this machine's run and artifact store is (store:, set by hylo store init PATH).

docs.title: plugins
docs.text:
Contract versions and plugin metadata (RFC-0005 part 4).

Every plugin group is a contract with a version (hylo.policy/v0.1, hylo.agent/v0.1, ...). A distribution declares which version of each contract its plugins implement, and what is known about them, in one dictionary exposed under the hylo.meta entry-point group (a module with no heavy imports, so listing plugins never loads them):

[project.entry-points."hylo.meta"]
hylo-policy-lerobot = "hylo.policies.lerobot:META"

META = {
    "contracts": {"agents": "hylo.agent/v0.1", "policies": "hylo.policy/v0.1"},
    "maturity": "implemented",                                  # the default for this distribution's plugins
    "plugins": {"agents/lerobot.steered": {"weights": "per checkpoint: ..."},
                "datasources/lerobot.dataset": {"maturity": "unverified", "notes": "..."}},
}

The code licence is the distribution's own (license in its pyproject); weights names the licence of model weights a plugin downloads or needs, which is often different. Maturity:

implemented     run end to end on its intended target (a real simulator or robot), with recorded runs
unverified      tests pass, but never run end to end on its intended target here
needs-hardware  needs hardware this lab has not connected yet
test-double     for tests and conformance only (`testing.*` names)

The registry refuses to load a plugin whose declared contract is incompatible with this core: another major version, or a newer minor version (a plugin written against features this core does not have). A plugin without a declaration still loads; hylo plugins shows it as undeclared and hylo plugin check warns.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text: Every plugin group's contract lives in hylo-core, so a plugin's contract comes from hylo-core alone. This page lists what a plugin must provide and the data that passes between the episode loop, environments and agents. The plugin system explains how plugins are registered; the interface notes explain the design behind each contract; the plugin catalogue lists what implements them.

docs.title: env
docs.text:
Environment contract. An Environment = Simulator + Task logic behind reset/step.

Optional capabilities are declared in EnvSpec.capabilities and exposed through separate protocols, never by duck-typing, so the kernel can refuse a run that needs a missing capability.

docs.title: policy
docs.text:
Policies (plugin group "policies"): action-chunk generators that agents run, steer and compose.

An Agent is what the kernel talks to (core.agent). A ChunkPolicy is the model inside: given an observation it draws action chunks, one per noise seed. Separating the two lets one policy be run, steered (seeded noise, sample-and-select, recovery rules), temporally ensembled (ACT), shadowed or memory-steered by agents in hylo-agents without the policy knowing, and lets one agent wrap any policy by configuration:

agent: {type: policy, params: {policy: {type: policy.flow, params: {path: artifacts/flow}}}}
agent: {type: steered, params: {sampler: {type: lerobot, params: {repo_id: lerobot/smolvla_libero}},
                                steering: {n_samples: 4, selector: medoid}}}

Deterministic policies (regression, retrieval, scripted) ignore the seeds and return identical samples. Stochastic ones (diffusion, flow matching, sampled tokens) must derive their randomness from the seeds only, so a candidate and its parent face the same noise on the same init state and an episode can be replayed.

docs.title: sample
docs.text:
sample(observation: Observation, seeds: list[int] | None, noise_scale: float) -> np.ndarray

(N, T, A) action chunks in the environment's units, one per seed (N = len(seeds), or 1 if None).

docs.title: reasoning
docs.text:
Reasoning plugin contracts, one per role (each its own plugin group and version):

  • reasoners (hylo.reasoner): the slow, event-triggered part of an agent; turns observations and memory into a Decision (a subgoal, a skill, an abort), with begin / deliberate / end around an episode.
  • choosers (hylo.chooser): which object an instruction refers to, among perceived or remembered objects.
  • planners (hylo.planner): decomposes an instruction into short sequential subgoals and judges when one is done.
  • reflectors (hylo.reflector): distils lessons from a campaign's diagnosis into operations on a lesson book.

Rule-based, LLM and VLM implementations satisfy the same protocols; the kernel never sees the difference. The agents that use them (composable object reach, SubgoalAgent, the experience generator) live in hylo-agents and hylo-evolve; the LLM ones in hylo-reasoner-llm and hylo-proposer-llm.

docs.title: Robots and scenes
docs.text: These data contracts connect environments with task-strategy tools and program agents. They do not import a simulator.

docs.title: robot
docs.text:
Robot description contract (hylo.robot/v0.1): what a manipulation environment tells tool-using agents about its robot, so the same perception, kinematics and planning tools (hylo-manip) work on every simulator and robot.

An environment that supports tool use puts a RobotSpec in EnvSpec.robot (so it also travels over the remote protocols) and follows the observation layout below. Nothing here changes how the kernel runs an episode: actions are still joint-position targets reviewed by the SafetyShield, one per control step.

Frames and units: metres and radians; the environment's world frame with +z up; poses are 4x4 homogeneous matrices given as nested lists. Cameras use the OpenCV optical frame (x right, y down, z forward).

The tool centre point (TCP) is defined the same way for every hand, so a grasp means the same on every robot:

  origin  where a held object's centre sits (between the pads of a parallel gripper; among the fingers of a
          dexterous hand, a few centimetres in front of the palm)
  +x      approach: the direction the hand moves to reach into an object
  +y      closing axis: the pads close along it (dexterous: the thumb-to-fingers direction)
  +z      x cross y

Observation layout of a manipulation environment (keys of Observation):

  state["q.<arm>"]           measured joint positions of that arm, in ArmSpec.joints order
  state["hand.<arm>"]        measured hand state in command units (parallel: one value, 0 closed .. 1 open), not the
                             last command: pads that stop short of closed tell the tools something is held
  state["base"]              [x, y, yaw] of a mobile base (only when RobotSpec.mobile_base)
  images["<cam>"]            RGB, (H, W, 3) uint8
  images["<cam>.depth"]      depth in metres along the optical axis, (H, W) float32; 0 or non-finite: no return
  images["<cam>.seg"]        instance ids, (H, W) int32, only when the environment was configured to give
                             segmentation (a privileged observation: it is part of the measured config)
  extra["cameras"]["<cam>"]  {"K": 3x3, "T_world_cam": 4x4}: intrinsics and the current camera pose
  extra["segments"]          {"<id>": "<label>"} for the instance ids above

Action layout: the concatenation, in RobotSpec.arms order, of each arm's joint targets followed by its hand command (ArmSpec.action_slice / hand_slice say where each sits).

docs.title: scene
docs.text:
Table-top scene contract (hylo.scene/v0.1): a manipulation task written as data, so a model can author it, a checker can validate it and an environment (bench: mujoco.panda_scene) can load it.

It lives in hylo-core because it crosses the harness / bench boundary: the harness writes and checks scenes (the scene builder of RFC-0006 part 8), bench environments load them, and neither side may import the other.

Frames and units: metres; ANGLES IN DEGREES (unlike hylo.robot, so hand-written and model-written files stay readable); world frame of the environment, +z up, table top at z = 0 unless the environment says otherwise.

A scene is a list of objects and a success predicate:

  object   one rigid body: a primitive (box, cylinder, sphere, capsule, mesh) or a ready-made container
           (tray: open box; cup: open cylinder), or a list of primitive `parts`; name (identifier), label (the
           words an instruction uses), colour, mass, friction
  pose     fixed start pose (pos [x, y] or [x, y, z]; z omitted: resting on the table or on `on`), or `region`:
           a box of start positions and a yaw range sampled from the episode seed (seeded variation)
  fixed    a fixture: does not move (no joint to the world)
  parent   attached to another object, rigidly or through one `joint` (slide or hinge): drawers, doors, lids,
           buttons; its pose is then in the parent's frame
  success  a declarative predicate over object poses and joint states, evaluated after every control step

Predicates (field op): on, inside, near, above, upright, lifted, row, joint_at_least, joint_at_most, not, all_of, any_of, sequence. Object predicates require the object at rest and released (not touching the hand) unless released: false. sequence latches: each term must become true after the previous ones did.

docs.title: instrument
docs.text:
Instruments (RFC-0004): learned components that measure or label instead of act.

A success judge or progress model labels episodes (so memory and training data can be written without simulator ground truth); a world model pre-screens candidates. Instruments are trusted through calibration, not the gate: hylo.learn.calibrate scores a judge against simulator outcomes on runs the judge was not built from and stores the CalibrationReport in the judge's artifact manifest. An instrument never decides a gate verdict: in simulation the gate always scores with ground truth, and a world model may only choose which candidates are worth real evaluation budget.

docs.title: learning
docs.text:
Learning pipeline contracts (RFC-0004): data source -> labeler -> learner -> sealed artifact -> candidate -> gate.

Contracts only. A learner turns development data into one artifact directory and seals it (artifact.write_manifest). Running jobs (in-process or with another venv's interpreter), calibration and data ingestion live in hylo-learn (hylo.learn).

docs.title: Learner
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Builds and seals one artifact from a job. Must refuse forbidden splits (use artifact.development_runs).

docs.title: OnlineLearner
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Learns by acting (policy search, on-policy RL, iterative self-training): each iteration it proposes agent specs to roll out, the runner evaluates them on a development split (recorded as ordinary runs) and hands back the results, the learner updates. seal writes the artifact; its provenance lists every rollout run.

Run by hylo.learn.online.run_online; a TrainJob whose learner has policies / update is online and carries the experiment config in params["experiment"].

docs.title: DataSource
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Episodes from outside the campaign's own runs (demonstrations, videos, other robots).

core.datasource.ingest turns them into a run under split external: with origin and licence. Episodes may lack actions (videos) or outcomes; labelers fill those in and say who produced each label.

docs.title: Labeler
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Adds labels an episode is missing (outcome, progress, latent actions). Labels from an instrument carry its artifact digest; an instrument never labels the data it was calibrated on.

docs.title: benchmark
docs.text: Benchmark = versioned set of TaskSpecs + evaluation protocol (splits, seeds, episodes); the benchmarks plugin contract (hylo.benchmark): a plugin is a factory that returns a Benchmark.

docs.title: standard_splits
docs.text:
standard_splits(train: int, validation: int, heldout: int) -> dict[str, tuple[int, ...]]

Disjoint seed ranges: train 0.., validation 10000.., heldout 20000..

docs.title: rsi_splits
docs.text:
rsi_splits(n_states: int = 50, bounds: tuple[int, int, int] = (20, 30, 40), replicates: int = 1, gate_looks: int = 1) -> dict[str, tuple[int, ...]]

RFC-0002 split of init-state indices: search (diagnosis), search_val (selection), gate (confirmation), heldout (report only). Replicate r reuses init state (seed % n_states) with new policy noise (seed + r * n_states). gate_looks > 1 adds gate_r1 .. gate_r{looks-1}: further noise replicates of the gate init states, evaluated only when an earlier look is inconclusive (group-sequential gate).

docs.title: scoring
docs.text:
The scorers and gate_tests plugin contracts (hylo.scorer, hylo.gate_test) and the data they exchange.

A scorer reads one episode's trace (never the agent or the environment) and returns a Score; a Score of None is an abstention (infra failure, agent error) and is excluded from metrics. A gate test compares per-episode values of one metric between a candidate and its parent, paired on (task, seed), and returns a PairedComparison. Implementations (success, steps, McNemar, sign, permutation) live in hylo-eval.

docs.title: improvement
docs.text:
The generators plugin contract (hylo.generator) and the records of an improvement campaign.

A generator (Proposer) reads a parent's diagnosis and the campaign's archive and proposes candidates: declarative patches of dotted config paths, each with a hypothesis. The cascade, the gate and the registry that decide what happens to a candidate live in hylo-evolve; these are the shapes a generator plugin sees and returns.

docs.title: safety
docs.text:
SafetyShield: the single, non-bypassable checkpoint between any Agent and any Environment.

  • Built by the kernel from the EnvSpec plus config; Agents never see or construct it.
  • Mandatory guards (finite check, bounds clamp) are always installed; config can only add guards or tighten limits. RSI candidates cannot target the safety.* config scope (evolve/candidate.py).
  • Extra guards are plugins ("guards" group): safety: {guards: [{type: keep_out, params: {...}}]}. They run between the mandatory finite check (first) and bounds clamp (last), so no plugin can let a non-finite or out-of-bounds action through. Built in: delta_limit, workspace, norm_limit, keep_out.
  • Rotation-aware: per-dimension clamping is refused for quaternion / rot6d dims (inspect-robots approver.py makes the same choice).

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text: EpisodeRunner is the one episode loop; evaluation, Studio's live sandbox and the workcell all use it. It runs an environment and an agent through the safety shield, in sync or realtime timing. Events go to an EventBus; a TraceStore writes them to the run's trace. See also the execution lifecycle.

docs.title: kernel
docs.text:
Execution kernel: the one episode loop, used for evaluation, learning rollouts and deployment.

env.reset -> agent.reset -> loop[ request a chunk (when the queue runs low) -> merge it when it arrives
                                  -> SafetyShield.review -> env.step -> agent.on_step ]
          -> episode.end -> agent.on_episode_end

Timing decides how policy time relates to robot time: - "sync" (default): the world waits for every policy call; a chunk is requested when the queue is empty and runs execution_steps actions. Deterministic; what benchmarks have always measured. - "realtime": the robot keeps moving while the policy thinks (LeRobot async inference, openpi's runtime, vla-eval's live runner): a chunk is requested when at most refill_steps actions remain, a chunk computed from the observation of step s that arrives at step t has its first t - s actions dropped (aligned merge), an empty queue executes a hold action, and a watchdog aborts after max_hold_steps consecutive holds. On the "virtual" clock the policy latency is measured (or fixed by latency_s) and the steps it would have taken run before the chunk is merged: deterministic, so benchmarks can measure deployment behaviour. On the "wall" clock the policy runs in a worker thread and the loop ticks at the control rate: the workcell next to a robot.

Both modes share the SafetyShield, the trace events, error classification and the operator channel (stop, latched e-stop, reset confirmation, outcome verdicts), so what the gate approved in simulation is what the robot runs.

This is "driven mode". In "served mode" (an external harness owns the loop) the same Agent + SafetyShield + trace are wrapped by a protocol adapter; see docs/execution-lifecycle.md.

Every observable thing in an episode is an Event. The Trace is the persisted event stream, so tracing, live dashboards and online critics all subscribe to the same bus.

docs.text:
EventBus()

Fan-out with failure isolation: a failing non-critical subscriber is detached, not fatal. Critical subscribers (the trace writer) propagate their exceptions.

docs.title: trace
docs.text:
Event-sourced, replayable episode trace.

Layout of a run directory

/manifest.json RunManifest (config hash, versions, seeds) /episodes/.jsonl one Event per line, arrays inline when small /blobs/.npy large arrays (images, point clouds), content-addressed /evallog.json aggregated scores; points back at episode files /seal.json optional: the run's file inventory, written by hylo seal

Hash chain (hylo.trace/v0.2): every event line carries prev (the previous line's hash, "" for the first) and h, the sha256 of the line's canonical JSON without h. Blobs are named by their own digest, so the chain covers them too. hylo.core.seal.verify_chain finds the first line that was changed, removed or reordered. Lines written before the chain existed have neither key and are reported as unchained, not as broken.

Scorers and shadow replay read only this; they never call the Agent or the Environment.

docs.title: memory_steer
docs.text:
Action-memory steering for a frozen flow VLA (RFC-0003 M1; mechanism after Retrieve-then-Steer, arXiv 2605.10094).

At every decision the sampler computes a retrieval key inside its own forward pass and calls back here: 1. retrieve the top-K verified segments by cosine similarity (same task by default) above a similarity floor; 2. drop candidates whose chunk is inconsistent with the others (median pairwise DTW over the executed prefix); 3. aggregate the rest into an elite prior with softmax-over-similarity weights (weighted mean for motion, weighted vote for the gripper, nearest neighbour when the vote is split); 4. map retrieval confidence (similarity, agreement) to a flow start time t0: confident -> small t0 -> strong guidance; nothing usable -> t0 = 1, i.e. the unchanged policy. The sampler then integrates the policy's own velocity field from x_t0 = (1 - t0) prior + t0 noise, so the current observation still decides the action: memory biases the sample, it never replays it.

docs.title: noise_steer
docs.text:
Noise-space steering (RFC-0004 W3): an offline, retrieval-based counterpart of DSRL for a frozen flow VLA.

DSRL learns a policy over the flow policy's initial noise and leaves the VLA untouched. Offline, from our own successes: every successful chunk was produced from a known seed, so its exact initial noise is recoverable. The bank (memory_build --store noise) keys those noises by the policy's own visual tokens. At decision time the agent retrieves the nearest same-task noises, averages them (similarity-weighted), rescales the mean to unit variance and hands it to the sampler, which starts the full flow from sqrt(w) * prior noise + sqrt(1 - w) * fresh noise. With w = 0 this is exactly the policy; nothing is retrieved below sim_floor.

Unlike an action prior, the chunk is still produced by the policy's velocity field for the current observation: the noise only biases which mode the flow lands in.

agent: {type: remote, params: {ref: hylo.policies.lerobot.experience_agent:make_noise_agent, params: {
    repo_id: lerobot/smolvla_libero, memory: {type: action_bank, params: {path: "artifact:l10-noise-search-v1@2687768f", frozen: true}},
    noise_steer: {weight: 0.5, k: 5, sim_floor: 0.95}, steering: {n_samples: 1, seed_noise: true}}}}

docs.title: policy_agents
docs.text:
Agents that run a policy (core.policy.ChunkPolicy) given by configuration.

  • "policy": draw one chunk per decision (seeded noise, so episodes replay and paired comparisons share noise) and execute its first execution_steps actions open loop. The plain way to run any policy plugin.

  • "temporal_ensemble": ACT's inference (Zhao et al. 2023): query the policy every step and execute, for the current step, the exponentially weighted average of every chunk predicted so far that covers it, w_i = exp(-m * i) with i = 0 the oldest prediction. Smoother motion at the price of one query per step.

    agent: {type: policy, params: {policy: {type: policy.bc, params: {path: artifacts/bc}}, execution_steps: 8}} agent: {type: temporal_ensemble, params: {policy: {type: policy.bc, params: {path: artifacts/bc}}, m: 0.1}}

docs.title: shadow
docs.text:
Shadow mode (RFC-0004 W4; roadmap v0.3): evaluate a candidate on real hardware without letting it act.

ShadowAgent executes the active agent and hands the same observation to a shadow (the candidate), whose chunk is never executed. Each decision emits an x.shadow event: how far the shadow's executed prefix would have been from what the robot actually did (mean / max absolute difference over arm dims, gripper agreement), and the shadow's latency. The shadow also receives the real step results, so it follows the episode the active agent produces.

With background=True the shadow runs in a worker thread and its result is emitted at the next decision, so the control loop never waits for it (on a robot the shadow must not add latency). The shadow's own events are prefixed x.shadow. so nothing it emits is mistaken for the active agent's.

docs.title: skills
docs.text:
SkillAgent (RFC-0003 M3): apply verified skills from a SkillLibrary to the agent it wraps, per episode.

At reset the library is matched against the task (instruction pattern, task tags, env). The best verified skill of each kind is applied for this episode only and undone at its end: - steering: a partial SteeringConfig merged into the nearest SteeredAgent in the wrapped chain; - recovery: trigger rules appended to that SteeredAgent's rules (the steering cap of 4 rules still holds); - plan: subgoal templates, filled with the trigger's slot bindings, given to the nearest SubgoalAgent. Weights skills are not swapped per episode (a policy reload); they are applied as config by the improvement loop. Each application is a skill.applied trace event, so outcomes can be attributed to the skill.

docs.title: steering
docs.text:
Steering a frozen stochastic policy (flow-matching / diffusion VLAs) without touching its weights.

SteeredAgent wraps any ChunkSampler (core.policy.ChunkPolicy: a "policies" plugin, given as a spec or an object) that can draw action chunks for given noise seeds: - seeded noise: chunk noise is derived from (task key, chunk index, sample index, resample round), so a candidate and its parent face the same randomness on the same init state (common random numbers for paired tests) and every episode is replayable; - sample-and-select: draw N chunks and execute their medoid ("medoid"), or keep the gripper-majority ones first ("gripper_vote_medoid", RoboMonkey-style vote); no extra work when N = 1; - runtime triggers: declarative rules over cheap features (still steps, grasp attempts, sample disagreement) that fire recovery actions (resample with more noise, or back off and reopen the gripper). Everything tunable is data (SteeringConfig), so the improvement loop can propose and gate it as config patches.

docs.text:
Benchmarking: run a policy under a fixed protocol and get a scorecard (core.scorecard) for a leaderboard.

The evaluation engine is hylo-eval; this package fixes what is measured (protocols), records it (scorecards) and ranks and compares results (leaderboards, paired comparison).

docs.title: protocol
docs.text:
Benchmark protocols (hylo.protocol/v0.1): everything about an evaluation except the policy.

A protocol fixes the benchmark and split (which tasks and init states), the environment, the safety limits, the trace options, the timing and the seed. The policy is the only free input, so two scorecards of the same protocol digest are comparable, episode by episode. timing decides whether the world waits for the policy (sync) or keeps moving while it thinks (realtime: what a workcell runs). Where the simulator runs (env.remote) is not measured.

Protocols ship with this package (protocols/*.yaml, by name) or are given as a YAML path. Changing anything measured is a new version; workers and description are not measured and do not change the digest.

import numpy as np

from hylo.core.safety import GuardVerdict, SafetyContext


class {cls}Guard:
    name = "{name}"

    def __init__(self, max_abs: float = 0.5) -> None:
        self.max_abs = float(max_abs)

from __future__ import annotations

from hylo.core.scoring import PairedComparison
from hylo.eval.scoring import one_sided_exact_mcnemar


class {cls}Test:
    name = "{name}"

    def __init__(self, metric: str = "success", direction: str = "higher") -> None:
        self.metric, self.sign = metric, 1.0 if direction == "higher" else -1.0

    def compare(self, candidate, parent) -> PairedComparison:
        keys = [k for k in candidate if k in parent and candidate[k] is not None and parent[k] is not None]
        d = [self.sign * (float(candidate[k]) - float(parent[k])) for k in keys]
        wins, losses = sum(x > 0 for x in d), sum(x < 0 for x in d)
        return PairedComparison(n_pairs=len(keys), candidate_wins=wins, parent_wins=losses,
                                p_value=one_sided_exact_mcnemar(wins, losses))

'), 'online_learner': ('learners', '{cls}Online', '"""Online learner plugin: propose agent specs, see their rollouts on a development split, update; then seal."""

from __future__ import annotations

import copy
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from hylo.core.artifact import ArtifactManifest, Provenance, write_manifest


class {cls}Online:
    name = "{name}@0.1"

    def start(self, job, agent) -> None:
        self.job, self.base = job, agent
        self.path = job.params.get("path", "params.kp")                # the agent parameter to search
        self.low, self.high = job.params.get("low", 0.1), job.params.get("high", 4.0)
        self.rng, self.best, self.tried = np.random.default_rng(0), None, []

    def _spec(self, v: float):
        spec = copy.deepcopy(self.base)
        node = spec
        *parents, leaf = self.path.split(".")
        for k in parents:
            node = node.setdefault(k, {{}})
        node[leaf] = float(v)
        return spec

    def policies(self):
        self.tried = list(self.rng.uniform(self.low, self.high, 3))  # random search; your method here
        return [self._spec(v) for v in self.tried]

    def update(self, results):
        for v, r in zip(self.tried, results):
            score = float(r["metrics"]["success_mean"])
            if self.best is None or score > self.best[0]:
                self.best = (score, v)
        return {{"best_score": self.best[0], "best": self.best[1]}}

    def finished(self) -> bool:
        return False

    def seal(self, out, sources) -> ArtifactManifest:
        Path(out).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        (Path(out) / "best.json").write_text(json.dumps({{"value": self.best[1], "score": self.best[0]}}))
        return write_manifest(out, kind="policy_params", role="behaviour", metrics={{"best": self.best[1], "score": self.best[0]}},
                              provenance=Provenance(builder=self.name, sources=sources,
                                                    params={{k: v for k, v in self.job.params.items() if k != "experiment"}}))

'), 'policy': ('policies', '{cls}Policy', '"""Policy plugin (core.policy.ChunkPolicy): draws action chunks, one per noise seed.

Run it:      agent: {{type: policy, params: {{policy: {{type: {name}}}}}}}
Steer it:    agent: {{type: steered, params: {{sampler: {{type: {name}}}, steering: {{n_samples: 4, selector: medoid}}}}}}
ACT-style:   agent: {{type: temporal_ensemble, params: {{policy: {{type: {name}}}, m: 0.1}}}}
Draw all randomness from the seeds, so episodes replay and paired comparisons share noise. A learned policy loads
its weights in __init__ (e.g. from an artifact path) and declares weights_license in its spec.

As generated it drives MuJoCo planar reach (hylo-bench) with analytic two-link IK. For your robot, change
required_state, action_semantics / action_dim and sample(), and check it with
`hylo plugin check policy {name} --experiment your_experiment.yaml`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np

from hylo.core.agent import AgentSpec, EpisodeContext
from hylo.core.types import ActionSemantics, Observation


class {cls}Policy:
    def __init__(self, gain: float = 0.3, horizon: int = 8, noise: float = 0.05, l1: float = 0.3, l2: float = 0.25,
                 max_step: float = 0.05) -> None:
        self.gain, self.horizon, self.noise, self.l1, self.l2, self.max_step = gain, horizon, noise, l1, l2, max_step

    def spec(self) -> AgentSpec:
        # what it reads and what its actions mean: checked against the environment before the first step
        return AgentSpec(name="{name}", version="0.1", required_state=("qpos", "target_pos"),
                         action_semantics=ActionSemantics(control_mode="joint_delta", frame="base"), action_dim=2,
                         components={{"policy": "{name}@0.1"}})

    def reset(self, ctx: EpisodeContext) -> None:
        pass

    def default_execution_steps(self) -> int:
        return max(1, self.horizon // 2)

    def _ik(self, x: float, y: float) -> np.ndarray:
        c2 = np.clip((x * x + y * y - self.l1 ** 2 - self.l2 ** 2) / (2 * self.l1 * self.l2), -1.0, 1.0)
        q2 = np.arccos(c2)
        return np.array([np.arctan2(y, x) - np.arctan2(self.l2 * np.sin(q2), self.l1 + self.l2 * np.cos(q2)), q2])

    def sample(self, observation: Observation, seeds: list[int] | None, noise_scale: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray:
        s = observation.state
        err = (self._ik(*np.asarray(s["target_pos"], float)[:2]) - np.asarray(s["qpos"], float) + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi
        a = np.clip(self.gain * err / self.max_step, -1.0, 1.0)
        rngs = [np.random.default_rng(x) for x in seeds] if seeds else [np.random.default_rng()]
        return np.stack([np.clip(a + self.noise * noise_scale * r.standard_normal((self.horizon, 2)), -1.0, 1.0)
                         for r in rngs])                                    # (N, T, A)

Write an agent when the decision logic is more than drawing chunks from one model (planning, memory, switching
between policies, a remote service); otherwise write a policy plugin and run it with the "policy" agent.

"""

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np

from hylo.core.agent import AgentBase, AgentSpec, EpisodeContext
from hylo.core.types import ActionChunk, ActionSemantics, Observation


class {cls}Agent(AgentBase):
    def __init__(self, gain: float = 0.3, horizon: int = 4, l1: float = 0.3, l2: float = 0.25, max_step: float = 0.05) -> None:
        self.gain, self.horizon, self.l1, self.l2, self.max_step = gain, horizon, l1, l2, max_step

    def spec(self) -> AgentSpec:
        return AgentSpec(name="{name}", version="0.1", required_state=("qpos", "target_pos"),
                         action_semantics=ActionSemantics(control_mode="joint_delta", frame="base"), action_dim=2,
                         components={{"policy": "{name}@0.1"}})

    def reset(self, ctx: EpisodeContext) -> None:
        self.ctx = ctx                                  # ctx.emit(type, payload) writes into the trace

    def act(self, observation: Observation) -> ActionChunk:
        s = observation.state
        x, y = np.asarray(s["target_pos"], float)[:2]
        c2 = np.clip((x * x + y * y - self.l1 ** 2 - self.l2 ** 2) / (2 * self.l1 * self.l2), -1.0, 1.0)
        q2 = np.arccos(c2)
        q = np.array([np.arctan2(y, x) - np.arctan2(self.l2 * np.sin(q2), self.l1 + self.l2 * np.cos(q2)), q2])
        err = (q - np.asarray(s["qpos"], float) + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi
        a = np.clip(self.gain * err / self.max_step, -1.0, 1.0)
        return ActionChunk(actions=np.repeat(a[None], self.horizon, axis=0), execution_steps=self.horizon,
                           provenance={{"model": "{name}"}})

docs.title: agents
docs.text:
Code-writing agents (RFC-0006 parts 4 and 5).

code.llm: a chat model writes one Python block per turn against the toolkit (robot), in a persistent restricted namespace; it sees what the block printed, errors, the robot's status and images it asked for, never the task's score. It ends the episode with finish() or when a budget runs out.

agent: {type: code.llm, params: {model: {backend: ollama, model: qwen3.5:35b-a3b, vision: true},
        max_turns: 30, max_cost_usd: 1.0, block_timeout_s: 60,
        skills: {type: skill_library, params: {path: runs/skills/manip, frozen: true}}}}

code.program: runs a frozen solve(robot) (from a sealed program artifact, or source in params for experiments) with the same toolkit and no model: free to run and reproducible.

agent: {type: code.program, params: {artifact: artifact:pick-place-sub2@1a2b3c4d}}

Both drive the robot through EpisodeBridge, so every motion is an ActionChunk the kernel executes step by step through the SafetyShield. tools names the toolkit factory (default hylo.manip.tools:Tools; tests use hylo.codeagents.fakes:FakeTools); it is called as factory(robot_spec, executor, control_hz=..., show=..., **params).

docs.title: bridge
docs.text:
The toolkit's Executor on top of the kernel (RFC-0006 part 4): a program moves the robot only through the kernel.

Two threads meet here. The kernel thread calls the agent (act, on_step, on_episode_end); the program thread (a model's turns, or a frozen solve(robot)) calls the Executor (observation, run, status) and finish:

program: robot.run(plan) -> bridge.run(actions) ---- posts a chunk, blocks ------------------+
kernel:  act(obs) blocks until a chunk is posted, returns it -> SafetyShield -> env.step x T |
         act(obs) again (the queue is empty): the chunk is done -> wakes the program <-------+
program: finish() -> a chunk marked END_EPISODE -> the kernel ends the episode ("agent_done")

While the program computes (or the model thinks) the kernel is blocked in act(): simulation time does not pass, and a robot runner holds. A chunk cut short (the shield modified an action and the kernel dropped the rest) wakes the program with interrupted: true. When the episode ends for any reason (task terminated, max_steps, an error, the operator), on_episode_end wakes the program: every later run() returns at once with ended: true. Needs the kernel's sync timing (realtime mode asks for chunks before the last one finished).

docs.title: fakes
docs.text:
Test doubles for code agents: a toy manipulation environment and a toolkit with the hylo.manip Tools signatures.

Not an evaluation environment (the real ones are hylo-bench's mujoco/manip-v0). The toy robot is Cartesian: its three "joints" are the TCP position, so a plan is a straight line and no kinematics are needed; the hand is a parallel gripper that stops half closed on a block (so holding works as on a real hand). Blocks and a bin lie on a table at z = 0; the task is "put the block in the bin". The toy observation carries object positions in extra["objects"] (perception for the fake toolkit), so programs written against the toolkit verbs run unchanged.

env:       {type: "hylo.codeagents.fakes:ToyManipEnv"}
benchmark: {type: "hylo.codeagents.fakes:toy_benchmark", params: {protocol: rsi}}
tools:     {type: "hylo.codeagents.fakes:FakeTools"}          (code.llm / code.program params)

docs.title: TOY_SOLUTION module-attribute
docs.text:
TOY_SOLUTION = '
def solve(robot):
    status = robot.status()
    words = status["instruction"].split()
    colour = words[words.index("block") - 1]
    view = robot.look()
    table = robot.table(view)
    block = robot.objects(view, robot.find(view, [colour + " block"]), table)[0]
    target = robot.objects(view, robot.find(view, ["bin"]), table)[0]
    grasp = robot.plan(robot.grasps("arm", block.points, table), table=table)
    robot.run(grasp)
    xy = target.points.mean(axis=0)[:2]
    robot.run(robot.plan(robot.place_at("arm", np.eye(4), block.points, xy, table=table), table=table))
    home = robot.Goal("home", "arm", joints=np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.3]))
    robot.run(robot.plan(home, table=table))
    print("placed", colour, "at", np.round(xy, 3))
'.strip('
')

docs.title: harness_evolution
docs.text:
Optional phase-guided program evolution, independently implemented from a design study.

Plan observable phases -> develop and repair solve(robot) -> seal evidence-linked repair notes -> return a code candidate to Hylo's existing gate. No upstream HarnessPAI code is included, no weight training is performed, and development success never activates code.

docs.title: PLAN module-attribute
docs.text:
PLAN = 'Plan observable phases for a robot control program. Return JSON only:
{"phases": [{"name": "...", "goal": "...", "completion": "...", "fallback": "...", "step_budget": 100}]}.
Use 1-12 phases. Completion checks must use deployment observations or public tool results,
never hidden simulator state, task IDs or evaluator success. Propose bounded handovers and
fallbacks. Use a frozen action-model tool only if the supplied toolkit actually provides
one; otherwise use its available control tools. Retrieved repairs are hypotheses with
limited provenance, not universal instructions. Do not infer phase competence from a
whole-task score. This is a plan for code generation, not an executable state machine.'

docs.title: DISTILL module-attribute
docs.text:
DISTILL = 'Summarize reusable repairs from the supplied development submissions and the
selected program. Return JSON only: {"repairs": [{"phase": "a supplied phase name",
"trigger": "observable failure pattern", "repair": "what changed and why it may help",
"limitation": "where it may not apply", "failure_refs": ["submission-1/case-0"],
"success_refs": ["submission-2/case-0"]}]}.
Use at most 8 notes, or an empty list when no repair is supported. Each note must cite a
failed case and a successful replay of that same case in the selected program. Cite only
provided evidence IDs. Do not claim cross-task transfer or independent phase validation.
Do not include executable code or hard-coded simulator coordinates in the repair text.'

docs.title: codeagents
docs.text:
Tool-using, code-writing agents (RFC-0006 parts 4-6).

  • sandbox: AST allow-list validation and a restricted, persistent namespace for model-written Python
  • bridge: the toolkit's Executor on top of the kernel (robot.run -> one ActionChunk through the SafetyShield)
  • agents: code.llm (a chat model writes one block per turn) and code.program (a frozen solve(robot), no model)
  • research: research sessions on development cases, frozen into program candidates (hylo research)
  • generator: research.llm, a research session as an improvement-campaign generator
  • skills: promoted programs as skills of the skill library
  • scene_check, scenes: the scene builder (hylo scene): a model writes a hylo.scene/v0.1 file, the checker validates it, code.llm solves it with privileged state

docs.title: motion
docs.text:
The motion studio (RFC-0006 part 8): a request (text, an image of a pose, or a reference video) -> a humanoid or robot motion, checked and rendered, by a chat model writing Python against motion tools.

hylo motion "wave with the right hand, then bow" --robot g1 --out runs/motion/wave
hylo motion "do this pose" --image pose.jpg --robot g1 --out DIR [--model SPEC] [--budget turns=12,cost=1]
hylo motion "copy the person" --video clip.mp4 --robot human --out DIR [--side-by-side] [--style mujoco]
hylo motion "jump and wave" --characters all --out DIR          the final motion on every character, one video
hylo motion --free "a looping dance from the clip" --video clip.mp4 --out DIR    (free mode: motion_free)

One agent loop (the code-agents sandbox and CodeLoop): each turn the model writes one Python block; the tools in its namespace are text_motion (NVIDIA Kimodo), video_motion and pose_from_image (the human tool), the motion edits of motion_ops, retarget (any character of motion_characters: humanoid robots from MuJoCo Menagerie, Hylo's capsule figure, rigged human characters driven in Blender), check (plausibility and a physics rollout), render (Blender Cycles on the CPU, MuJoCo fallback), lineup (one render per character, composed into a labelled grid) and look; finish(motion) ends it. Slow tool calls do not count against the block time limit. The run directory gets log.jsonl (turns and tool calls), motion.npz, check.json, motion.mp4 (+ split.mp4 with --side-by-side) and summary.json (turns, cost, wall time, time per tool). With --characters the final motion is also retargeted to, checked on and rendered with each of those characters: characters.json and lineup.mp4 (with --video and --side-by-side, split.mp4 puts the source clip next to each character) instead of motion.mp4.

This module is the agent loop and the CLI; the tools, their backend and the final report are in motion_tools, the characters in motion_characters (mapping files) and the retargeting in motion_retarget / motion_sim / motion_blender. Tests pass a fake backend. SPEC is a chat-model spec (JSON or shorthand, hylo.reasoners.llm.chat); default Ollama qwen3.5:35b-a3b with vision.

docs.title: SYSTEM module-attribute
docs.text:
SYSTEM = 'You are a motion director. You turn a request into a humanoid motion for a robot by writing Python that
calls motion tools, then check it and render it.

Tools (already in your namespace; motions are objects, print them to see a summary):
- text_motion(prompt, seconds=4.0, seed=0) -> Motion. A text-to-motion model (NVIDIA Kimodo, ~1 min per call).
  Describe one person's movement plainly ("a person waves with the right hand"). For a sequence, pass a list of
  prompts and a list of seconds (one per segment): it makes one continuous motion.
- video_motion(path="video", start=0.0, seconds=None) -> Motion from the reference video (pose estimation).
- pose_from_image(path="image") -> a one-frame Motion: the pose of the person in the image.
- Edits (return new motions): concat(m1, m2, ..., blend=0.3), blend(a, b, seconds=0.5), loop(m, times=2),
  mirror(m) (left <-> right), retime(m, speed=None, seconds=None), trim(m, start=0.0, end=None),
  hold(pose, seconds=1.0) (stand still in the last frame of pose), keyframe(m, pose, at, width=0.8) (make m pass
  through pose at time `at` seconds), motion_from_array(joints, fps) (your own (T, 17, 3) keypoints, names NAMES).
- A Motion has .seconds, .frames, .fps, .joints (T, 17, 3 metres, z up, ground z = 0, facing +x at the start),
  .summary() (path length, turn, pelvis and hand heights), .pose(t), .joint(name).
- retarget(m, robot=None) -> RobotMotion for a character (CHARACTERS lists them: robots g1, h1, t1, apollo, n1,
  "human" (a capsule figure) and rigged human characters); the run's robot by default.
- check(m) -> {"problems": [...], "kinematics": {...}}. problems lists real defects (floor penetration,
  sliding feet, self-collision, joint limits, poor retargeting); kinematics has the metrics
  (com_outside_support_frac is static balance and is high for any dynamic motion: not a defect). The studio
  adds a physics rollout to the final report; you do not need it. Never change or drop part of the request to
  make the motion calmer or more stable.
- render(m, camera="track", style=None) -> path of an MP4 (minutes; optional). A still frame is shown to you
  if you can see images.
- lineup(m, characters=None) -> path of an MP4 with the motion on several characters side by side (minutes).
- look(path, n=4) shows you n frames of a video in your next feedback.
- finish(m, note="") -> the final motion. The studio then checks and renders it (you do not have to).

How to work:
- Reply with a short thought, then exactly ONE fenced block ```python ... ```. It runs at once; you see what it
  printed and any error, then you write the next block. Variables persist between blocks.
- Only math and numpy can be imported; no files, no classes, no names starting with an underscore.
- print() what you need to see. Look at the summary: does the motion do what was asked (duration, path length,
  turn angle, hand heights)? If not, try a clearer prompt, another seed, or edit it.
- Be economical: on this busy CPU every text_motion call takes 5-20 minutes and a render a few minutes. A good
  plan uses 2-3 blocks: generate (and edit), check, finish.
Ending: call finish(motion) as soon as the motion does everything the request asks.'

docs.title: motion_characters
docs.text:
Target characters of the motion studio: humanoid robots (MJCF) and rigged human characters (Blender), each described by a short mapping file in motion_characters/.json.

A mapping names, for every role of the studio's skeleton (pelvis, chest, head and, per side, hip, knee, ankle, toe, shoulder, elbow, wrist), where that point is on the character:

  • kind "mjcf" (a robot or a simulated humanoid): bodies maps a role to a body, or to [body, [x, y, z]] (an offset in the body frame, e.g. the toe in front of the ankle); feet are the two foot bodies (contact, sole flat); clearance keeps hands and elbows that far from the body's midline (metres); the asset is a MuJoCo Menagerie folder at a pinned commit (menagerie: a manifest beside this module with a digest per file) or a builtin model.
  • kind "rig" (a skinned character, driven in Blender): joints maps a role to a bone end ("Bone.head" or "Bone.tail"); drive says which bones move: pelvis (placed and turned with the hips), spine (bones that share the turn from the hips to the chest), neck, and per side upper_arm, forearm, thigh, shin, foot (turned so the segment between their joints points like the source's); attach pins a bone's head to another bone's end (an IK foot of the original rig); colours overrides material base colours (sRGB, by material name). height_m scales the character to that height. The asset is an archive fetched from its original page (archive: url, sha256, members to extract).

Every mapping records licence and credit. Robots are fetched from MuJoCo Menagerie and characters from their authors' uploads, verified by digest, into the asset cache; nothing is vendored.

docs.title: motion_free
docs.text:
Free mode of the motion studio: the model composes its own pipeline as scripts in its run directory.

hylo motion --free "REQUEST" --out DIR [--video V] [--image I] [--model SPEC] [--budget turns=12]
            [--max-tool-calls 40] [--script-timeout-s 900] [--max-wall-s S]

Each turn the model writes one Python script; motion_scripts checks it, saves it as scripts/turnNN.py and runs it in a guarded process in the run directory (motion_freerun). Scripts import the kit (from studio import *, motion_freekit) and may do their own processing with numpy and scipy, writing any files inside the run directory. Every tool call is a request answered here by FreeTools (an allowed tool, every path inside the run directory, the tool-call budget), run with the studio's tools (motion_tools.StudioTools) and logged in log.jsonl with every script. finish(motion, characters) ends the session; the studio then reports each character (retargeting error, joint-limit hits, plausibility) and renders the lineup (motion_tools.finalize). Inputs are copied into inputs/.

docs.title: SYSTEM module-attribute
docs.text:
SYSTEM = 'You are a motion director with a studio of tools. You turn a request into a humanoid motion shown on
robots and human characters, by writing Python scripts. You decide the pipeline: which tools, which processing,
which characters.

Each turn: a short thought, then exactly ONE fenced ```python``` block. The studio saves it as scripts/turnNN.py
and runs it as a separate process in your run directory (the current directory). You see what it printed, any
error, and images you asked to look at. Scripts do not share variables: save what you need to files (save_motion,
np.save, json) and load it in the next script.

Start every script with `from studio import *`. The studio kit:
- Sources (each returns a Motion): text_motion(prompt, seconds=4.0, seed=0) (NVIDIA Kimodo; a list of prompts
  and a list of seconds makes one continuous motion; several minutes per call), video_motion(path, start=0.0,
  seconds=None) (pose estimation from a video of one person), pose_from_image(path) (a one-frame Motion).
- Other tools: hands(video), depth(image), segment(image, prompts), human(video) -> {"outputs", "files"}.
- Motion: .joints (T, 17, 3) metres, z up, ground z = 0, facing +x at the start; .fps; .frames; .seconds;
  .summary(); .joint(name); .pose(t). NAMES lists the 17 keypoints. motion_from_array(joints, fps) wraps your
  own array. save_motion(m, path=None) -> path, load_motion(path).
- Edits (return new motions): concat(m1, m2, ..., blend=0.3), blend(a, b, seconds=0.5), loop(m, times=2),
  mirror(m), retime(m, speed=None, seconds=None), trim(m, start, end), hold(pose, seconds), keyframe(m, pose, at,
  width=0.8). You can also write your own processing with numpy and scipy (filters, blending, stylising, looping)
  on m.joints; keep bone lengths plausible and the feet on the ground (z >= 0).
- characters() lists the characters; retarget(m, character) -> metrics (keypoint error, limb angle error,
  joint-limit hits); check(m, character) -> {"problems", "kinematics"}.
- render(m, character, camera="track") -> MP4 path (Blender, minutes); lineup(m, characters) -> one MP4 with
  the motion on several characters side by side (minutes per character). look(path, n=4) shows you frames of a
  video or an image in your next feedback: look at your renders and fix what is wrong.
- finish(m, characters=[...], note="") ends the session; the studio then checks the motion on each of those
  characters and renders them together. A ToolError means a request was refused or failed.

Rules: work only inside the run directory (relative paths; inputs are in inputs/). Imports allowed: numpy, scipy,
math, json, statistics, itertools, functools, collections, random, re, copy, pathlib, studio, and your own
modules in lib/ (write them with open("lib/name.py", "w")). No processes, network or eval. Each script has a
time limit (tool time excluded) and the session a tool-call budget. print() what you need to know.
Be economical: plan in few scripts, generate once, process, check on the characters, render once and look, then
finish. Never drop part of the request to make the motion easier.'

docs.title: motion_ops
docs.text:
Motion data and edits for the motion studio (pure numpy): one keypoint skeleton, converters from the motion tools and edits on joint trajectories.

Skeleton: 17 keypoints (NAMES, SOMA joint names), metres, z up, ground z = 0. canonical puts a motion on the ground, at the origin, facing +x at its first frame, so edits can align clips by root position and heading. Edits (concat, blend, loop, mirror, retime, trim, hold, keyframe) work on positions: clips are aligned (the next clip starts where and facing where the last one ended) and cross-faded over a short window.

docs.title: EDITS module-attribute

keyframe(m: Motion, pose: Motion, at: float, width: float = 0.8, root: bool = False) -> Motion

docs.title: motion_retarget
docs.text:
Retargeting math shared by every target character (pure numpy, no Hylo imports): the MuJoCo worker (motion_sim) uses it for robots, the Blender script (motion_blender) for rigged characters; both load this file by path, Hylo code imports it as hylo.codeagents.motion_retarget.

Skeleton points are arrays (..., K, 3) indexed by idx (keypoint name -> column), metres, z up, facing +x.

  • body_frames: the pelvis and chest frames of a skeleton (forward, left, up columns).
  • proportional_targets: source keypoints -> target points with a character's proportions: the root path scaled by the leg-length ratio, each limb segment along the source's direction with the character's own length, hips and shoulders placed as on the character, turned with the source's pelvis and chest.
  • lock_feet / smooth: clean-ups of the source before the fit (no sliding while a foot is down; video noise).
  • segment_angles: limb direction error between two skeletons (a scale-free retargeting error).
  • ground_correction: a per-frame height offset that keeps the lowest foot point on the floor while the source's feet are down, and never below it.

docs.text: TREE = [('LeftLeg', 'Hips', 'pelvis'), ('RightLeg', 'Hips', 'pelvis'), ('Chest', 'Hips', 'dir'), ('Head', 'Chest', 'chest'), ('LeftArm', 'Chest', 'chest'), ('RightArm', 'Chest', 'chest'), *[(c, p, 'dir') for p, c in LIMBS]]

Pelvis and chest frames (..., 3, 3) of points P (..., K, 3); columns forward, left, up. Pelvis: left = right -> left hip, up = hips -> chest; chest: left = right -> left shoulder, up = chest -> mid-shoulders.

docs.title: lock_feet

While a foot keypoint stays near the ground (within tol of its low height), hold its horizontal position at the run's mean, eased over 3 frames at each end: removes the source's foot sliding.

docs.title: ground_correction
docs.text:

(T,) height offsets: the lowest foot point (low) on the floor whenever the source's feet (src_feet, at target scale) are near the ground, interpolated in between (jumps keep their flight), never below the floor.

docs.title: motion_scripts
docs.text:
Model-written scripts run in a directory, under a guard, with tool calls served over a pipe (free mode of the motion studio; nothing here is specific to motion).

  • check_source: the static check before anything runs: imports from an allow-list or the run directory's lib/ (checked too), no eval / exec / getattr, no dunder or private attributes, no async code.
  • ScriptRunner.run(code): saves the script as scripts/turnNN.py and runs it with motion_freerun.py (python -I, cwd = the run directory, resource limits, an audit hook refusing files outside the directory, processes, sockets and ctypes). The script talks to handler(op, args) in this process through two pipes (one JSON line per request and per answer); PermissionError from the handler is reported as a refusal. The time limit excludes the time spent in handler calls. Returns the code-agents BlockResult, so a CodeLoop can drive it.
  • inside: resolve a path given by a script, refusing anything outside the run directory.

docs.title: motion_tools
docs.text:
The motion studio's tool layer (RFC-0006 part 8), shared by the guided studio (motion.py) and free mode (motion_free.py): the model-facing tools, the backend that runs them, and the final report of a run.

  • RobotMotion: a motion retargeted to one character (robot qpos, or a rigged character's posed keypoints).
  • ToolBackend: the real tools, each in its own environment: hylo-tools workers (text_motion kept loaded, human, render and the perception tools), the MuJoCo worker (motion_sim: retarget, check, validate) and the media worker (motion_media: clip, compose, rig). Tests pass a fake with the same methods.
  • StudioTools: what the model calls: text_motion, video_motion, pose_from_image, retarget (any character of motion_characters), check, render (robots through the hylo-tools render tool, rigged characters through Blender), lineup (the same motion on several characters, one labelled video grid), look (frames of a video for the model), finish. Every call is logged and timed; slow calls pause the sandbox's block clock.
  • finalize: the final motion -> motion.npz, check.json, a report per character (characters.json) and the videos.

docs.title: preflight
docs.text:
hylo preflight: check, before a tool-agent run, everything that can be checked without running it.

hylo preflight CONFIG [--out DIR] [--no-model] [--no-env]
hylo preflight --model ollama:qwen3.5:35b-a3b [--vision]

Each check prints PASS / FAIL / SKIP with what it found; the exit code is 1 when any check failed, and with --out the results go to DIR/preflight.json (the run directory, so the evidence of a run includes its preflight):

  config        the experiment file loads and its plugins (env, agent, benchmark) are installed
  source        the git commit and whether the working tree has uncommitted changes (a warning, not a failure)
  storage       free space where the run writes (>= 2 GiB) and in the asset cache (>= 1 GiB)
  model         a live probe of the agent's chat model: a text reply, an image (vision models), a tool call with
                valid JSON arguments, and an answer that uses a tool result
  environment   the env builds and publishes a RobotSpec (tool agents need one), and its first reset works

docs.title: prompt
docs.text:
What code-writing models are told: the robot, the toolkit's API, the rules, and the feedback after each block.

Task-agnostic: the robot comes from RobotSpec, the API from the toolkit itself (hylo.manip.api_reference, else the Tools signatures and docstrings), the task from the instruction. No task names, no success signal.

docs.title: RULES module-attribute
docs.text:
RULES = "How to work:
- Reply with a short thought, then exactly ONE fenced block: ```python ... ```. It runs as soon as you send it; you
  see what it printed, any error, and the robot's status, then you write the next block. There are no tools or
  functions to call through the chat: write the code as text in your reply, inside the fence.
- Variables, functions and imports persist between blocks. Preloaded: `robot` (the toolkit), `np` (numpy), `math`.
  The only imports allowed are math and numpy. No files, no network, no class definitions, no names that start
  with an underscore.
- Each block may compute for at most {block_s:g} s; time the robot spends moving is not counted.
- Every turn is one model call, which can be slow: when you are confident, do several steps in one block (perceive,
  plan, run a motion, check it) and print what you need to verify.
- `robot.run(plan)` is the only call that moves the robot: it returns when the motion is done. The simulation is
  paused while you think, so take the time you need.
- print() what you need to see: values you do not print are not shown to you.{vision}"

docs.title: replay
docs.text:
Replay to sim (RFC-0006 part 8): a recorded episode -> tracked objects and hand -> MuJoCo scene -> replay -> checks.

hylo replay SOURCE --out DIR [--profile libero|droid|video] [--camera KEY] [--agent] [--model SPEC]
                   [--labels "red block,plate"] [--step K] [--max-frames N] [--stub] [--no-video]
                   [--hand g1|allegro|<name>]

SOURCE: a saved recording folder, panda:TASK:SEED (records one of our episodes with the privileged oracle, ground truth kept for evaluation), hf:REPO:EPISODE (a LeRobot dataset episode; --camera names the image key), or a video file (a human hand demonstration). See replay_data.py.

Steps (each a method of ReplayPipeline, callable on its own and in this order by run()): labels a vision chat model names the objects in the first frame (fallback: the instruction's noun phrases) segment SAM 3 masks for those labels (best mask per label, duplicates and table-sized masks dropped) lift depth (recorded, or MoGe-2 per frame rescaled to frame 0), the camera in a +z-up frame (recorded pose, or GeoCalib gravity refined by the RANSAC table plane), the table plane hands (human videos) hand keypoints -> metric scale from the hand's size -> parallel-gripper TCP and opening; with --hand also the keypoints in the world retargeted onto a multi-finger robot hand (hylo.manip.retarget: finger joints per frame and the palm pose; the hand's side follows the detected handedness) track object poses through the video (mask propagation + ICP on the per-frame depth) register (robot videos without a camera pose) scale, yaw and offset to the robot frame from the carried object's path and the TCP path; IK of the TCP path on the Panda (base pose fitted when unknown) objects per object: mesh (mesh tool) -> convex parts (convex tool) + a support part down to the table grasps (--hand) each recorded grasp refined with the dexterous grasp planner on the object's convex parts at the grasp moment, the plan nearest the retargeted hand chosen; the palm path is bent onto it (pre-pose, straight approach, then the hand-relative offset kept while carrying), the fingers open before it, close to the plan's squeeze command and hold until the release scene MJCF with the table, the objects (moving ones free, others fixed), the camera and the Panda, a free-floating gripper or (--hand) a free-floating multi-finger hand replay kinematic replay (recorded motion written into qpos) and physics replay (joint targets / TCP path, hand closed between grasp and release; objects move only by contact) checks pose error per object over time (sim vs tracked, and vs ground truth when known), contact events (grasp, lift, place) matched to the recording, final-state success, mesh size error (ground truth) video side-by-side MP4, recording | simulation, rendered with the render tool

With --agent a chat model drives the same steps from a sandboxed Python session (the code-agents sandbox and turn loop): it sees each step's summary and overlay images, may change labels, masks, tracking mode or thresholds and re-run steps, and calls finish() when the checks are done. Without it the steps run in order with defaults. Writes DIR/report.json, DIR/scene.xml (+ meshes/), DIR/tracks.npz, DIR/replay.mp4 and DIR/overlays/*.png.

docs.title: AGENT_SYSTEM module-attribute
docs.text:
AGENT_SYSTEM = 'You turn a recorded manipulation video into a physics simulation and check it. You work in a
Python session (only math and numpy can be imported) through the object `replay`, whose methods run the workflow's
steps and return short summaries (dicts). Images (masks, tracked models) are attached to your next message.

Steps, normally in this order:
  replay.info()                         the recording: frames, fps, task text, what the source provides
  replay.labels(names=None)             propose object labels from the first frame (or set them: a list of str)
  replay.segment(labels=None, keep=None)  masks for the labels in frame 0; keep=[indices] keeps some of them
  replay.lift()                         depth, camera frame, table plane
  replay.hands()                        human videos only: hand -> gripper (call after lift)
  replay.track(mode="yaw", gate=0.04)   object poses through the video; mode "xyz", "yaw" or "full"
  replay.register()                     camera to robot frame, IK of the robot path (when needed)
  replay.events()                       grasp / lift / release / place from the gripper and object motion
  replay.objects()                      meshes and convex collision parts
  replay.grasps()                       with a multi-finger hand (--hand): plan grasps, bend the hand's motion
  replay.scene()                        the MuJoCo scene
  replay.replay()                       kinematic and physics replay
  replay.checks()                       pose errors, matched contact events, final-state success
  replay.video()                        the side-by-side video
  finish(note)                          end the session with a one-paragraph note on what reproduced

Check each result before moving on: are the masks on the objects the task is about (look at the image)? Did a
tracked object get lost for many frames or jump? Did registration use enough pairs with a small rmse? If a check
fails, change what you control (labels, kept masks, tracking mode or gate) and run the step again; later steps must
then be re-run too. Do not invent results: report what the checks say. Write one ```python block per reply, with a
sentence of reasoning before it. Keep blocks short and print what you need.'
