docs.title: g1_oracle
docs.text:
oracle.g1_table: a privileged scripted agent for mujoco/humanoid-v0 (an upper bound, not a method).

It reads object poses and the goal from extra["privileged"] (env param privileged_obs: true) and moves the G1's arms and fingers with ordinary joint-position actions:

  • pick_place: the hand on the block's side comes down over it with the claw open (thumb behind, fingers in front), closes to the power grasp, carries the block over the plate and opens;
  • two_hands: each hand picks the block on its side and puts it on the plate on its side, both at once (param sequential: true runs them one after the other);
  • press_button: the nearer hand closes and pushes the cap down with the underside of its curled fingers from above (a pointing index finger needs the hand turned fingers-down, which this arm reaches over too little of the table to be reliable).

docs.title: g1_table
docs.text:
The Unitree G1 humanoid standing at a table, working with both arms and three-finger hands: mujoco.g1_table.

The robot is the MuJoCo Menagerie unitree_g1 model with hands (g1_with_hands.xml, BSD-3-Clause, fetched at a pinned commit into the asset cache on first use, see assets.py). Upper-body manipulation only: the pelvis is fixed in place (no floating base, mobile_base false) and the leg and waist joints are made rigid at zero, so the torso, head and shoulders never move; each arm (7 joints) with its hand (7 finger joints) is one ArmSpec with a dexterous HandSpec. Arm bodies compensate gravity, so the position servos track planned motions closely. The table, objects and cameras are ours.

World frame: the floor at z = 0, the robot's pelvis at the origin's vertical (x forward, y to the robot's left), the table top at z = TABLE_TOP in front of it. Hand command: the seven finger joint targets in radians, in HandSpec.joints order (thumb 0-2, index 0-1, middle 0-1); open is the claw ready to grasp from above; presets name a power grasp, a pinch, a pointing index and a flat hand.

Observation: q.left, hand.left, q.right, hand.right (measured finger joints), RGB-D from head (on the torso, looking down at the table) and front (across the table), segmentation and privileged state on request.

docs.text:
Dexterous robot hands from MuJoCo Menagerie, each as a HandSpec plus its model, and the floating-hand robot built from one: the hand on a six-joint base (three slides, then yaw, pitch and roll hinges) that mujoco.dex_table drives like an arm and that the replay-to-sim workflow loads as its hand model.

hand_names()                -> ["allegro_left", "allegro_right", "g1_left", "g1_right"]
resolve("allegro", "left")  -> "allegro_left"
hand_spec("g1_right")       -> HandSpec (finger joints, open / closed commands, presets, TCP)
floating_hand_file(name)    -> Path of the floating-hand MJCF (written once into the asset cache)

Hands (folders fetched and verified by assets.py, never vendored): g1_left / g1_right Unitree G1 three-finger hands (unitree_g1, BSD-3-Clause): thumb (3 joints), index and middle (2 each); the claw commands and TCP of mujoco.g1_table. allegro_left / _right Wonik Robotics Allegro Hand (wonik_allegro, BSD-2-Clause): four fingers of four joints each.

The floating-hand model marks the human wrist's place on the hand with a site wrist on the hand body (used by retargeting); finger servos are renamed <joint>_servo, the base servos dex_<joint>_servo.

docs.title: humanoid_tasks
docs.text:
The mujoco/humanoid-v0 task family on mujoco.g1_table: a humanoid's hands at a table.

Task Success pick_place the named block rests on the named plate, released (one hand, a multi-finger grasp) two_hands each named block on its named plate, both released, within the step limit: each block and its plate lie on one hand's side, and the limit is shorter than two pick-and-place motions one after the other press_button the button of the named colour pressed down (a pointing index finger); pressing another one fails at once

Each task samples positions, yaw, sizes, colours and the instruction from the episode seed. Failures end the episode early: an object falls off the table or a wrong button is pressed.

docs.title: manip_tasks
docs.text:
The mujoco/manip-v0 task family on mujoco.panda_table (RFC-0006 part 3).

Each task samples a layout from the episode seed (positions, yaw, colours, distractors), realises a natural-language instruction and evaluates its success predicate after every control step. Predicates need the objects at rest and released (no contact with the fingers), so a block still in the hand above the plate is not a success.

Task Success pick_place the named object rests on the named plate stack two or three blocks stacked in the named order, the bottom one on the table put_in_bowl the named object inside the named bowl push_to_zone the large box (too wide to grasp) inside the named zone press_by_number buttons pressed in the order the instruction gives (a wrong press fails at once) sort_by_colour every block in the tray of its colour

Episodes end early with failure when an object falls off the table or a button is pressed out of order.

docs.title: multi_oracle
docs.text:
Scripted motion for privileged oracles of robots with several arms (oracle.aloha_table, oracle.g1_table).

An oracle task is a generator of segments: each segment is {arm: (T, joints + hand) rows}; arms left out hold their last command, and the shorter arm of a segment holds its last row until the longer one finishes, so the arms of one segment start together. Feedback (did the grasp hold?) comes from the observation current when the generator is resumed. Motions are damped-least-squares IK on each arm's model (oracle.Kinematics) along straight TCP lines with minimum-jerk timing, capped in joint speed, as in oracle.panda_table.

docs.title: oracle
docs.text:
oracle.panda_table: a privileged scripted agent for mujoco/manip-v0 (an upper bound, not a method).

It reads object poses and the goal from extra["privileged"] (the env must run with privileged_obs: true) and solves each task with damped-least-squares IK on the arm model named by RobotSpec (loaded with MuJoCo) and straight-line TCP motions with minimum-jerk timing. It acts only through ordinary actions (joint targets and hand commands, one chunk per motion segment), so it proves every task is solvable by the robot as simulated.

When an attempt ends without success (a slipped grasp, a box that turned while pushed), the next act plans a new attempt from the current state: only what is still undone (remaining buttons, unsorted blocks, upper levels).

docs.title: packs
docs.text:
Robot packs (hylo.pack/v0.1): every robot a stage can name, with what is known about driving it.

A pack points at an asset manifest (MuJoCo Menagerie folder at a pinned commit, verified by digest, fetched on first use; see assets.py) and its model file, and says how the world controls it:

  family     arm, gripper, hand, bimanual, quadruped, humanoid, drone, mobile_manipulator
  base       fixed (bolted to the world or to the entity it is mounted on) or free (a floating base)
  home       the model's keyframe used as the start posture (none: zero joints)
  drive      position (position servos: a target is a ctrl value) or torque (motors: the world closes a PD loop
             with `gains`) or thrust (drones)
  gripper    {actuator, open, closed}: the ctrl values of an open and a closed hand, when it has one
  tcp        {site} or {body, offset}: the tool point an arm moves (`tcp` actions)
  legs       quadrupeds: per leg the hip, thigh and calf joints, for the trot controller
  base_joints  mobile bases driven through joints (x, y, yaw)
  controls   the actions the world accepts for it (joints, gripper, tcp, walk, fly, base, hold)
  status     usable (checked in the world tests) | partial (some controls only; `notes` says which) | unverified

Readiness is separate from priority: a pack is usable when its listed controls passed the world's checks on this workstation (tests/test_world.py), not because it is a common robot.

docs.title: panda_scene
docs.text:
mujoco.panda_scene: the Panda table of mujoco.panda_table with the objects and the success predicate of a scene file (hylo.scene/v0.1, hylo.core.scene), and the benchmark type mujoco/scenes-v0 that turns a directory of scene files into tasks with seeded RFC-0002 splits.

The robot, the table, the cameras, segmentation, the observation layout, control and RobotSpec are panda_table's (this class reuses PandaTableEnv's robot half and its attach_panda / scene_xml); what differs is the model: one compiled per scene file, its bodies built from the file's objects (primitives, trays, cups, meshes, compound parts, children on slide / hinge joints). Free objects get a free joint; fixtures and the roots of articulated fixtures are mocap bodies, so seeded start poses never need a recompile. Each episode samples the start poses from the seed (regions), rests objects on the table or on their on support, applies joint start values, then settles 0.2 s.

The success predicate is evaluated after every control step (sequence progress is part of the episode state and of snapshots). An episode fails early when a movable object falls off the table. With privileged_obs=True the observation carries extra["privileged"]: every object's pose, extents, world bounding box, container interior and joint state, contacts that penetrate, placement problems and the predicate's terms (for checkers and for agents run with privileged state; env params are part of the experiment digest, so such runs are never ranked with others).

Params: scene (path to a .json / .yaml scene; a task's params["scene"] overrides it), plus PandaTableEnv's cameras, width, height, segmentation, privileged_obs, control_hz, depth, mesh_detail.

docs.title: panda_table
docs.text:
MuJoCo Franka Panda at a table: the manipulation environment of RFC-0006 part 3 (mujoco.panda_table).

The arm and its parallel hand are the MuJoCo Menagerie model (Apache-2.0, fetched at a pinned commit into the asset cache on first use, see assets.py); the table, the objects and the cameras are ours. One model holds a pool of objects (blocks, cylinders, plates, bowls, trays, a large box, zones, numbered buttons); each episode activates the ones its task needs and parks the rest inside the table, so the model never changes shape and snapshots are cheap.

Control: joint-position targets at control_hz (20 Hz; 25 physics steps of 2 ms underneath). Action = 7 joint targets (rad) + 1 hand command in [0, 1] (0 closed, 1 open). Observation layout follows hylo.core.robot: q.arm, hand.arm (measured, command units), RGB-D images per camera, <cam>.seg with segmentation=True, and camera intrinsics and poses in extra["cameras"]. With privileged_obs=True the observation also carries object poses and the task goal in extra["privileged"] (for the oracle agent; a privileged run is never ranked with an unprivileged one because env params are part of the experiment digest).

Rendering needs an OpenGL backend: MUJOCO_GL=egl, or on CPU MUJOCO_GL=osmesa PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=osmesa with LD_LIBRARY_PATH pointing at an OSMesa build (bench/scripts/install-osmesa-user.sh). cameras=[] needs none.

docs.title: policies
docs.text:
Pretrained locomotion policies in the stage world (RFC-0008 part 8): inspected without running them, matched to a robot before use, and executed on the CPU with numpy.

Weights files are never deserialised by a general unpickler and never executed:

  sniff(path)           the format from its bytes: onnx (protobuf), safetensors (length-prefixed JSON header),
                        torchscript (a zip with code/), torch-checkpoint (a zip with data.pkl and no code/), unknown
  read_torchscript      the tensors of a TorchScript archive as numpy arrays: its tensor index (data.pkl) is read by
                        an unpickler that knows only tensor rebuilding and stand-ins for module objects (anything
                        else is refused), and the raw storages are read as little-endian arrays
  NumpyPolicy           the network rebuilt from those tensors: an optional LSTM memory (one layer) followed by an
                        MLP (Linear / ELU), the common shape of exported locomotion policies

A LocoPolicy says what the network expects: the robot pack, the controlled joints in order, their default angles, PD gains, the observation layout (base angular velocity, projected gravity, command, joint offsets, joint velocities, last action, gait phase) with its scales, the action scale and the control period. match(policy, robot) lists every difference between that and the robot in the world (joints, drive, timestep, free base) as {path, expected, actual}; the world refuses a policy action while the list is not empty.

docs.title: table_reach
docs.text:
MuJoCo table-top reaching with language, occlusion and disturbances.

A planar 2-link arm over a table with three coloured pads. Each episode samples pad colours and positions, a target pad, and a natural-language instruction (direct: "touch the red pad", or indirect: "touch the pad the colour of a ripe tomato"). Pads are only observable for the first visible_steps steps; afterwards the agent must rely on memory. Optionally the arm is pushed.

Task logic (init distribution, instruction, success / failure predicates) lives here; MuJoCo is the Simulator. Success = fingertip dwells on the target pad; touching another pad long enough fails.

docs.title: world
docs.text:
The stage world (RFC-0008 part 3): a running MuJoCo simulation of a stage that tools act on through actions with receipts.

world = World(stage, root=stage_dir)          # compiles the stage; generation 1
r = world.act({"action_id": "a1", "expected_generation": 1, "robot": "arm", "kind": "tcp",
               "position": [0.5, 0.0, 0.3]})
r["status"], r["steps"], r["measured"]
world.capture(["overview"])                    # RGB-D, segmentation by entity, K, camera pose

Rules: - Every action names the generation it was decided on. A world that was rebuilt (a new stage revision) or reset has a new generation, and an action for an older one is refused as stale: observe again first. - action_id makes an action idempotent: sending the same id again returns the stored receipt. - One action per robot at a time; act_batch runs actions of several robots in the same steps (all start together, each ends on its own; the receipt of each says when). - Time passes only inside actions (the clock is manual): the world holds still between tool calls. - A receipt reports what was measured in the simulation after the action, never what was intended.

docs.title: world_tools
docs.text:
The stage world as typed tools (RFC-0008 part 5): what a model (or a person through the Studio, or a coding agent over MCP) calls to build a scene, run robots in it, look at it and check it.

Registered as the surface mujoco.world (entry point group hylo.surfaces). One Workspace holds a stage store, the stage being worked on and the world built from one of its revisions:

  stage      stage_show, stage_history (read); stage_edit (a patch against the revision you read: compare and swap),
             stage_restore (act)
  packs      packs: the robots a stage can name, with their controls and status
  world      world_build (compile the newest revision: a new generation), world_reset (act); world_state (read)
  robots     act: one action per robot, or several robots in the same steps; every action names the generation
             it was decided on and comes back with a measured receipt
  time       advance: let time pass (people walk, objects settle), optionally recording a video
  people     people: goto / stop / resume a person
  eyes       capture (camera images with depth and segmentation by entity), view (a free viewpoint),
             pixel_to_world (a pixel of a capture as a world point and the entity it shows)
  checks     check (a goal predicate: satisfied, or which atoms failed and why), gate (before starting: refuse a goal
             naming missing entities, flag one already satisfied), overlaps (penetrations at the start)
  data       export (camera frames over time as a dataset: samples.jsonl, rgb png, depth npy, seg png, calibration)
Images (capture, view) come back to vision models; files go under the workspace's output folder.

docs.title: env
docs.text:
RoboCasa Environment adapter with the robot contract (hylo.robot/v0.1). Runs inside the RoboCasa venv (bench/envs/robocasa: RoboCasa 1.0.1 on robosuite 1.5) behind an EnvServer; the main process never imports either. The contract's machinery is hylo.envs.robosuite_contract; this module builds RoboCasa's kitchens and labels them.

Robot: RoboCasa's PandaOmron (a Panda arm on a mobile base with a torso lift). The contract drives the arm only: the base and the torso get zero commands and stay where the scene put them. World frame: the arm's mount (body robot0_link0), +x forward, +z up; counters are typically 0.2-0.3 m below it (RobotSpec.table_height is not given: it varies by kitchen, the tools measure it). After RoboCasa's reset the arm glides from RoboCasa's stretched start posture to the contract's home posture (ready_posture), before the agent's first observation. One environment instance serves one task (param task).

A seed fixes an episode: the adapter reseeds RoboCasa's generator with it before the reset, so the kitchen (layout and style), the objects and their placement, the robot's spawn offset and the task's choices (which drawer, which burner) follow from the seed. Splits as in the other Hylo benchmarks: protocol "rsi" (default) gives RFC-0002 search / search_val / gate / heldout over rsi_states seeds plus a validation split; "standard" gives train / validation / heldout.

docs.title: tasks
docs.text:
The RoboCasa atomic tasks this adapter offers and how their scenes are labelled (pure Python).

Seven atomic tasks over the four skills RoboCasa's atomic set covers on a counter: pick and place, opening or closing an articulated fixture (a drawer, a hinged cabinet door), turning a knob or lever (a stove burner, a sink faucet) and pressing a button (a microwave). Step budgets are RoboCasa's own task horizons (v1.0.1).

Labels: objects by their RoboCasa category ("bottled_water" -> "bottled water"); fixtures by kind ("sink", "stove", "drawer", "cabinet", ...); a fixture the task refers to keeps the plain kind and other fixtures of the same kind get "other " (the instruction's "the left drawer" is the one labelled "drawer"); parts of referenced fixtures get their own labels (PARTS); counters are the support (id 1, "counter").

Success: every door closed.'), Task('turn_on_stove', 'TurnOnStove', 'turn on the <position> burner of the stove', 450, 'knob', "Each burner has a knob on the stove's front or top; a knob turns about its own axis. Success: the named burner's knob turned on."), Task('turn_on_sink_faucet', 'TurnOnSinkFaucet', 'turn on the sink faucet', 600, 'lever', "The faucet's handle is a lever on the spout; lift or swing it. Success: the water on."), Task('turn_on_microwave', 'TurnOnMicrowave', 'press the start button on the microwave', 450, 'button', "The start and stop buttons are on the microwave's front panel; press the start button in.")]}

docs.title: env
docs.text:
robosuite Environment adapter with the robot contract (hylo.robot/v0.1). Runs inside the robosuite venv (bench/envs/robosuite) behind an EnvServer; the main process never imports robosuite. The contract's machinery (action and observation mapping, model export, cameras, segmentation) is hylo.envs.robosuite_contract; this module only says which robosuite task to build and how it is laid out.

One environment instance serves one task (param task, a key of tasks.TASKS): the RobotSpec depends on it (one or two arms, where the second arm stands, which hand). World frame: robot0's base. A seed fixes the episode: robosuite's generator is reseeded with it before the reset. Success is robosuite's _check_success(); Wipe also ends on robosuite's own failure check (the arm touching the table, a joint at its limit).

docs.title: suites
docs.text:
robosuite tasks as a Hylo Benchmark (pure Python: the main process enumerates tasks without importing robosuite).

A seed fixes an episode completely: the adapter reseeds robosuite's random generator with it before the reset, so object placements (and the hammer's size in the handover, the dirt path in Wipe, the arm's start noise) follow from the seed alone. Splits use disjoint seed ranges like the other Hylo benchmarks: protocol "rsi" (default) gives the RFC-0002 search / search_val / gate / heldout splits over rsi_states seeds plus a separate validation split for plain evaluation; protocol "standard" gives train / validation / heldout.

docs.title: stats
docs.text:
Gate tests (plugin group "gate_tests"): the paired statistic the improvement protocol uses to decide.

A gate test compares candidate and parent on the same (task, seed) keys and returns a PairedComparison: candidate_wins / parent_wins (pairs where one side is better, used by early rejection and futility), and a one-sided p_value for H1 "the candidate is better". The protocol around it (cascade, group-sequential looks, alpha spending, Holm, regression and safety vetoes, held-out report) is unchanged whichever test is chosen.

protocol: {gate_test: {type: sign, params: {metric: steps, direction: lower}}}

Built in: - mcnemar (default): exact one-sided McNemar on a binary metric (success); - sign: exact one-sided sign test on any metric, with a direction and an optional minimum difference; - paired_permutation: sign-flip permutation test on the mean paired difference of a continuous metric.

docs.title: campaign
docs.text:
Multi-cycle improvement campaigns: config, resume, budgets, manual approval (RFC-0002 §5).

A campaign repeats run_cycle: each promoted candidate becomes the next cycle's parent. State lives in the campaign directory (registry, archive, campaign_state.json, per-cycle runs), so run_campaign resumes where it stopped. With approval="manual", a candidate that passes the gate is parked in pending_approval.json and promoted only by an explicit approve() (e.g. hylo evolve approve DIR): the default for anything that will run on hardware. Every change of the active version is published as active.json (core.deployment), which is all a deploying process (the policy server) reads.

docs.title: candidate
docs.text:
Improvement candidates and the candidate registry.

  • A Candidate is declarative: a patch of dotted config paths (v0.1). A code candidate (RFC-0006 part 5) is still a patch: it may change only the agent, and its program must be a sealed program artifact (validated and run in the restricted namespace of hylo-code-agents), never inline source.
  • ProtectedScope: candidates may not touch safety, benchmark, scoring or trace configuration.
  • Registry: immutable versions with parent links, an active pointer, an append-only ledger, and rollback as a first-class operation (no upstream project implements rollback).

docs.text:
Chunk-critic proposer (RFC-0002 L3): learn Q(s, chunk) from the campaign's own development traces and propose steering the frozen VLA with it (sample N chunks, execute the best-valued one).

proposer: {type: critic.chunk_value, params: {data_roots: [runs/rsi-libero10/runs], n_samples: 4}}

The critic is trained in a subprocess (hylo.learn.critic) on search / search_val episodes only, so the gate still judges it on unseen init states. The offline same-state pair accuracy is recorded as evidence; a critic that cannot rank chunks from identical states better than chance (min_pair_accuracy) is not proposed.

docs.title: experience
docs.text:
Turn improvement-loop outcomes into skills (RFC-0003 M3: the point where memory and RSI meet).

Every archived candidate becomes a skill version whose status follows the evidence, never a model's opinion: - promoted -> verified (gate statistics as evidence) - gated_fail, effect <= 0 -> refuted - gated_fail, effect > 0 -> proposed (promising but underpowered: worth re-testing with more episodes) - rejected (stage-1 deficit) -> refuted - archived (not significant on search_val) -> proposed Refuted skills stay in the library so proposers can see what was tried and failed.

hylo skills <campaign dir | archive.jsonl> --out runs/skills/libero10 --tags libero libero_10 --env libero

docs.title: learning
docs.text:
Generic learning proposer (RFC-0004): train an artifact from this cycle's development runs and propose using it.

proposer: {type: learn, params: {
    learner: critic.chunk_value,                       # "learners" plugin (runs in `python`'s venv)
    params: {image_camera: agentview, task_prefix: libero/libero_10/},
    python_path: agent.params.python,                  # or python: envs/libero/.venv/bin/python
    require: {cv.same_state_pair_accuracy: 0.55},      # manifest metrics gate (offline sanity, not the RSI gate)
    patch: {agent.params.ref: lerobot.critic_steered,
            agent.params.params.critic: {path: "{artifact}", beta: 0.5}},
    variants: [{agent.params.params.critic.beta: 0.0}],
    hypothesis: "a critic ranking same-state chunks {metrics.cv.same_state_pair_accuracy} picks better chunks"}}

The learner seals its output (artifact.json: kind, role, digest, the runs it read); the proposer verifies it before proposing, and stage 0 of the gate verifies it again. Development splits only; a job whose artifact is already sealed with the same job digest is reused (campaign resume). CriticProposer and ExpertIterationProposer are the two original special cases of this pattern.

docs.title: loop

A single improvement cycle on standard splits: Execute(train) -> Diagnose -> Propose -> Check -> Validate -> Held-out -> Promote. Split discipline: diagnosis reads the train split (privileged state allowed); candidate selection uses the validation split (paired, same seeds); heldout is only reported.

docs.title: protocol
docs.text:
RSI evaluation protocol v2 (RFC-0002 §4): four-way split, cascade evaluation, archive, confirmatory gate.

search split      -> diagnosis and proposer feedback (the proposer may read these traces)
search_val split  -> candidate selection (metrics never shown to the proposer)
gate split        -> one confirmatory paired test per selected candidate (Holm if several)
heldout split     -> report only

Lessons applied (our research notes): no single-shot acceptance; selection and confirmation on different seeds; held-out sealed; novelty check before spending rollouts; every candidate kept in an archive with its hypothesis and evidence; promotion only through the gate; budget accounting.

docs.title: selftrain
docs.text:
Expert-iteration proposer (RFC-0002 L4): improve the policy's weights from its own successes.

Each call collects the parent's episodes on the search split with full camera recording, fine-tunes the policy on the successful ones in the policy's own venv (hylo.policies.lerobot.selftrain), and proposes the new weights as a config patch. The candidate then goes through the same cascade and sequential gate as any steering change, so a fine-tune that only memorised the search states is rejected on unseen init states.

proposer: {type: selftrain.expert_iteration, params: {steps: 300, batch_size: 8, lr: 1.0e-5}}

Only development splits are trained on; the proposer reuses the parent's search traces if they already have per-step images, otherwise it records a fresh collection run (trace.image_every = 1).

docs.title: critic
docs.text:
Chunk value critic (RFC-0002 L3): a small learned Q(s, chunk) that re-ranks the N chunks a frozen VLA samples.

V-GPS-style test-time steering, scaled to CPU and to the data we already have: - data: our own traces. Each agent.chunk event plus the observation before it is one (state, chunk) sample; the target is the discounted success-to-go gamma**(steps until success), 0 if the episode failed (Monte Carlo, no bootstrapping: the behaviour policy is the policy being steered). - features: proprio state, episode progress, task one-hot, a summary of the chunk's executed part (net translation / rotation, gripper level and flips), optionally a coarse camera thumbnail. - model: an ensemble of small numpy MLPs; selection maximises mean - beta * std (pessimism against the critic's own extrapolation, the role Cal-QL's conservatism plays in V-GPS). Weights are .npz + JSON metadata (no pickle), so the critic loads in any venv. The agent that steers with it is hylo.agents.critic.CriticSteeredAgent:

agent: {type: remote, params: {ref: hylo.policies.lerobot.critic_agent:make_critic_steered, params: {
    repo_id: ..., steering: {n_samples: 4, execution_steps: 25}, critic: {path: critics/l10-v1, beta: 0.5}}}}

A judge decides "is the task done?" from what a real robot has: camera frames, proprio state and the task. It never sees privileged simulator state, the episode length or the termination reason (in LIBERO an episode ends the moment it succeeds, so length alone would leak the answer).

Model: the critic's numpy MLP ensemble over proprio + task one-hot + grayscale thumbnails of each camera. Trained by the "judge.trace" learner in hylo-learn (hylo.learn.judges).

docs.title: instruments
docs.text:
Hylo instruments: learned models that measure or predict but never act.

Success judges (judges), chunk value models (critic) and world models (world_model). They are trained by hylo-learn, used by the improvement loop (labels, pre-screening) and by agents that consult them (hylo.agents.critic.CriticSteeredAgent).

docs.title: world_model
docs.text:
World model (RFC-0004 W2): an action-conditioned model of the environment, learned from our own traces.

StateWorldModel predicts the next proprioceptive / object state from (state, action) with an ensemble of small MLPs (their disagreement is the model's uncertainty), and the probability that the task is complete in a state. WorldModelEnvironment wraps it behind the Environment protocol, so the unchanged kernel can run an agent inside the model: episodes start from initial states recorded in development runs and end when the model says the task is complete or the step budget runs out.

It is an instrument. Its use in the improvement loop is pre-screening (protocol.prescreen): candidates the model predicts to be clearly worse than the parent are dropped before any real rollout; the gate never sees model results. This version models low-dimensional state, so it can host agents that act on state (MuJoCo / test baselines, planners); a VLA acting on camera images needs a video world model (GPU), which plugs into the same protocol later.

env: {type: world_model, params: {path: "artifact:world_model@<digest>"}}     # trained by the "world_model.state"
                                                                    # learner (hylo.learn.world_model)

docs.title: critic
docs.text:
Train a ChunkCritic from Hylo traces.

python -m hylo.learn.critic --runs runs/rsi-libero10/runs runs/evolve/libero10-llm         --out critics/l10-v1 [--image-camera agentview] [--task-prefix libero/libero_10/]

Protocol integrity (RFC-0002): only episodes whose split is in --splits (default: search, search_val) are read; gate and held-out episodes never reach the critic, so a critic-steered candidate is still judged on unseen init states. The critic is fit on search and evaluated on search_val, then refit on both. The output directory is sealed as a value_model artifact (RFC-0004) listing the runs it was trained on; CriticLearner is the same trainer behind the learner interface ("critic.chunk_value").

Reports the offline diagnostics that decide whether re-ranking can help at all: - val AUC / Brier of the predicted value against the episode's final success; - the same for a state-only model: if (state + chunk) is no better than state alone, the critic cannot tell chunks apart and steering with it is noise.

docs.title: data
docs.text:
External data (RFC-0004): demonstrations, videos and other robots' logs, ingested as ordinary runs.

A DataSource yields ExternalEpisodes (frames with state and camera images, actions if the source has them, an outcome if the source states one). ingest writes them into the trace store as a run whose split is external:<name>, so every builder reads them through the same split guard, and seals the run as a dataset artifact recording origin and licence. Nothing external enters a gate or held-out split.

Two checks guard what external data may be used for: - labels say who produced them: "source" (the dataset says so), "judge:" (a calibrated instrument, see label_run), or none; an unlabeled episode is never treated as a success; - contamination_report compares each external episode's initial state with the initial states of protected (gate / held-out) episodes of the same task; an external source that reproduces protected init states must not be used to build anything that is then gated on them.

python -m hylo.learn.data ingest SPEC.json      # {"source": {"type": ..., "params": ...}, "name": ..., "out": ...}

Write episodes as a run under split external: and seal it. Returns the run summary.

assume_success: label every episode a success on the source's authority (curated demonstrations); otherwise an episode is a success only if the source says so, and is left unlabeled when it says nothing.

docs.title: judges
docs.text:
Learner "judge.trace": a success judge trained on development traces (RFC-0004 A3).

Training data, from development-split runs only: - the last recorded frame of every finished episode, labelled with the simulator outcome; - early frames (progress < negative_before) of successful episodes as extra negatives: same scene, task not yet done, which teaches the scene change rather than the scene identity. The sealed artifact is loaded at run time by hylo.instruments.judges.TraceSuccessJudge.

docs.title: TraceJudgeLearner

docs.title: online
docs.text:
Online learning runner (extension point): propose -> roll out -> update, then seal.

The rollouts are ordinary evaluations of a development split (search by default; gate and held-out are refused), recorded under <out>/rollouts/iter-NNN/ like any run, so replay, judges and the catalog see them and the sealed artifact's provenance lists them. The learner decides what to try and how to update: policy search (CEM), on-policy RL (a GRPO-style learner would return its current policy and update from the rollouts' traces), iterative self-training. Episodes per evaluation are the split's.

TrainJob(learner="examples.cem", inputs=[], out="runs/learned/cem", params={
    "experiment": <ExperimentConfig as dict>, "iterations": 4, "split": "search", ...learner params})

docs.title: Goal dataclass
docs.text:
Goal(verb: Verb, arm: str | None = None, tcp: ndarray | None = None, pre: ndarray | None = None, hand_before: Sequence[float] | None = None, hand: Sequence[float] | None = None, joints: ndarray | None = None, rank: float = 0.0, free: Literal['x', 'z'] | None = None, attached: ndarray | None = None)

One motion the planner may choose. verb: grasp, place, reach, lift, push, press, retreat, home. arm: arm name (None: the robot's only arm). tcp: (4, 4) TCP pose to end at. pre: (4, 4) approach pose: the planner reaches pre around obstacles, then moves in a straight line to tcp (that line is checked against the table and the robot only, not observed points, so it may touch the object). Without pre, verbs lift, retreat, push and press move in a straight line from the current TCP; other verbs plan a collision-free joint path to tcp. joints: a joint-space goal instead of tcp (e.g. home). hand_before: hand command while moving (None: keep the current one). hand: hand command at the end, held until the hand settles (None: no change). rank: lower is tried first among goals passed together. free: "x" or "z" lets the planner rotate freely about that TCP axis (e.g. "x" for a top-down approach to a round object). attached: (N, 3) points of a held object in the TCP frame: they move with the hand and are checked against the table and observed points like the hand itself (place_at fills it); observed points of the object where it is now are ignored.

docs.title: dexgrasp
docs.text:
Multi-finger grasp planning for any dexterous hand (a HandModel: HandSpec plus its MJCF) on an object given as points or a mesh.

Object: one or more convex parts (the hull of the points, of the mesh, or of each given part), so the signed distance to the object is the smallest of the parts' hull distances and a ray's entry into the object is exact. A partial point cloud seen from above is extruded down to the table first (the hidden underside is solid).

Planning, per candidate hand pose: 1. sample: approach directions (+x of the TCP) over the sphere, minus those from below the table, times rolls about the approach (the +y closing axis); the TCP aims at the object's centre (plus offsets during refinement); 2. approach: the open hand (a rigid point set) slides along the approach until its first point would enter the object or the table (ray-hull entry distances, exact), never past the centre; 3. close: each finger moves from the open command towards the closing command (HandSpec.closed for "power", the "pinch" preset for "pinch") until its links touch the object (a sweep, then bisection per finger); 4. score: contacts are the finger and palm samples within a few millimetres of the surface (one per link, the hull facet's normal); the epsilon measure of their friction-cone wrenches (force closure when positive), the total normal force needed to hold the object against gravity, penetration, how many fingers touch, and an optional preferred approach direction or pose; 5. refine: the best few are perturbed (offset, tilt, roll) for a couple of rounds and re-scored (a short cross-entropy search over the pose; the fingers re-close each time).

plan() returns DexGrasp records, best first; to_goals() turns them into toolkit Goals (pre-pose back along the approach with the hand open, then the hand closing to a squeeze command past the contact angles).

docs.title: grasp_quality
docs.text:
Grasp quality from contacts: point contacts with Coulomb friction, their friction cones as a few edge forces, the wrenches those forces exert on the object, force closure and the largest-ball (epsilon) measure of the wrench hull, and the effort needed to hold the object against gravity.

Conventions: a contact is a point p on the object surface and the unit normal n pointing INTO the object (the direction the finger pushes). Forces are unit normal force plus friction up to mu (friction cone edges f_j = n + mu (cos t_j u + sin t_j v)). Torques are taken about the object's reference point c and divided by a length rho (usually the object's radius), so forces and torques are commensurate: w = [f, (p - c) x f / rho]. The epsilon measure is the distance from the origin to the nearest facet of the convex hull of every contact's edge wrenches: the largest wrench of any direction the grasp resists with unit total normal force (summed over contacts, an L1 bound). It is positive exactly when the grasp is force closure; zero or negative otherwise.

docs.title: handmodel
docs.text:
A dexterous hand on its own: the subtree of an arm model's hand body, cut out of any MJCF (or URDF) with MuJoCo's model editor and hung under a mocap root so its pose in the world can be set freely. The grasp planner and the retargeting solver work on it.

hand = HandModel.from_arm(robot_spec.arm("right"))      # the hand of an arm, as its ArmSpec describes it
hand = HandModel(model_path, "palm", hand_spec)          # any model file, its hand body and a HandSpec
hand.set(T_world_tcp, q)                                 # place it (TCP pose) with finger joints q
pts, link = hand.surface()                               # collision surface samples in the world, link per point

Fingers are found from the kinematic tree: each child chain of the hand body that holds finger joints is one finger (its joints in HandSpec.joints order, its links, its tip: the collision point of its last link farthest from the finger's first joint). The thumb is the finger whose names say so ("thumb", "th"), else the one whose base lies farthest from the others; the other fingers are named by hints in their body and joint names (index / ff, middle / mf, ring / rf, little / lf), else in order. The human wrist's place on the hand (for retargeting) is a site named "wrist" on the hand body when the model has one, else the end of the palm's collision geometry opposite the fingers.

docs.title: handpath
docs.text:
Editing a hand's motion so it holds what it should: a retargeted (human) trajectory of TCP poses and finger joints bent onto a planned grasp around the grasp moment.

tcp, fingers, info = bend_onto_grasp(tcp, fingers, grasp, start=a, end=b, fps=15.0)

Phases (frame indices; grasp is a DexGrasp from hylo.manip.dexgrasp): ramp [a - ramp, a - approach): from the retargeted pose to the pre-pose (6 cm back along the approach), fingers to the grasp's open pre-shape; approach [a - approach, a): straight in along the approach to the grasp pose, fingers open; hold [a, b): the grasp's offset from the retargeted TCP at frame a rides on the retargeted motion (the hand carries the object as the human hand does), fingers close to the squeeze command over close_s; release [b, b + open_s): offset kept, fingers back to the pre-shape; return then over ramp: back to the retargeted motion. Frames outside these phases are unchanged.

docs.title: Goal dataclass
docs.text:
Goal(verb: Verb, arm: str | None = None, tcp: ndarray | None = None, pre: ndarray | None = None, hand_before: Sequence[float] | None = None, hand: Sequence[float] | None = None, joints: ndarray | None = None, rank: float = 0.0, free: Literal['x', 'z'] | None = None, attached: ndarray | None = None)

One motion the planner may choose. verb: grasp, place, reach, lift, push, press, retreat, home. arm: arm name (None: the robot's only arm). tcp: (4, 4) TCP pose to end at. pre: (4, 4) approach pose: the planner reaches pre around obstacles, then moves in a straight line to tcp (that line is checked against the table and the robot only, not observed points, so it may touch the object). Without pre, verbs lift, retreat, push and press move in a straight line from the current TCP; other verbs plan a collision-free joint path to tcp. joints: a joint-space goal instead of tcp (e.g. home). hand_before: hand command while moving (None: keep the current one). hand: hand command at the end, held until the hand settles (None: no change). rank: lower is tried first among goals passed together. free: "x" or "z" lets the planner rotate freely about that TCP axis (e.g. "x" for a top-down approach to a round object). attached: (N, 3) points of a held object in the TCP frame: they move with the hand and are checked against the table and observed points like the hand itself (place_at fills it); observed points of the object where it is now are ignored.

Oriented box around object points: minimum-area xy rectangle (size[0] >= size[1], yaw in (-pi/2, pi/2]), top from the points, bottom at the table when given (hidden sides are filled down to it). box.pose: 4x4.

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(model_points: ndarray, observed: ndarray, init: ndarray | None = None) -> Fit

Rigid ICP of a known shape (model points, its own frame) onto observed world points; partial views fit. Without init it tries 12 yaws about +z from the centroids. fit.T maps model to world.

docs.title: grasps
docs.text:
grasps(points: ndarray, table: Table, scene: ndarray | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> list[Goal]

Ranked grasp goals (best first) for a parallel hand from an object's points: top-down across the narrow side, across the long side if it fits, side grasps from the robot's side for tall objects. TCP depth is up to 3 cm below the top (half the height if shorter); width must fit the open hand; candidates whose open hand (at the goal or the 10 cm pre-pose) hits the table, the object or scene points are dropped. Each Goal has pre, hand_before=open, hand=closed. Empty: no grasp fits. arm: which arm (None: the only one).

docs.title: grasp_at
docs.text:
grasp_at(tcp: ndarray, hand: Sequence[float] | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> Goal

A grasp goal at a TCP pose you chose: pre-pose 10 cm back along the TCP's +x (approach), hand opens before moving and closes (or goes to hand) at tcp.

docs.title: hand_grasps
docs.text:
hand_grasps(points: ndarray, table: Table, kind: str = 'power', arm: str | None = None) -> list[Goal]

Dexterous hand: top-down grasp goals, TCP at the object's mid height, closing axis across its box faces (four directions; first the one nearest the arm base frame's +x, e.g. a humanoid's forward: thumb on the near side, fingers on the far side). Opens to HandSpec.open on the way, closes to preset kind.

docs.title: dex_grasps
docs.text:
dex_grasps(points: ndarray, table: Table, hand: str | None = None, scene: ndarray | None = None, arm: str | None = None, mesh: tuple[ndarray, ndarray] | None = None, top: int = 8) -> list[Goal]

Multi-finger grasp goals (best first) for a dexterous hand from an object's points (or mesh = (V, F)): hand poses sampled around the object (approach directions times rolls, none from below the table), the open hand slid in until it touches, each finger closed until it touches, scored by the friction-cone wrench hull (force closure), the force needed to hold the object against gravity, penetration and fingers in contact, then refined by a short search over the pose. hand: closing style, "power" (all fingers wrap, palm may touch), "pinch" (the pinch preset) or None for both. Approaches from the arm's side and from above rank higher. Each Goal: pre 10 cm back along the approach with hand_before = the open pre-shape, tcp, hand = a squeeze command past the contact angles. Empty: no grasp found. arm: which arm (None: the only one).

docs.title: retarget
docs.text:
retarget(keypoints: ndarray, arm: str | None = None, valid: ndarray | None = None, side: str | None = None, scale: float | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

Human hand keypoints (T, 21, 3) in the MediaPipe layout (wrist 0, thumb 1-4, index 5-8, middle 9-12, ring 13-16, little 17-20; metres, world frame) -> this arm's hand: {"hand": (T, n) finger commands, "tcp": (T, 4, 4) TCP poses that put the robot palm where the human palm is, "ee": (T, 4, 4), "tip_error_mm": (T,) fingertip error per frame, "summary": {...}}. Fingertip and thumb-to-finger vectors are matched (scaled to the robot hand's size; scale overrides it) within joint limits, smooth across frames. side: "left"/"right" human hand (a mismatch mirrors it); valid: frames with keypoints.

docs.title: hand_points
docs.text:
hand_points(hand: Sequence[float] | str | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> np.ndarray

Hand surface points (N, 3) in the TCP frame at command hand (a preset name; None: open). [:, 0].max(): how far the hand reaches past the TCP along +x (e.g. to push a button with it).

docs.title: place_at
docs.text:
place_at(obj_in_tcp: ndarray, obj_points: ndarray | Box, xy: Sequence[float], yaw: float | None = None, table: Table | None = None, hover: float = 0.03, scene: ndarray | None = None, support: float | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> Goal

Where the TCP must go so the held object rests at xy. obj_in_tcp: the object frame in the TCP frame at grasp time (inv(grasp_tcp) @ box.pose). obj_points: the object's Box (its pose is the object frame; best: the hidden bottom counts) or its points in that frame (apply inv(box.pose) to its world points). The object keeps its current tilt; its yaw becomes yaw (world, None: unchanged); its lowest point ends hover metres above the support: support (a height), else the top of scene points (e.g. view.points; robot, table and the held object ignored) under the object's footprint at xy (a plate, a block to stack on), else the table (table, else the robot's table height). Pre-pose 10 cm above; hand opens at the goal; the object rides along as attached geometry (checked against the table and observed points).

docs.title: plan
docs.text:
plan(goals: Goal | Sequence[Goal], table: Table | None = None, scene: ndarray | None = None) -> Plan | None

The first reachable goal by rank: IK (seeds: current joints, home, random), a collision-free joint path to pre (or tcp) avoiding the table and scene points (pass view.points: the robot, the table and points within 8 cm of the hand are ignored), the straight approach to tcp, then the final hand command. Timed to control steps within velocity and acceleration limits; other arms hold. None: no goal reachable (robot.why() says why). Deterministic for a given seed.

docs.title: why
docs.text:
why() -> str

Why the last plan() returned None (empty after a success).

docs.title: hold
docs.text:
hold(steps: int, hand: dict[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None) -> np.ndarray

(steps, action_dim) joint targets that keep every arm where it is now; hand {arm: command} sets those hands (others keep their last command). Run it with run_actions (a gripper command, a pause).

docs.title: run_actions
docs.text:
run_actions(actions: ndarray) -> dict[str, Any]

Execute raw joint targets (from hold) through the kernel and the shield; remembers the hand commands.

docs.title: reach
docs.text:
reach(tcp: ndarray, arm: str | None = None, free: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

Can the arm put its TCP at tcp (4x4)? IK only (no collision check, no path): {"ok", "pos_err" (m), "rot_err" (rad), "q"}.

docs.title: together
docs.text:
together(plans: dict[str, Plan] | Sequence[Plan], sync: bool = False) -> Plan | None

One plan moving several arms at once: each arm follows its own plan from the same moment (a shorter one then holds its last command). sync=True re-times the arms to start and stop together with their TCPs in step (both hands on one object: plan each arm's motion, e.g. two "lift" goals, then together(..., sync=True)). Every step is checked for arms touching each other or the robot; None when they would (robot.why()).

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run(plan: Plan | dict[str, Plan] | Sequence[Plan], sync: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]

Execute a plan (through the kernel and the safety shield) and wait. Returns {"steps", "ended", "success", "reason", "q", "hand", "tcp": {arm: 4x4}, "tcp_error": {"pos": m, "rot": rad} vs the goal's tcp, None for a joints goal}. Refuses ("error", steps 0) if the robot moved more than 0.05 rad since planning: plan again. Several arms at once: run({"left": plan_l, "right": plan_r}, sync=...) runs together(...) first (refused with "error" when the arms would touch); tcp_error is then {arm: ...}.

docs.title: holding
docs.text:
holding(arm: str | None = None) -> bool | None

Parallel hand: True when the measured pads stopped between open and closed after a close command (something is between them); False when open, opening or fully closed. Dexterous hand: True when, after a command nearer closed than open, at least two finger joints stopped more than 0.12 rad short of it.

docs.title: carried
docs.text:
carried(view: View, points: ndarray, tcp_before: ndarray, tcp_now: ndarray, table: Table) -> dict[str, Any]

Did the object move with the hand? points: its world points seen before the motion; view: a look() after it. Returns {"carried": bool, "match": fraction of rigidly-moved points seen in the view, "left_behind": fraction still seen at the old place, "lifted": TCP z change (m), "offset": (3,) mean observed - expected}.

docs.title: retarget
docs.text:
Hand motion retargeting: human hand keypoints (the 21-point MediaPipe layout) -> joint angles of a robot hand and the pose of its palm.

Frames. Both hands get a palm frame from the same recipe: origin at the wrist, x towards the middle finger's base (knuckle), y across the knuckles from the index towards the outermost finger, z = x cross y (out of the palm on a right hand, anatomically the same side on both). The robot's wrist point, finger bases and fingertips come from its model (HandModel); for a three-finger hand the outermost finger is its middle finger.

Per frame the finger joints q minimise, in the robot palm frame, sum_i w_tip |tip_i(q) - o - a Rv(k_tip_i - k_wrist)|^2 wrist-to-tip vectors + sum_j w_ij |(tip_j(q) - tip_thumb(q)) - a Rv(k_tip_j - k_tip_thumb)|^2 thumb-to-finger vectors + w_smooth |q - q_prev|^2 + w_rest |q - q_open|^2 within the joint limits (bounded least squares, analytic Jacobians from MuJoCo). a scales the human hand to the robot's (middle finger plus palm length, measured once per sequence), Rv expresses human palm-frame vectors in the robot palm frame; w_ij grows as the human thumb and finger close in, so pinches stay pinches. Robot fingers map to human fingers by name (thumb, index, middle, ring, little); a robot with fewer fingers uses the first ones.

The palm pose in the world aligns the robot palm frame with the human one, palm centres (wrist and knuckles) together. A left human hand on a right robot hand (or the reverse) is mirrored: finger shapes reflected through the palm plane, the palm's normal kept (the thumb then sits on the other side).

rt = Retargeter(hand_model("allegro_right"))
out = rt.run(keypoints)            # (T, 21, 3) metres, any frame (camera or world)
out.q (T, n), out.ee (T, 4, 4) palm (ee frame) poses, out.tcp, out.tip_error_mm (T,), out.ms_per_frame

docs.title: tools
docs.text: The Tools facade (RFC-0006 part 2): the verbs a program uses as robot. Stateless: the program keeps its own list of objects and of what each hand holds; every verb reads the robot afresh. The implementations live in the modules beside it (kinematics, collision, planning, perception, grasping); api_reference(tools) renders the verbs' docstrings as the reference a code-writing model reads.

docs.title: TYPES module-attribute
docs.text: TYPES = (View, CameraView, Mask, Table, Detection, Box, Fit, Plan)

docs.title: EXAMPLE module-attribute
docs.text:
EXAMPLE = 'view = robot.look(); table = robot.table(view)
obj = robot.objects(view, robot.find(view, "red block"), table)[0]
box = robot.box(obj.points, table)
plan = robot.plan(robot.grasps(obj.points, table, scene=view.points), table, view.points)
if plan is None: print(robot.why())
else: out = robot.run(plan); print(out["tcp_error"], robot.holding())
up = out["tcp"]["arm"].copy(); up[2, 3] += 0.10
robot.run(robot.plan(robot.Goal("lift", tcp=up), table, view.points))
obj_in_tcp = np.linalg.inv(plan.goal.tcp) @ box.pose
view = robot.look()                                # rests on whatever is under (0.5, 0.2): table, plate, block
goal = robot.place_at(obj_in_tcp, box, xy=(0.5, 0.2), yaw=0.0, table=table, hover=0.01, scene=view.points)
robot.run(robot.plan(goal, table, view.points))'

docs.title: TWO_ARM_EXAMPLE module-attribute
docs.text:
TWO_ARM_EXAMPLE = 'view = robot.look(); table = robot.table(view)
a = robot.objects(view, robot.find(view, "red block"), table)[0]
b = robot.objects(view, robot.find(view, "blue block"), table)[0]
pl = robot.plan(robot.grasps(a.points, table, scene=view.points, arm="left"), table, view.points)
pr = robot.plan(robot.grasps(b.points, table, scene=view.points, arm="right"), table, view.points)
out = robot.run({"left": pl, "right": pr})         # both arms at once; out["error"] if they would touch
print(out.get("error"), robot.holding(arm="left"), robot.holding(arm="right"))
st = robot.status(); ups = {}
for arm in ("left", "right"):
    t = st["tcp"][arm].copy(); t[2, 3] += 0.10
    ups[arm] = robot.plan(robot.Goal("lift", arm, tcp=t), table)
robot.run(ups, sync=True)                          # start and stop together, TCPs in step'

docs.title: Goal dataclass
docs.text:
Goal(verb: Verb, arm: str | None = None, tcp: ndarray | None = None, pre: ndarray | None = None, hand_before: Sequence[float] | None = None, hand: Sequence[float] | None = None, joints: ndarray | None = None, rank: float = 0.0, free: Literal['x', 'z'] | None = None, attached: ndarray | None = None)

One motion the planner may choose. verb: grasp, place, reach, lift, push, press, retreat, home. arm: arm name (None: the robot's only arm). tcp: (4, 4) TCP pose to end at. pre: (4, 4) approach pose: the planner reaches pre around obstacles, then moves in a straight line to tcp (that line is checked against the table and the robot only, not observed points, so it may touch the object). Without pre, verbs lift, retreat, push and press move in a straight line from the current TCP; other verbs plan a collision-free joint path to tcp. joints: a joint-space goal instead of tcp (e.g. home). hand_before: hand command while moving (None: keep the current one). hand: hand command at the end, held until the hand settles (None: no change). rank: lower is tried first among goals passed together. free: "x" or "z" lets the planner rotate freely about that TCP axis (e.g. "x" for a top-down approach to a round object). attached: (N, 3) points of a held object in the TCP frame: they move with the hand and are checked against the table and observed points like the hand itself (place_at fills it); observed points of the object where it is now are ignored.

docs.title: Mask dataclass
docs.text:
Mask(label: str, camera: str, mask: ndarray, score: float = 1.0, instance: int | None = None)

An instance mask in one camera: label (the text label it answers), camera, mask (H, W) bool, score in [0, 1] (1: exact label match), instance (the environment's instance id, when known; label: view.segments[instance]).

docs.title: Plan dataclass
docs.text:
Plan(goal: Goal, actions: ndarray, start_q: dict[str, ndarray], info: dict[str, Any] = dict(), path: dict[str, list] = dict())

A timed motion: goal (the one chosen; several arms: the first, all in info["goals"]), actions (T, action_dim) joint targets at control rate, start_q {arm: q} it was planned from (run refuses if the robot moved away), info (ik residual, path length, duration, method), path {arm: joint waypoints} before timing.

docs.title: Table dataclass
docs.text:
Table(height: float, normal: ndarray, extent: ndarray | None = None)

The support plane: height (z), normal (3,) (+z for a level table), extent [[xmin, xmax], [ymin, ymax]].

docs.title: View dataclass
docs.text:
View(cams: dict[str, CameraView], points: ndarray, segments: dict[int, str] = dict(), step: int = 0)

One observation: cams {name: CameraView}; points (N, 3) world points fused from every depth camera (voxel-downsampled, robot included); segments {instance id: label} when given; step at which it was taken.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tools(spec: RobotSpec, executor: Executor, *, segmenter: Any | None = None, control_hz: float = 20.0, show: Callable[[ndarray, str], None] | None = None, max_vel: float | Sequence[float] = 1.0, max_acc: float | Sequence[float] = 2.0, seed: int = 0)

robot in programs. executor moves the robot; segmenter answers find (default: the environment's segmentation when the observation has it, else colour names); show collects images for the model. max_vel and max_acc (per joint or scalar, rad/s and rad/s^2) bound planned motions; seed makes planning repeatable.

docs.title: status
docs.text:
status() -> dict[str, Any]

Robot and episode now: {"step", "max_steps", "instruction", "ended", "q": {arm: (n,) joint positions}, "hand": {arm: measured hand state, 0 closed .. 1 open}, "tcp": {arm: (4, 4) TCP pose in the world}}.

docs.title: look
docs.text:
look() -> View

The latest observation: per-camera RGB, depth, intrinsics, pose and segmentation (view.cams), fused world points of every depth camera (view.points, 5 mm voxels; includes table and robot), view.segments.

docs.title: find
docs.text:
find(view: View, labels: str | Sequence[str]) -> list[Mask]

Instance masks for text labels (one Mask per instance per camera). With environment segmentation a label matches segment labels with the same content words (score 1), else those sharing the most words (score = word overlap); with the colour segmenter only the colour word counts. Empty list: nothing matched.

docs.title: table
docs.text:
table(view: View) -> Table

The support plane from view.points by RANSAC (near-horizontal planes only; near RobotSpec.table_height when given): height, normal, xy extent of its inliers.

docs.title: objects
docs.text:
objects(view: View, masks: Sequence[Mask], table: Table) -> list[Detection]

Per label (and instance when known): the masked depth as world points, table points and outliers removed (flat markings on the table, e.g. zones, keep their points at table height), cameras merged, split into separate 3D clusters (one Detection each, largest first).

docs.title: box
docs.text:
box(points: ndarray, table: Table | None = None) -> Box

Oriented box around object points: minimum-area xy rectangle (size[0] >= size[1], yaw in (-pi/2, pi/2]), top from the points, bottom at the table when given (hidden sides are filled down to it). box.pose: 4x4.

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(model_points: ndarray, observed: ndarray, init: ndarray | None = None) -> Fit

Rigid ICP of a known shape (model points, its own frame) onto observed world points; partial views fit. Without init it tries 12 yaws about +z from the centroids. fit.T maps model to world.

docs.title: grasps
docs.text:
grasps(points: ndarray, table: Table, scene: ndarray | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> list[Goal]

Ranked grasp goals (best first) for a parallel hand from an object's points: top-down across the narrow side, across the long side if it fits, side grasps from the robot's side for tall objects. TCP depth is up to 3 cm below the top (half the height if shorter); width must fit the open hand; candidates whose open hand (at the goal or the 10 cm pre-pose) hits the table, the object or scene points are dropped. Each Goal has pre, hand_before=open, hand=closed. Empty: no grasp fits. arm: which arm (None: the only one).

docs.title: grasp_at
docs.text:
grasp_at(tcp: ndarray, hand: Sequence[float] | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> Goal

A grasp goal at a TCP pose you chose: pre-pose 10 cm back along the TCP's +x (approach), hand opens before moving and closes (or goes to hand) at tcp.

docs.title: hand_grasps
docs.text:
hand_grasps(points: ndarray, table: Table, kind: str = 'power', arm: str | None = None) -> list[Goal]

Dexterous hand: top-down grasp goals, TCP at the object's mid height, closing axis across its box faces (four directions; first the one nearest the arm base frame's +x, e.g. a humanoid's forward: thumb on the near side, fingers on the far side). Opens to HandSpec.open on the way, closes to preset kind.

docs.title: dex_grasps
docs.text:
dex_grasps(points: ndarray, table: Table, hand: str | None = None, scene: ndarray | None = None, arm: str | None = None, mesh: tuple[ndarray, ndarray] | None = None, top: int = 8) -> list[Goal]

Multi-finger grasp goals (best first) for a dexterous hand from an object's points (or mesh = (V, F)): hand poses sampled around the object (approach directions times rolls, none from below the table), the open hand slid in until it touches, each finger closed until it touches, scored by the friction-cone wrench hull (force closure), the force needed to hold the object against gravity, penetration and fingers in contact, then refined by a short search over the pose. hand: closing style, "power" (all fingers wrap, palm may touch), "pinch" (the pinch preset) or None for both. Approaches from the arm's side and from above rank higher. Each Goal: pre 10 cm back along the approach with hand_before = the open pre-shape, tcp, hand = a squeeze command past the contact angles. Empty: no grasp found. arm: which arm (None: the only one).

docs.title: retarget
docs.text:
retarget(keypoints: ndarray, arm: str | None = None, valid: ndarray | None = None, side: str | None = None, scale: float | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

Human hand keypoints (T, 21, 3) in the MediaPipe layout (wrist 0, thumb 1-4, index 5-8, middle 9-12, ring 13-16, little 17-20; metres, world frame) -> this arm's hand: {"hand": (T, n) finger commands, "tcp": (T, 4, 4) TCP poses that put the robot palm where the human palm is, "ee": (T, 4, 4), "tip_error_mm": (T,) fingertip error per frame, "summary": {...}}. Fingertip and thumb-to-finger vectors are matched (scaled to the robot hand's size; scale overrides it) within joint limits, smooth across frames. side: "left"/"right" human hand (a mismatch mirrors it); valid: frames with keypoints.

docs.title: hand_points
docs.text:
hand_points(hand: Sequence[float] | str | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> np.ndarray

Hand surface points (N, 3) in the TCP frame at command hand (a preset name; None: open). [:, 0].max(): how far the hand reaches past the TCP along +x (e.g. to push a button with it).

docs.title: place_at
docs.text:
place_at(obj_in_tcp: ndarray, obj_points: ndarray | Box, xy: Sequence[float], yaw: float | None = None, table: Table | None = None, hover: float = 0.03, scene: ndarray | None = None, support: float | None = None, arm: str | None = None) -> Goal

Where the TCP must go so the held object rests at xy. obj_in_tcp: the object frame in the TCP frame at grasp time (inv(grasp_tcp) @ box.pose). obj_points: the object's Box (its pose is the object frame; best: the hidden bottom counts) or its points in that frame (apply inv(box.pose) to its world points). The object keeps its current tilt; its yaw becomes yaw (world, None: unchanged); its lowest point ends hover metres above the support: support (a height), else the top of scene points (e.g. view.points; robot, table and the held object ignored) under the object's footprint at xy (a plate, a block to stack on), else the table (table, else the robot's table height). Pre-pose 10 cm above; hand opens at the goal; the object rides along as attached geometry (checked against the table and observed points).

docs.title: plan
docs.text:
plan(goals: Goal | Sequence[Goal], table: Table | None = None, scene: ndarray | None = None) -> Plan | None

The first reachable goal by rank: IK (seeds: current joints, home, random), a collision-free joint path to pre (or tcp) avoiding the table and scene points (pass view.points: the robot, the table and points within 8 cm of the hand are ignored), the straight approach to tcp, then the final hand command. Timed to control steps within velocity and acceleration limits; other arms hold. None: no goal reachable (robot.why() says why). Deterministic for a given seed.

docs.title: why
docs.text:
why() -> str

Why the last plan() returned None (empty after a success).

docs.title: hold
docs.text:
hold(steps: int, hand: dict[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None) -> np.ndarray

(steps, action_dim) joint targets that keep every arm where it is now; hand {arm: command} sets those hands (others keep their last command). Run it with run_actions (a gripper command, a pause).

docs.title: run_actions
docs.text:
run_actions(actions: ndarray) -> dict[str, Any]

Execute raw joint targets (from hold) through the kernel and the shield; remembers the hand commands.

docs.title: reach
docs.text:
reach(tcp: ndarray, arm: str | None = None, free: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

Can the arm put its TCP at tcp (4x4)? IK only (no collision check, no path): {"ok", "pos_err" (m), "rot_err" (rad), "q"}.

docs.title: together
docs.text:
together(plans: dict[str, Plan] | Sequence[Plan], sync: bool = False) -> Plan | None

One plan moving several arms at once: each arm follows its own plan from the same moment (a shorter one then holds its last command). sync=True re-times the arms to start and stop together with their TCPs in step (both hands on one object: plan each arm's motion, e.g. two "lift" goals, then together(..., sync=True)). Every step is checked for arms touching each other or the robot; None when they would (robot.why()).

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run(plan: Plan | dict[str, Plan] | Sequence[Plan], sync: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]

Execute a plan (through the kernel and the safety shield) and wait. Returns {"steps", "ended", "success", "reason", "q", "hand", "tcp": {arm: 4x4}, "tcp_error": {"pos": m, "rot": rad} vs the goal's tcp, None for a joints goal}. Refuses ("error", steps 0) if the robot moved more than 0.05 rad since planning: plan again. Several arms at once: run({"left": plan_l, "right": plan_r}, sync=...) runs together(...) first (refused with "error" when the arms would touch); tcp_error is then {arm: ...}.

docs.title: holding
docs.text:
holding(arm: str | None = None) -> bool | None

Parallel hand: True when the measured pads stopped between open and closed after a close command (something is between them); False when open, opening or fully closed. Dexterous hand: True when, after a command nearer closed than open, at least two finger joints stopped more than 0.12 rad short of it.

docs.title: carried
docs.text:
carried(view: View, points: ndarray, tcp_before: ndarray, tcp_now: ndarray, table: Table) -> dict[str, Any]

Did the object move with the hand? points: its world points seen before the motion; view: a look() after it. Returns {"carried": bool, "match": fraction of rigidly-moved points seen in the view, "left_behind": fraction still seen at the old place, "lifted": TCP z change (m), "offset": (3,) mean observed - expected}.

docs.title: show

Attach an image (an RGB array, or a View: its cameras side by side) to your next turn, with a note.

docs.title: action_bank
docs.text:
ActionBank: an in-memory, numpy-backed ActionMemory (RFC-0003).

Keys are L2-normalised vectors stored as float16 (cosine similarity = dot product); chunks keep their own length. Capacity is enforced FIFO (Retrieve-then-Steer: a 5k FIFO bank matches an unlimited one). A saved bank is bank.npz + bank.json (no pickle) and is frozen when loaded for evaluation: add raises, and snapshot() is the content digest that goes into the agent spec.

docs.title: episode
docs.text:
Exact event recall above a durable SQLite evidence journal (RFC-0009).

Independent implementation of public event/sequence memory ideas; no external project code. The journal cannot turn missing/ambiguous perception into ground truth. No automatic summary replaces evidence, and budget exhaustion fails explicitly rather than dropping an early cue.

docs.title: frames
docs.text:
Bounded visual retrieval over an episode's observed RGB frames.

Keep demonstration coverage and diverse rollout evidence separately. This is an image-only heuristic, not a detector of task-relevant events; the lossless evaluation trace remains the source of truth when a retrieval budget omits a cue.

docs.title: lessons
docs.text:
LessonBook: language lessons from the agent's own experience, curated by delta operations (RFC-0003 M4).

After ExpeL (ADD / UPVOTE / DOWNVOTE / EDIT insight lists) and ACE (itemised playbook with helpful / harmful counters, incremental deltas instead of rewrites, which avoids "context collapse"). An LLM reflector proposes operations; this class applies them deterministically: - ADD whose title is near-identical (ratio >= dedup) to an active lesson in the same scope becomes an UPVOTE; - UPVOTE / DOWNVOTE move the counters (outcome feedback: candidates that cited a lesson and were promoted or refuted); - EDIT replaces the content and keeps the counters; RETIRE removes it from retrieval; - a lesson with harmful >= helpful + retire_margin retires itself. Every applied operation is appended to ops.jsonl (audit trail); lessons.json is the current state.

lessons: {type: lesson_book, params: {path: runs/lessons/libero10, frozen: true}}

SimpleMemVLA's frame-indexed video memory, independent of other Hylo memories.

Sampling and padding reproduce OpenBMB/SimpleMemVLA commit 453d6ec293e63318bbc2bce545d0b9256ab1bc51. See THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in hylo-memory for the upstream MIT attribution. This is a streaming visual memory, not a semantic MemoryStore implementation.

docs.title: skills
docs.text:
SkillLibrary: verified, versioned procedures for task families (RFC-0003 M3).

A skill is data, never code: a plan template, a steering or recovery config patch, a weights reference, or a reference to a sealed program artifact (kind "program", RFC-0006 part 6: run only by code agents, in their sandbox). Program skills have no trigger pattern; similar ranks them by instruction similarity. Lifecycle: proposed -> verified (only through the RSI gate, with its statistics as evidence) | refuted; verified -> deprecated. match returns verified skills only, with the slot bindings captured by the trigger's instruction pattern. Usage feedback (useful / misleading / not_applicable) accumulates per version.

Storage: /@.json, one file per skill version. A library opened with frozen=True (evaluation) refuses every write, and snapshot() is the content digest recorded in the agent spec. export_skill_md writes one SKILL.md per verified skill (name + description front matter, body below) so an LLM can scan the index and read bodies on demand.

skills: {type: skill_library, params: {path: runs/skills/libero10, frozen: true}}

docs.title: SQLiteMemoryStore
docs.text:
SQLiteMemoryStore(path: str | Path = ':memory:')

Single-owner store. Facts replace only the same (kind, key, scope, clock).

docs.title: visual
docs.text:
Evidence-linked visual reports for frozen-model planners.

Reports are fallible model interpretations, never simulator facts. The journal records that a model emitted a report, with its original confidence and frame citations intact. Retrieval keeps early cues and recent updates without replacing the append-only evidence history.

VisualReportMemory(journal: EventMemory, *, max_chars: int = 8000)

An episode-scoped, bounded prompt view over durable, unverified reports.

Frame IDs are monotonically assigned by the observation adapter. Only citations actually supplied to the model in the current request are accepted. No success flag, reward, task oracle, environment instance, or model-generated completion claim can advance a counter.

docs.title: app
docs.text:
Hylo playground: a local web UI over the existing system (FastAPI backend + React frontend).

hylo-playground --root runs --port 8765            # then open http://127.0.0.1:8765

Read-only pages go through the catalog API (hylo.catalog), never through other packages' internals. Actions go through public paths only: live episodes through the kernel and SafetyShield, components through the plugin registry, jobs and approval / rollback through the hylo command. Protected settings (safety, benchmark, trace, scoring) cannot be overridden from the UI. Binds to 127.0.0.1 by default; with --token every API call needs it.

Research sessions and code-agent runs (research.py) are read from their own files: the runs directory and any --sessions [LABEL=]DIR.

It is also the control plane for workcells and policy servers (control.py): --workcell name=url, --policy name=url, and per-role tokens (--role-token viewer=... operator=... approver=...).

docs.title: control
docs.text:
Control plane (S4): the playground backend as the operator's single entry point to workcells and policy servers.

It never sends actions. It lists workcells and policy servers, starts episodes on a workcell (choosing the policy endpoint), relays operator events (reset confirmation, verdicts, stop, e-stop, clearing a fault) and proxies a workcell's live event stream to the browser.

Roles, by token (--role-token viewer=... --role-token operator=... --role-token approver=...): - viewer: read everything, and press the e-stop (stopping is never gated behind a higher role); - operator: start episodes, reset / verdict / stop / clear a fault, live sandbox, jobs; - approver: everything, plus promote / roll back campaign versions. Without role tokens (and without --token) the local user has every role.

docs.title: live
docs.text:
Live sandbox: run one episode of any experiment config and stream it to the browser as it happens.

The episode runs through the unchanged kernel (EpisodeRunner, SafetyShield). A bus subscriber turns events into compact messages (camera frames as JPEG every step); the trace keeps every trace.image_every-th frame like any run, in runs/playground/live/, under split "playground", which no learner ever reads. Environment and agent are kept warm between episodes of the same configuration (loading a VLA takes tens of seconds).

User controls: task and seed from the benchmark, config overrides (protected scopes refused), an instruction override (the agent sees the user's text; the environment's task and success check are unchanged), stop.

docs.title: research
docs.text:
Research sessions and code-agent runs, read straight from their directories (plain JSON and JSONL files).

A research session directory holds log.jsonl (one record per turn, reset, submission and the end; images as PNG files under images/), submissions/sub-NN/ (solve.py, results.json), frozen/<name>/ (the sealed program: solve.py, program.json, artifact.json) and summary.json. Scene-builder runs keep their turns in turns.jsonl with solve.json / build.json, motion-studio runs in log.jsonl (records keyed by event) with summary.json, replay runs in agent_turns.jsonl with report.json. Each of those may hold MP4 videos.

Nothing here imports the code that wrote the files: the formats are read as data, and every field is optional. Sessions are found under the playground's runs directory and any extra roots (--sessions); a session id is its path relative to its root, prefixed with <label>: for an extra root. Files are only served from inside a discovered session directory, with a fixed set of extensions.

docs.title: online
docs.text:
Example online learner: the cross-entropy method over an agent's numeric parameters.

Each iteration samples a population of parameter vectors from a Gaussian, rolls each one out on the development split (the runner does that), keeps the elite fraction by score and refits the Gaussian to the elites. The sealed artifact holds the best parameters found; a LearningProposer turns them into a candidate, which the gate then judges on init states the search never saw.

proposer: {type: learn, params: {learner: examples.cem, online: true, python: <this venv>,
           params: {space: {kp: {path: params.kp, low: 0.1, high: 6.0}}, population: 6, iterations: 3},
           patch: {agent.params.kp: "{metrics.best.kp}"}}}

The same contract fits on-policy RL: policies() returns the current policy, update() reads the rollouts' traces (run_dir) and takes a gradient step, seal() writes the weights.

docs.title: policies
docs.text:
Policy plugins (group "policies"): one written from scratch, one composed from other registered policies.

  • examples.ik_reacher: a scripted chunk policy for MuJoCo planar reach, with seeded exploration noise.

  • examples.mixture: several policies behind one name. mode "sample": each seed picks one member (with weights), so steering's sample-and-select chooses among the members' proposals; mode "mean": the members' chunks averaged (an ensemble).

    agent: {type: steered, params: {sampler: {type: examples.mixture, params: {members: [...]}}, steering: {n_samples: 4, selector: medoid}}}
