docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deployment configures an agent or campaign version on a policy server and workcell. Validate the target robot, assets and runtime dependencies separately from simulation results or skill-library verification.

This page takes you from a simulated arm to a real one, and back to the recorded episodes on your workstation. A reference section follows the steps. Commands run from the workspace directory unless a step says otherwise.

Two services and a control plane split the work:

  • A policy server (hylo serve policy) runs an agent, usually on a GPU machine, and answers observations with action chunks.
  • A workcell (hylo serve workcell) runs next to the robot or simulator. It owns the environment, the episode loop with its safety shield, and the trace. It reaches the policy server over a WebSocket.
  • Studio (hylo playground) is the control plane. It starts episodes and relays operator input over HTTP. It never sends actions.

The workcell's runs are copied to the store on the workstation.

With clock: wall (step 2), the workcell handles a slow network on its own: if the policy server is slow, the arm holds its position, and if it stops answering, the watchdog ends the episode. An e-stop stays latched in the workcell until an operator clears it. Where these layers stop is on the safety page.

docs.title: 1. Simulated setup
docs.text:
Clone the deployments template next to the other repositories, once. Studio's web UI also needs a one-time build (installation).

git clone https://github.com/HyloAI/hylo-deployments-template.git deployments-template

Then run three processes, each in its own terminal:

uv run hylo serve policy --agent '{"type": "bringup.wave", "params": {"amplitude": 8}}' --port 8002
uv run hylo serve workcell --config deployments-template/workcells/sim_arm.yaml --port 8102
uv run hylo playground --repo bench --workcell sim-arm=http://127.0.0.1:8102 --policy wave=ws://127.0.0.1:8002/hylo
  • bringup.wave is not a task policy. It moves one joint in a small sine wave around the pose where the episode starts, amplitude degrees each way.
  • sim_arm is a simulated arm with five joints and a gripper, in degrees. It goes through the same LeRobot robot adapter as a real arm, with real_robot safety.
  • Studio opens at http://127.0.0.1:8765.

In Studio's Operator station, pick sim-arm and wave, and start an episode with the instruction wave. The sim_arm config asks for reset confirmation and a verdict, so the episode goes through every operator step:

  1. The workcell waits in awaiting_reset. Confirm the reset.
  2. The arm moves to its home pose, then waves until max_steps.
  3. The environment cannot judge success, so the workcell waits in awaiting_verdict. Give a verdict.

Without Studio, the same flow with curl:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8102/episodes -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"instruction": "wave", "max_steps": 120}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8102/operator -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"type": "reset_done", "by": "me"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8102/operator -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"type": "verdict", "verdict": "success", "by": "me"}'
curl -s localhost:8102/status

After the verdict, /status is back to idle and reports the episode:

"state": "idle", "last": {"status": "success", "steps": 120, "holds": 1, "chunks": 12, "safety_interventions": 0, ...}

The episode is in runs/workcell/workcell-sim-arm/.

docs.title: 2. Robot setup
docs.text:
The robot computer needs:

  • Hylo with the serve packages. Install hylo-core, hylo-serve and hylo-env-lerobot-robot (plus hylo-policy-openpi to reach an openpi policy server), for example as a subset of the repositories.

  • A venv for the robot SDK. It holds LeRobot with your robot's extras (lerobot[feetech] for SO-100/101), hylo-core and hylo-env-lerobot-robot. Register it as the robot runtime of this machine's execution profile:

    uv run hylo profile set-runtime robot --python ~/robot/.venv/bin/python

  • A calibrated arm. Calibrate it with LeRobot's own tools. The calibration is keyed by the robot id in the workcell config.

  • Your lab's deployments repository, created from deployments-template. Start from workcells/so101.yaml and set the serial port, the robot id, the cameras, the action limits and the home pose for your arm (deployments repository).

Set clock: wall on hardware

The default clock is virtual. With it, the episode loop does not pace itself to control_hz: it sends actions as fast as the robot's I/O returns. It blocks in each policy call and sends no commands while it waits, so the watchdog cannot fire. A stalled policy server ends the episode only when the call times out, after 600 s on the hylo protocol. On a real robot, always set runtime: {clock: wall} in the workcell config. The so101 and sim_arm templates already do.

Keep the robot's own limits (LeRobot's max_relative_target, torque limits) and a hardware e-stop within reach. The safety shield is not a certified safety function (safety).

The LeRobot robot adapter has run only with the simulated arm (plugin catalogue).

docs.title: 3. Policy server
docs.text:
On the GPU machine, serve the agent of an experiment config, or the promoted version of a campaign:

uv run hylo serve policy --config bench/examples/configs/libero10_steered.yaml --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --token $POLICY_TOKEN
uv run hylo serve policy --campaign bench/runs/evolve/libero10-steering --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --token $POLICY_TOKEN
  • --config serves only the config's agent. The workcell brings its own environment and safety settings.
  • --campaign serves the campaign's active version and follows promotions and rollbacks. It rebuilds the agent between sessions, never during one (campaigns).
  • The server checks compatibility when the workcell resets the episode, before any motion. It refuses the session if the agent does not fit the environment's spec: action space, control mode, cameras, state keys.
  • It serves one session at a time. A second client is refused.

The workcell config points at the server with policy: {url: "ws://gpu-box:8000/hylo", protocol: hylo}. Give the token per episode rather than in that config (security).

docs.title: 4. Workcell
docs.text:
Start the workcell on the robot computer, and point Studio at it and at the policy server:

uv run hylo serve workcell --config workcells/so101.yaml --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8100 --token $HYLO_TOKEN
uv run hylo playground --repo bench \
    --workcell so101=http://robot-host:8100#$HYLO_TOKEN --policy smolvla=ws://gpu-box:8000/hylo#$POLICY_TOKEN

An episode starts with a StartEpisode request to POST /episodes. It names either a task_id from the workcell's benchmark (with a seed), or a free-form instruction. With a task_id, an instruction changes only what the agent hears, not the task or its success check. policy overrides the configured endpoint.

A workcell moves through these states:

State When Leaves when idle no episode an episode is requested starting the environment and the policy connection are being set up setup ends; a setup failure returns to idle awaiting_reset require_reset_confirm is on, before the move to home the operator sends reset_done; stop ends the episode instead running the arm moves to home, then the episode runs the episode ends awaiting_verdict the environment cannot judge success and verdict_timeout_s is above 0 a verdict arrives, or verdict_timeout_s passes fault an e-stop is latched the operator sends clear_fault

Confirm the reset only when the path to the home pose is clear: the move to home does not pass through the safety shield. While an episode runs or a fault is latched, POST /episodes answers 409.

Operator events go to POST /operator:

Event Effect stop end the episode as safety_abort; the arm holds its measured position estop the same, and latch a fault: no episode starts until clear_fault clear_fault clear the latched fault reset_done the scene is reset; the episode may start verdict success, failure or partial, for an episode the environment could not judge

Studio's Operator station sends these events. Every Studio role can press the e-stop; the other events need the operator role (security).

docs.title: 5. Recordings
docs.text:
All episodes of a workcell go into one run, <output_dir>/workcell-<name>/. Unlike hylo run, which writes a new run each time, the workcell appends a trace per episode and updates evallog.json after each one. Replay, judges and Studio work on it like any run. Episodes get the split deployment, which no learner reads unless asked.

The operator's verdict becomes the episode's label (labels.success.by: operator:<by>); partial counts as failure. A workcell run scores unlabeled, safety_abort and error episodes differently from hylo run (episode statuses).

To bring the runs to the workstation, make the workcell's output directory the robot computer's store and pull from it:

uv run hylo store init runs                                  # on the robot computer, where output_dir lands
uv run hylo store pull robot-host:/path/to/runs              # on the workstation: new runs, and new episodes of runs it has

docs.title: Policy server
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning --agent JSON / --config FILE / --campaign DIR one required what to serve: an agent spec, an experiment config's agent, or a campaign's active version --port 8000 --openpi-inputs libero preset name, or a JSON mapping from openpi observation keys to observation fields

--host and --token are described on the security page. One server answers on several paths:

Path Wire format Clients /hylo JSON: the Hylo agent protocol (spec, reset, act, on_step, on_episode_end) workcells, remote.ws agents /openpi msgpack-numpy: openpi's protocol (metadata, then an observation dict in and {"actions": (H, A)} out) openpi clients (DROID, RoboArena, openpi's examples) /healthz HTTP liveness, no token needed /meta HTTP, JSON the served agent's spec

On /openpi the server only computes chunks. There is no safety shield and no compatibility check: the openpi client runs its own control loop and applies its own limits. openpi has no reset message, so the agent is reset on connect, when the prompt changes, or when the client sends {"reset": true}.

docs.title: Workcells
docs.text: See Workcell configuration for YAML fields, defaults, runtime settings and a complete example. Deployments repository explains how to keep those files.

docs.title: Workcell API
docs.text: Endpoint Body / reply Notes GET /healthz {"ok": "yes"} no token needed GET /status name, state, episode, last result, latched fault, run id, policy, split, runtime, tasks POST /episodes StartEpisode → {"task_id", "policy"} 409 while an episode runs or a fault is latched POST /operator OperatorEvent (type, by, verdict, note) → {"fault", "state"} 400 for an unknown or malformed event WS /events one JSON event per message observations (JPEG), actions, chunks, safety, operator events, done

docs.title: Develop a program
docs.text:
Write and run a task program using Hylo's perception, grasping and motion-planning tools. Start with the task, robot, observations and success conditions, then test the program across initial states.

code.program executes a hand-written or frozen solve(robot) program. code.llm writes and executes code one turn at a time during an episode. For policy and tool-calling alternatives, see Agents. For repeated development cases and frozen submissions, follow Program skills.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use the development workspace, with harness and bench installed. It includes hylo-manip, hylo-code-agents and hylo-tools. Camera-based tasks need an off-screen renderer. Robot models are downloaded into the asset cache on first use; a reference program needs no language model. code.llm and research additionally need a configured chat backend, such as a local Ollama endpoint or a supported API.

Start with a supported MuJoCo manipulation task. LIBERO uses a separate runtime. Check the adapter validation records before choosing another environment; an available adapter alone does not establish task success.

docs.title: Robot tools
docs.text:
The environment publishes a RobotSpec: arms, hands, cameras, frames and action layout. The robot facade provides tools over that contract:

Work Tools Observe and locate status, look, find, table, objects, box Choose a manipulation goal grasps, hand_grasps, grasp_at, place_at, Goal Plan and execute plan, run, together Check and inspect holding, carried, show

robot.run sends an action chunk back to the kernel. Every executed action passes the SafetyShield and is recorded. Tools use the robot contract; the environment retains the task's success predicate. See the toolkit API for parameters and return types.

Simulator segmentation is privileged perception. Keep it explicit in the environment config and compare runs with the same observation conditions. A result using segmentation is not a like-for-like comparison with an RGB-only policy.

docs.title: Run a program
docs.text:
From the workspace root, after configuring rendering:

uv run python harness/adapters/hylo-code-agents/examples/programs/run_programs.py \
    --suite manip --tasks pick_place --workers 1 --parallel 1 --out runs/strategy-pick-place

This evaluates the hand-written reference solve(robot) on the validation split, records traces, and writes results.json, results.md and generated experiment configs under the output directory. It demonstrates the toolkit; it is not evidence that a model independently discovered the strategy. Suites bimanual and humanoid use the same runner.

To develop your own program, use the generated config as a starting point. code.program takes source text in agent.params.source for experiments, or a sealed program in agent.params.artifact. Source text is the program itself, not a Python filename. Keep the benchmark and environment fixed while changing the strategy.

For a model that writes code during the episode, use agent.type: code.llm and a model specification in its params.

docs.title: Model tools
docs.text:
hylo tool exposes segmentation, depth, meshes, motion extraction and rendering. Each heavy model runs in a separate worker environment; the first call can install dependencies and download weights. Current mesh, hand and human tools have fallback backends because their primary models have access or registration requirements. The tools README records backends, licences and timings.

For experimental scene generation, replay and motion-authoring workflows, consult the validation records for supported conditions and known failures.

docs.title: Tool agents
docs.text:
code.llm and tools.llm use the same robot tools. code.llm writes Python blocks, which suits tasks a program can express in a few lines and keeps the code for reuse. tools.llm calls one tool at a time with JSON arguments; every action is refused or confirmed with a measured receipt before the model decides again, which suits models trained for tool calls and makes each step visible. See Tool-calling agents.

To try a task with another robot or in another scene first, build it as a world: 24 robot packs, cameras, people, goals checked with reason codes.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Inspect task success, steps, safety interventions and traces across more than one initial state. Record the robot, task, observation conditions and program version. Development successes do not establish generalisation; freeze the program and evaluate separately before making that claim.

For a first skill, compare the frozen implementation with the task's success and safety requirements. For an improved skill version, also compare it with the previous implementation. A promoted program can become a verified program skill for later code agents; deployment on a target workcell remains a separate check.

Programs execute in a restricted Python namespace in the host process. This is not operating-system isolation and does not limit memory. Read Security before running generated code.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:

  • Experiments: run a program under explicit task conditions.
  • Skills: retain and reuse verified capabilities.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Run a configured agent against specified tasks and initial states, then inspect the recorded outcomes and traces. Use development runs to iterate and separate validation runs to measure capability. An experiment config names the benchmark, environment, agent, timing and safety settings.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Commands on this page run from bench/, so runs land in the store registered during installation:

cd bench
uv run hylo run examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml

hylo run prints one line per finished episode on stderr, then a JSON summary on stdout:

[20] mujoco/planar_reach_random seed=10009 success (32 steps)
{
  "run_dir": "runs/mujoco-reach-validation-2342f91d706e83e9-5c6b71",
  "config_digest": "2342f91d706e83e9",
  "success_mean": 1.0,
  "safety_interventions_mean": 0.0,
  "steps_mean": 35.25,
  "n_episodes": 20,
  "n_scored": 20
}

n_scored counts the episodes that have a success value; success_mean is taken over those only.

Option Meaning --split SPLIT run another split of the benchmark (default: benchmark.split in the config) --set KEY=VALUE dotted-path override, value parsed as YAML; repeatable (--set agent.params.kp=0.1 --set workers=8) --output DIR where the run directory goes (default: the config's output_dir, runs)

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
A run directory is named <name>-<split>-<digest>-<6 hex> and contains:

File Content evallog.json run and benchmark ids, the agent's spec, aggregate results, and one sample per episode (task, seed, status, steps, scores, trace path) manifest.json the measured config and its digest, the git commit, Python, platform and package versions, and the resolved store ids episodes/<episode_id>.jsonl the episode's events. Large arrays (camera images, point clouds) are stored once in blobs/<sha256>.npy.

Each episode ends with a status:

Status When Success score success / failure the environment says so, or the episode reached the task's max_steps 1 / 0 safety_abort the safety shield or the operator ended the episode (safety) 0 error the agent failed, or the realtime watchdog fired none infra_invalid the environment faulted or the simulator diverged; not the policy's fault none unlabeled realtime mode only: the environment cannot judge success, and no operator verdict came 0

An unlabeled episode keeps that status in its trace and is recorded as failure in evallog.json. An operator's partial verdict also counts as failure.

A workcell run scores differently. There, unlabeled, safety_abort and error episodes have no success value, so the run's success_mean covers only success and failure episodes (deployment).

Read runs with hylo trace RUN_DIR [EPISODE_ID] or in Studio.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
schema_version: hylo.experiment/v0.1
name: mujoco-guarded
benchmark: {type: mujoco/reach-v0, split: validation}      # a benchmark plugin, its params, the split
env: {type: mujoco.planar_reach}                           # an environment plugin
agent: {type: baseline.planar_ik, params: {kp: 0.3}}       # an agent plugin
safety: {max_delta: 0.5, guards: [{type: norm_limit, params: {max_norm: 1.2}}]}
trace: {record_privileged: true, image_every: 1}
timing: {mode: sync}
seed: 0
workers: 8
output_dir: runs
Key Default Measured Meaning name required yes the experiment's name; starts every run directory name benchmark required yes {type, params, split}; split defaults to validation. params.protocol: rsi (a benchmark setting, not an evaluation protocol) selects the four campaign splits. env required yes, except env.remote {type, params, remote} agent required yes, except placement {type, params}; type is a plugin name or module:attr safety {} yes extra guards and limits (safety) trace record_privileged: true, image_every: 1 yes store privileged simulator state; keep camera images every N steps (0 = never) timing sync yes sync or realtime seed 0 yes tags () yes free labels workers 1 no parallel episode workers, each with its own environment and agent output_dir runs no where run directories go

The full schema is the experiment config schema. hylo schema experiment prints it as JSON Schema.

docs.title: Preflight checks
docs.text:
uv run hylo conformance examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml            # the environment against its contract
uv run hylo conformance examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml --agent    # and the agent (two full episodes)

--nondeterministic skips the same-seed comparison of the agent check. --spec-budget (default 2 s) limits how long spec() may take, which matters for remote environments. --split and --set work as in hylo run. What each check covers is in extending.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
One episode loop runs every episode, in benchmarks and on robots. In sync mode (the default) the world waits for each policy call. In realtime mode the robot keeps executing while the next chunk is computed. Actions for steps that already passed are dropped. An empty queue executes a hold action: the environment's hold_action, the last target for absolute control, or zero motion (gripper kept) for delta control.

Key Default Meaning mode sync sync or realtime clock virtual realtime only. virtual: simulated latency, deterministic; the loop blocks in each policy call. wall: a real control loop at control_hz, with the policy in a worker thread. Use wall on hardware. control_hz the environment's control rate of the realtime loop refill_steps 2 request the next chunk when this many queued actions remain adaptive_refill true or earlier, when the queue covers only the recent latency plus one step latency_s measured virtual clock only: a fixed inference latency per chunk instead of the measured one max_hold_steps 100 watchdog: the episode ends as error after more than this many hold steps in a row

Two more keys, require_reset_confirm and verdict_timeout_s, matter only on workcells (deployment).

uv run hylo run examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml \
    --set 'agent={type: policy, params: {policy: {type: examples.ik_reacher, params: {horizon: 16}}}}' \
    --set timing.mode=realtime --set timing.latency_s=0.1

A realtime episode records at its end how many hold steps it needed (holds) and how many chunks it requested (chunks). Protocols that score in realtime fix latency_s, because a measured latency depends on the machine and its load (protocols).

An agent that returns one action per call, such as baseline.planar_ik or temporal_ensemble, does not work in realtime mode with any latency: each action arrives after its step has passed, so the arm only holds until the watchdog ends the episode.

docs.title: Process placement
docs.text:
An environment or an agent can run in another process, with another interpreter. Name a runtime from this machine's execution profile, so the config stays the same on every machine:

EnvironmentAgent 
env:
  type: libero
  remote: {runtime: libero-sim}          # the simulator runs in the libero-sim venv

remote: {} runs the environment in a subprocess of the current interpreter (examples/configs/mujoco_reach_remote.yaml).

agent:
  type: remote
  params:
    ref: lerobot.steered                 # the agent plugin to build in the other process
    runtime: lerobot
    params: {repo_id: lerobot/smolvla_libero, steering: {n_samples: 1, seed_noise: true}}

python: and env: entries set the interpreter and extra environment variables directly, and override the runtime's. They tie the config to one machine, so prefer a runtime.

A component on another machine runs behind a WebSocket server, started in the component's own venv:

uv run hylo serve env libero --params '{"image_size": 256}' --port 8770
uv run hylo serve agent lerobot --params '{...}' --port 8771 --token-env HYLO_TOKEN

The config then uses {type: remote.ws, params: {url: "ws://host:8770"}} as the environment or the agent. Each connection gets its own component instance. --token-env names an environment variable that holds the token (security).

docs.title: Comparability
docs.text:
The config digest is a short hash of everything the experiment measures. Left out are where results go (output_dir), parallelism (workers), and where components run: env.remote, and a remote agent's runtime, python and env. A remote.ws component is the exception: its URL replaces the component in the config, so it is hashed and changes the digest. Changing any measured value changes the digest. timing is measured; a config that leaves it at the default (sync) has the same digest as one that omits it.

Two runs with the same digest used the same config. Compare them episode by episode only if both hold:

  • Every artifact id is pinned (artifact:<name>@<digest>). An unpinned id such as artifact:policy.flow enters the digest as written. If the artifact with that name is replaced in the store, the digest stays the same but the behaviour changes. The manifest records the full id each run actually used (store).
  • The code versions match. Code is not part of the digest. Compare the git commit and package versions in the two manifests.

docs.title: Learning
docs.text:
A learner turns recorded runs into an artifact: a sealed directory whose manifest (artifact.json) records what it is, a digest of its content, and where it came from: the learner, its parameters, and the runs it read. External data enters as runs too, so every artifact traces back to runs.

Task programs use a separate research session to produce a frozen artifact. Campaigns compare proposed changes before promotion.

docs.title: Run a learner
docs.text:
A learner job is a JSON file. Commands on this page run from bench/, so runs and artifacts land in the store you registered during installation.

examples/policies/jobs/flow.json
{"learner": "policy.flow", "inputs": ["runs/policies/demos"], "out": "runs/policies/artifacts/flow",
 "params": {"chunk": 8, "epochs": 300, "integration_steps": 10}}

Record demonstrations on a development split, then run the job:

cd bench
uv run hylo run examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml --split search \
    --output runs/policies/demos --set benchmark.params.protocol=rsi
uv run hylo learn examples/policies/jobs/flow.json
Output
{
  "out": "runs/policies/artifacts/flow",
  "kind": "policy_params",
  "role": "behaviour",
  "digest": "218d7147b2d05110",
  "splits": ["search"],
  "metrics": {"episodes": 80, "samples": 2858, "obs_dim": 8, "chunk": 8, "action_dim": 2,
              "train_flow_mse": 0.128}
}
Field Meaning learner a learners plugin name, or module:attr inputs run directories, directories to search for runs, or store ids (run:<id>) out the artifact directory this job seals splits the splits it may read (default search, search_val) params the learner's parameters

A finished job is not run again: if out already holds an artifact sealed by the same job, hylo learn skips it. A job that stopped halfway starts over.

Use --python when the learner's dependencies live in another venv, such as LIBERO's:

uv run hylo learn my-job.json --python envs/libero/.venv/bin/python

docs.title: Use an artifact
docs.text:
uv run hylo artifact runs/policies/artifacts/flow     # check the digest and sources, print the manifest
uv run hylo store ref runs/policies/artifacts/flow    # its store id: artifact:policy.flow@218d7147b2d05110

hylo artifact fails if the content no longer matches the digest or a source is a gate or held-out run. hylo store ref needs the directory to be inside this machine's store.

Configs name the artifact by its store id:

sampler: {type: policy.flow, params: {path: "artifact:policy.flow@218d7147b2d05110"}}

Keep the @digest (why).

docs.title: Data boundaries
docs.text:
By default a learner reads only search and search_val runs. It reads synthetic runs (produced inside a learned model) and external runs (ingested data) only when the job lists them in splits.

Gate and held-out runs are refused three times: when the job starts (asking for them fails, and a directory scan skips them), when the artifact is sealed, and in a campaign's stage-0 checks, for every artifact a candidate references. Who else reads which split: campaign splits.

docs.title: Artifact roles
docs.text:
Role Kinds Changes Trusted when behaviour action_memory, value_model, noise_policy, policy_weights, policy_params what the robot does the gate promotes a candidate that uses it instrument success_judge, progress_model, world_model what is measured or labelled it is calibrated against known outcomes proposal lesson_book, skill_library only what generators propose campaign outcomes, including gate results, curate it: lessons cited by promoted candidates gain credit, those cited by refuted ones lose it data dataset what learners can read its labels come from the source or a calibrated judge

The two trust paths are separate. A gate verdict never makes an instrument trusted, and calibration never activates a behaviour artifact.

A mutable artifact keeps changing after it is sealed, such as a lesson book a campaign is curating. Its digest is not enforced: hylo artifact and the stage-0 checks do not compare its content with the manifest.

docs.title: Calibrate judges
docs.text:
A success judge (an instrument) labels episodes from their traces when no simulator can, on a robot or in external data. Train one with judge.trace, then calibrate it on simulator runs:

judge-job.json
{"learner": "judge.trace", "inputs": ["runs/libero10"], "out": "runs/judges/l10-trace",
 "params": {"cameras": ["agentview", "wrist"]}}

uv run hylo learn judge-job.json
uv run hylo calibrate --judge '{"type": "judge.trace", "params": {"path": "artifact:l10-trace@<digest>"}}' \
    --runs RUN_DIR [RUN_DIR ...] --artifact artifact:l10-trace@<digest>

Calibration reads search and search_val runs by default (--splits) and compares the judge's scores with the simulator's outcomes. It reports AUC, Brier score, expected calibration error, and the lowest threshold that reaches the target precision (--target-precision, default 0.95), with the recall there.

The judge is ready to label when all three hold:

  • at least 50 episodes were scored;
  • the target precision is reachable;
  • the recall at that threshold is at least 0.3.

With --artifact, runs the judge was trained on are left out, and the report is stored in the judge's manifest, where hylo label reads it.

docs.title: External data
docs.text:
Demonstrations, videos and other robots' logs enter as ordinary runs with split external:<name>. Each is sealed as a data artifact that records its origin and licence. Data sources are datasources plugins.

spec.json
{"source": {"type": "video.frames", "params": {"root": "data/kitchen-videos"}},
 "name": "kitchen-videos", "licence": "CC-BY-4.0", "out": "runs/external",
 "image_every": 1, "assume_success": false}

uv run hylo ingest spec.json                       # --python VENV_PYTHON if the source needs another venv
uv run hylo label RUN_DIR --judge artifact:l10-trace@<digest>
uv run hylo contamination EXTERNAL_RUN_DIR --protected PROTECTED_RUNS_DIR

assume_success: true labels every episode a success on the source's authority. Otherwise an episode is a success only if the source says so.

hylo label refuses a judge that is not ready and labels only ingested runs the judge was not trained on. Episodes scoring at or above the calibrated threshold are labelled successes. The rest stay unlabelled, never failures. --threshold can raise the threshold but not lower it. Labels are written into the run's evallog.json, each marked by: judge:<digest>. No new artifact is made.

hylo contamination compares each external episode's initial state with the gate and held-out episodes of the same task under --protected (default runs). It prints a report and exits with code 3 when it finds a match. It does not block anything. Do not use matching external data to build anything gated on those states.

docs.title: Built-in learners
docs.text:
Learner Builds policy.knn, policy.bc, policy.flow, policy.tokens reference policies (policies) world_model.state a state world model, for policy.mpc and world-model pre-screening critic.chunk_value a chunk critic for critic steering judge.trace a success judge from traces lerobot.action_memory, lerobot.noise_prior action memories and noise priors for LeRobot steering lerobot.expert_iteration fine-tuned LeRobot weights from successful episodes

How far each is tested: plugin catalogue. To write your own: adding a learner.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Hylo is organised around Physical RSI, Worlds, Agents, Memory and Skills. Physical RSI is the improvement loop connecting the other four: agents act in worlds, memory carries experience forward, and skills make verified capabilities reusable. The operational terms used by commands and configs are listed below.

docs.title: Physical RSI
docs.text: Physical recursive self-improvement uses task outcomes to propose changes, verify their effects and carry adopted changes into later rounds. A campaign implements the comparison and promotion process; learning supplies new artifacts. Read Physical RSI for the loop and its boundaries, then Campaigns to run an improvement experiment.

docs.title: Worlds
docs.text: A world is a simulation built from a scene description with robots, objects, cameras and goals. It provides a place for agents to act and receive measured feedback. Benchmark environments provide fixed tasks for comparison; robot adapters connect execution to hardware. See Worlds.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: An agent decides actions from observations and instructions. It can run a policy, execute a program or let a model call typed tools. Policies, planners and memory are components an agent may use. See Agents to choose an approach.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Memory carries observations and experience into later decisions: spatial facts, successful action segments and lessons from previous attempts. Different memories have different write and retrieval rules; evaluation must respect their data boundaries. See Memory.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: A skill is a reusable task capability with stated applicability and evidence. Supported library records let agents reuse programs, recipes and other verified changes. Memory answers what was observed or learned; skills describe what can be applied to do a task. See Skills and the Skill library. Library support depends on the implementation and consuming agent.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
These terms name the mechanisms used to operate the five concepts. Follow the linked guides for their rules.

Execution: experiments, agents and records Term Meaning Experiment A config naming the benchmark split, environment, agent, safety and timing; each execution produces a run. See Experiments. Environment The simulator or robot interface supplying observations, actions and control rate. Agent The logic deciding actions, using a policy, program or model with tools. Policy A model or controller producing actions from observations. See Policies. Run The record of an execution: manifest, episode results and traces. Episode One attempt at a task from an initial state until termination. Trace The episode's event log: observations, proposed and executed actions, checks and outcomes. Safety shield The action checkpoint between the agent and environment. See Safety. Timing Whether simulation waits for inference (sync) or continues while it computes (realtime). See Timing. Digest A hash of measured config settings; it excludes most placement settings but includes a remote.ws URL. It does not cover code versions. See comparability. Development and reuse Term Meaning Robot skill A task capability under stated robot, scene and observation conditions, with implementation and evidence. Task strategy The task logic implemented by a policy, controller or program. Robot contract and tools The robot description and tools for perception, grasping, planning and execution. Program agent code.program executes a task program; code.llm writes code during an episode. See Programs. Research session Model-assisted program development on development cases, producing a qualifying frozen submission. See Program skills. Program skill A library record referencing a promoted program, its applicability and evidence. Coding-agent skill A SKILL.md instruction file teaching a software agent to operate Hylo. Improvement and evaluation Term Meaning Artifact A sealed derived result with a digest and provenance, such as weights, a memory bank or a program. See Learning. Campaign A process proposing changes, evaluating them and promoting at most one per cycle after its gate. See Campaigns. Learner A plugin producing an artifact from permitted data; the split guard refuses gate and held-out runs. Judge An instrument labelling outcomes without ground truth, calibrated against known outcomes. Generator and candidate A generator proposes candidate config changes; the YAML key is proposer. Protected settings cannot be changed by candidates. Split A named set of initial states. Campaigns use search, search_val, gate and heldout; see access rules. Gate The confirmatory paired test on the gate split, with regression and safety vetoes. Active version The campaign version recorded in active.json; manual approval delays activation. Activation alone does not deploy a robot. Evaluation protocol Fixed episodes, seeds, timing and scoring for comparable scorecards. A leaderboard ranks results under one protocol. See Benchmarking. Deployment and configuration Term Meaning Workcell The process next to a robot or simulator that runs episodes, records them and accepts operator commands. See Deployment. Policy server Serves an agent over the network; with --campaign, it follows the active version. Store id A run or artifact reference resolved to a local path on each machine. See Store. Runtime and execution profile A runtime names an interpreter and environment; the profile locates runtimes and the store on a machine. See Profiles. Plugin An installed implementation found through a registered name. See Extending.

  • Architecture: how the implementation connects these concepts.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
This page shows how to run your model in Hylo and which agent to wrap it in.

A policy is a model or controller used by an agent. This guide covers configuring policy agents; the agent overview also covers programs and typed tool calls.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Complete Installation. From bench/, run the shipped CPU controller:

uv run hylo run examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml

The command prints episode outcomes and a run directory. The quickstart explains the expected result. To use your own compatible policy, replace the agent block as shown below; artifact:policy.bc and artifact:policy.flow refer to artifacts you must first build or register.

docs.title: Policy and agent
docs.text:
A policy returns action chunks from an observation. An agent holds a policy and decides how to use its chunks (concepts). Each wrapper requires a compatible policy contract.

See Agents for the control modes and their relationship to programs and tool calls.

The optional simplememvla agent combines an episode video-history buffer with a compatible frozen video-conditioned checkpoint. It uses the released Panda controller interface and an explicit shared-batch runtime. Configuration, model requirements and verification limits are in Video memory.

docs.title: Agent types
docs.text:
Agent Runs the policy Key params policy chunk by chunk, with seeded noise policy, execution_steps, seed_noise, noise_scale temporal_ensemble every step, exponentially weighted over overlapping chunks (as in ACT) policy, m (weight decay; 0 = plain average) steered draws n_samples seeded chunks per decision and executes one, with optional recovery rules sampler, steering policytemporal_ensemblesteered 
agent:
  type: policy
  params:
    policy: {type: policy.bc, params: {path: "artifact:policy.bc"}}
    execution_steps: 8

agent:
  type: temporal_ensemble
  params:
    policy: {type: policy.bc, params: {path: "artifact:policy.bc"}}
    m: 0.01

agent:
  type: steered
  params:
    sampler: {type: policy.flow, params: {path: "artifact:policy.flow"}}
    steering: {n_samples: 4, selector: medoid}

sampler takes a policy spec, like policy in the other two agents.

A policy returns chunks of T actions. policy and steered execute the first execution_steps of each chunk (default: the policy's default_execution_steps(), capped at T). temporal_ensemble asks at every step.

Use policy to run a policy chunk by chunk. The other two fit these cases:

  • temporal_ensemble gives smoother motion from a deterministic chunk policy, at the price of one policy call per step. It returns one action per call, so it works only with sync timing (experiments).
  • steered suits stochastic policies (flow matching, diffusion), when you can afford n_samples calls per decision. Everything in steering is data, so a campaign can propose and gate changes to it.

steering keys:

Key Default Meaning n_samples 1 chunks drawn per decision (1 to 8; cost grows linearly on CPU) selector first first, medoid, or gripper_vote_medoid (keep the chunks that agree with the gripper majority, then take their medoid) noise_scale 1.0 scale of the initial noise execution_steps the policy's actions executed from each chunk seed_noise true derive the noise from seeds (see below) rules [] up to 4 recovery rules

A rule watches one feature and fires an action when the feature crosses a threshold:

steering:
  n_samples: 4
  selector: gripper_vote_medoid
  rules:
    - {name: unstick, feature: still_steps, op: ">=", value: 20, action: resample, params: {noise_scale: 1.5}}
    - {name: regrasp, feature: grasp_attempts, value: 3, action: backoff, params: {steps: 8, dz: 0.5}, max_fires: 1}
  • Features: still_steps, grasp_attempts, disagreement (spread between samples), steps. eef_key and gripper_key rename the state keys the first two read (default eef_pos, gripper_qpos).
  • Actions: resample (with params.noise_scale) and backoff (up along action dimension 2 and open the gripper; end-effector delta control only, such as LIBERO).
  • cooldown (default 30 steps) and max_fires (default 3 per episode) limit firing.

docs.title: Policy contract
docs.text:
A policy is a policies plugin with four methods:

class ChunkPolicy(Protocol):
    def spec(self) -> AgentSpec: ...
    def reset(self, ctx: EpisodeContext) -> None: ...
    def default_execution_steps(self) -> int: ...
    def sample(self, observation: Observation, seeds: list[int] | None, noise_scale: float) -> np.ndarray:
        """(N, T, A) action chunks in the environment's units, one per seed."""

Deterministic policies (regression, retrieval, scripted) ignore the seeds. Stochastic ones (diffusion, flow matching, sampled tokens) must take their randomness from the seeds only. Agents compute the seeds from the task, the chunk index and the sample index. So two agents compared on the same init state draw the same noise, which keeps paired comparisons fair.

uv run hylo plugin new policy NAME      # scaffold a policy package
uv run hylo plugin check policy NAME    # conformance: shape, finiteness, seed determinism

The adding a policy tutorial walks through one, and extending lists what the check covers.

docs.title: Reference policies
docs.text:
hylo-policies ships one small, weights-free implementation of each common policy family, in numpy only. You train them from your own runs and they are sealed as artifacts. They are not the published architectures at scale.

Plugin Family Idea (reference) Stochastic policy.knn retrieval nearest neighbours in observation space, averaged chunks (VINN) no policy.bc regression BC MLP from observation to an action chunk, MSE (BC with chunking) no policy.flow flow matching velocity field from noise to the chunk, Euler integration (pi0, SmolVLA action experts) yes policy.tokens tokenized actions each dimension binned, categorical heads, sampled (RT-1, OpenVLA-style) yes policy.mpc model-based planning cross-entropy method over action sequences in a learned world model (MPC) yes

Learners of the same names build policy_params artifacts from successful episodes. world_model.state builds the world model that policy.mpc plans in (learning).

docs.title: Train and evaluate
docs.text:
All at onceStep by step 
cd bench
uv run python examples/policies/compare.py    # data -> every learner -> mujoco-reach scorecards -> leaderboard (~3 min)

cd bench
uv run hylo run examples/configs/mujoco_reach.yaml --split search --output runs/policies/demos \
    --set benchmark.params.protocol=rsi                    # demonstrations, from a development split
uv run hylo learn examples/policies/jobs/flow.json           # a sealed policy_params artifact
uv run hylo store ls --kind artifact                         # its id: artifact:policy.flow@<digest>
uv run hylo run examples/configs/mujoco_policy_flow_steered.yaml
uv run hylo bench run mujoco-reach --name flow-steered \
    --policy examples/configs/mujoco_policy_flow_steered.yaml

The example uses the name-only id artifact:policy.flow. Pin its digest before comparing runs.

Compare two scorecards with hylo bench compare A.json B.json (an exact paired McNemar test) before reading a difference into them. The results of compare.py are on the leaderboard.

docs.title: Model adapters
docs.text:
LeRobot (SmolVLA, pi0, ...)openpi

The hylo-policy-lerobot adapter runs LeRobot policies on CPU, in the lerobot runtime that bench's LIBERO setup installs. It registers lerobot twice:

  • as a policy, for Hylo's agents (policy: {type: lerobot, ...}), with noise from Hylo's seeds;
  • as an agent (type: lerobot), which runs chunk by chunk, LeRobot's way, with unseeded noise.

The factories below wrap the policy in an agent for you:

Agent What it adds lerobot the policy, chunk by chunk lerobot.steered the steered agent: seeded noise, sample-and-select, recovery rules lerobot.critic_steered samples n_samples chunks and executes the one a learned chunk critic values most lerobot.memory_steered starts flow sampling from an action retrieved from its own successes (action memory) lerobot.noise_steered biases the initial noise towards noise that produced similar successful chunks 
agent:
  type: remote
  params:
    ref: lerobot.steered
    runtime: lerobot
    params: {repo_id: lerobot/smolvla_libero, num_threads: 4, steering: {n_samples: 1, seed_noise: true}}

openpi (hylo-policy-openpi) is an agent that calls an openpi policy server over WebSocket. Its params are url (default ws://127.0.0.1:8000) and an input preset (default libero). The plugin catalogue says how far it is verified.

SmolVLA (lerobot/smolvla_libero) on a LIBERO-10 task, every 10th camera frame of one episode.

Weight licences differ per checkpoint: PaliGemma-based pi0 and pi0.5 checkpoints are under the Gemma Terms of Use. The plugin catalogue lists each plugin's maturity and licences.

docs.title: Develop a program skill
docs.text: Improve an existing task program with a model, let a campaign evaluate the frozen candidate, and make a promoted program available to a later agent. The supplied example starts from a deliberately weak stacking program. Promotion depends on the results; a new model session may produce no qualifying candidate.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
You need the workspace, camera rendering and an Ollama endpoint serving gpt-oss:20b. The shipped campaign names that model and uses automatic approval in simulation. All commands below run from the workspace root and write under runs/campaign/. Use a fresh output directory for a new experiment; reusing an existing campaign directory can resume its state.

The model receives the parent's source and develops on three search cases. The campaign evaluates frozen programs as code.program, without model calls during their execution. The example uses simulator-provided observations; keep those conditions explicit when comparing agents. See the recorded case for its measured scope.

docs.title: 1. Develop
docs.text:
research.llm is a candidate generator for the ordinary campaign cascade. It can expose a code.program parent's source to the model, freeze a submission and propose it as a code candidate. The campaign owns the subsequent validation, paired gate, held-out report, approval and version registry.

uv run hylo evolve run harness/adapters/hylo-code-agents/examples/campaign/campaign.yaml
uv run hylo evolve status runs/campaign/campaign

The shipped example uses one cycle and automatic approval in simulation. Its output paths are relative to the working directory. Keep them consistent when resuming. For deployment, review approval and rollback and Security; an approval happens after candidate evaluation.

docs.title: 2. Verify
docs.text:
Inspect runs/campaign/campaign/cycle-01/cycle_report.json and the status printed above. A successful path has a promoted candidate and an active.json pointing to it. If no candidate passes, inspect the research session under runs/campaign/research/; do not derive or claim a verified program skill from an unsuccessful run.

The gate supports the comparison with this parent under the declared conditions. A held-out report is kept for review. For hardware use, configure approval: manual before running the campaign and validate the target setup.

docs.title: 3. Reuse
docs.text:
Derive a skill-library record from the promoted candidate. It binds the name, version, applicability, sealed program and gate evidence:

uv run hylo research skills runs/campaign/campaign --library runs/skills --family stack

Configure a later code.llm agent with agent.params.skills: runs/skills. Verified program skills are retrieved by instruction similarity and made available as skills.<name>(robot). A skill references the sealed program and its gate evidence; it is not a new trained checkpoint. Applicability and validation are limited to the recorded robot, task and observation conditions. Revalidate when those conditions change.

Create runs/stack-skill-reuse.yaml with this complete configuration, keeping the model endpoint available:

schema_version: hylo.experiment/v0.1
name: stack-skill-reuse
benchmark: {type: mujoco/manip-v0, split: validation, params: {tasks: [stack], validation: 3}}
env: {type: mujoco.panda_table, params: {cameras: [front, side, wrist], segmentation: true}}
agent:
  type: code.llm
  params:
    model: {backend: ollama, model: gpt-oss:20b, vision: false, reasoning_effort: low}
    skills: runs/skills
trace: {record_privileged: false}
output_dir: runs/skill-reuse

uv run hylo run runs/stack-skill-reuse.yaml

Inspect the printed run directory with hylo trace. Check whether the agent retrieved and actually called the skill, as well as the task verdict. Retrieval does not force the model to use a skill. These validation episodes are development observations; they are not a new paired estimate of the skill's benefit.

docs.title: Inspect sessions
docs.text:
uv run hylo playground --repo . --sessions research=runs/research

The Research page reads recorded sessions: turns, code, output, camera views, submissions, frozen source, usage and cost. It also links campaign candidates when their evidence names the session. It does not provide an interactive model-development editor or start research sessions from this page.

A research session's turns, submissions and frozen program; the campaign that promoted it; the verified program skill in the library.

docs.title: Standalone development
docs.text:
Prepare the tools, environment and model backend. From the workspace root, the existing stacking experiment can be used as a development environment:

uv run hylo research harness/adapters/hylo-code-agents/examples/campaign/experiment.yaml \
    --model ollama:gpt-oss:20b --dev 3 --budget turns=30,resets=6,submits=3 \
    --out runs/research/stack

This command requires that model at the configured Ollama endpoint. It uses search cases and does not automatically pass the experiment's parent program to the model. A campaign's research.llm generator can pass the parent program in the campaign workflow above. The command returns a nonzero status if no program qualifies for freezing.

During a session:

  • robot is the manipulation toolkit on the live episode.
  • reset(case) starts another development attempt and reports the previous outcome.
  • submit(source) validates a program and evaluates it on the development cases without model calls.
  • finish() ends development; turn, reset, submission, token and cost budgets can also end it.

Inspect summary.json, log.jsonl, the submissions/ directory and, when one qualifies, frozen/. A frozen program records its source, entry point, artifact digest and provenance. It has not been promoted merely by being frozen.

docs.title: Evaluate a program
docs.text:
hylo research --evaluate search_val evaluates after the session; --with-parent also evaluates the configured agent for a paired comparison. Post-session outcomes are not fed back into that session's model. Evaluation can also be run later with code.program and its sealed artifact.

Use development and validation results while iterating. Reserve gate and held-out states for a predeclared decision and final report. Once you use a result to choose or edit a program, it is no longer independent evidence for that choice. A standalone --evaluate command does not run the campaign promotion protocol.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Whenever Hylo runs the episode loop (in hylo run, benchmarks, campaigns, the Studio live sandbox and workcells), every action passes through the safety shield before it reaches the environment. The episode loop builds the shield from the environment's spec and the experiment's safety: config. Agents never see or build it.

The shield does not cover two cases:

  • When hylo serve policy answers an external openpi client on /openpi, Hylo only computes action chunks. The client runs its own control loop and applies its own limits (deployment).
  • A config can load any Python code by module:attr. The shield checks actions, not the code that produces them (security).

Not a certified safety function

The shield is a software layer. On a real robot, keep the robot's own limits (for example LeRobot's max_relative_target and torque limits) and a hardware e-stop within reach.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
One checkpoint, owned by the loop. Actions come from many sources: policies, language models, recovery rules, campaign candidates, hold actions. They all pass the same shield, and the shield belongs to the episode loop, not to any agent. Letting a benchmark or a model framework own the loop instead would leave safety and timing to code Hylo does not control.

An order that cannot be undone by configuration. The finite check comes first, because a NaN cannot be repaired. The bounds clamp comes last, so no configured guard can push an action out of the action space. Guards added in a config sit in between: they can make an action safer, never loosen the mandatory limits.

Correct in simulation, stop on a robot. In simulation a small correction is recorded and the episode goes on, without the rest of the agent's plan, which no longer matches what will happen. On a real robot any intervention ends the episode: a policy that had to be corrected once is not one to keep running on hardware.

Safety runs where the robot is. On a workcell the shield runs in the process next to the robot, so a network fault between the policy server and the robot cannot bypass it.

Improvements cannot buy their score with safety. Campaign candidates may not change the safety settings, and the gate vetoes a candidate that needs noticeably more interventions than its parent.

Every review is evidence. Each review is a trace event with the proposed and the approved action and the reason, and interventions are counted in every score, so safety is measured as well as enforced.

docs.title: Action checks
docs.text:
• Mandatory guards. A NaN or infinite action aborts the episode. The bounds clamp runs last, so no guard can push an action out of the environment's action space.
  • Rotations. If the action space uses quaternions or rot6d, the bounds check clamps nothing. Any out-of-bounds dimension aborts the episode, even a gripper slightly over its limit, and the clip tolerance does not apply.
  • Environment guardrail. An environment that declares a workspace gets a workspace guard, always on. It zeroes delta-position components that would move the controlled point further outside the workspace.
  • Configured guards run in between, in the order given.

Hold actions, which the episode loop executes when no policy action is ready, pass through the shield too. Every review is recorded in the trace as a safety.review event: the proposed and approved actions, whether the action was modified, and why.

docs.title: Interventions
docs.text:
A guard that changes an action makes a safety intervention. The rest of the agent's planned chunk is discarded, because the plan no longer matches what will happen. A bounds clip within clip_tolerance (default 0.05) is not an intervention: it is recorded in the review, and the chunk is kept.

These events end the episode at once as safety_abort: a non-finite action, an out-of-bounds rotation, a hold under absolute control with no target to hold, an intervention on a real robot (below), and an operator stop or e-stop. A watchdog abort ends it as error (episode statuses).

The episode's safety_interventions score counts the modified actions, plus one if the episode ended in any of these aborts, the watchdog included. Campaigns compare this score in their safety veto (below).

An environment that declares itself a real robot (real_robot in its spec) changes the rules. The clip tolerance becomes 0, and any intervention ends the episode as safety_abort.

After any abort, the watchdog included, the loop calls the environment's stop(). Its effect depends on the environment plugin. The LeRobot robot adapter commands the arm's current measured position.

docs.title: Configure guards
docs.text:
safety:
  max_delta: 0.5                 # shorthand for a delta_limit guard
  clip_tolerance: 0.05
  guards:
    - {type: norm_limit, params: {max_norm: 1.2}}
    - {type: keep_out, params: {state_key: eef_pos, low: [0.3, -0.1, 0.0], high: [0.5, 0.1, 0.3], action_dims: [0, 1, 2], margin: 0.02}}

Built-in guards:

Guard Params Effect delta_limit max_delta (scalar or per dimension) rate limit: each action stays within max_delta of the previous one norm_limit max_norm, dims (default: all) scales the selected dimensions down so their Euclidean norm stays within max_norm (a speed limit) keep_out state_key, low, high, action_dims, margin when the next step would land inside the box (grown by margin), zeroes the delta components that move into it or deeper into it workspace state_key, low, high, action_dims the workspace guard, configured explicitly

keep_out adds the action to the position in state_key. So it only works when the action is a delta of that position, in the same units. It does not protect a box under joint-space or absolute control, such as the SO-101 template.

Guard plugins from other packages work the same way (extending).

docs.title: Robot operation
docs.text:
On a robot, three layers act, each with its own job:

Layer What it does Safety shield Reviews every action. Because the environment sets real_robot, any intervention aborts the episode. Episode loop With clock: wall, holds the arm when the policy is late, and ends the episode as error after more than max_hold_steps holds in a row (the watchdog; runtime.max_hold_steps in a workcell config). Workcell Gives the operator stop, a latched e-stop that blocks new episodes until cleared, reset confirmation and verdicts (deployment).

Hold and watchdog need clock: wall

On the default virtual clock, the loop blocks in each policy call and sends no commands while it waits. The watchdog cannot fire during that wait. A stalled remote policy ends the episode only when its call times out (600 s by default for a remote.ws policy), as error, without calling stop(). Set clock: wall on hardware (deployment).

The move to the home pose at the start of an episode does not pass through the shield. The LeRobot robot adapter interpolates to home in small steps and clips each step to the action box only. Confirm the reset only when the path to home is clear.

Keep-out zones and limits for a cell belong in the lab's deployments repository.

docs.title: Campaign protection
docs.text:
A campaign proposes changes to an experiment config as patches. It rejects any candidate whose patch touches one of these top-level keys:

safety, benchmark, trace, scorers, env, evolution, schema_version

Everything else can change. In particular:

  • agent is not protected. A patch can replace the agent, including with any module:attr.
  • timing is not protected. A patch can raise timing.max_hold_steps and so loosen the watchdog.

The gate's safety veto rejects a candidate whose mean safety interventions per episode exceed the parent's by more than max_safety_increase. The default, 1.0, lets a candidate need up to one more intervention per episode than its parent. Set it in the campaign's top-level protocol: block, which holds the gate settings (campaigns).

docs.text:

  • Deployment: bring a workcell up, first without hardware.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Who can make Hylo do what, over the network or through a config, and how to deploy it safely. This page is the reference for tokens and Studio roles. Robot limits are on safety.

A config is code

A config can name a component by module:attr instead of a plugin name, and Hylo imports and calls it with the config's params. So a config, a --set override or a campaign patch can run any importable Python function, as the user running Hylo. Treat everyone who can submit a config as someone with a shell on that machine.

docs.title: Access boundaries
docs.text:
Every service binds to the loopback interface unless you pass --host 0.0.0.0. No service terminates TLS or manages user accounts, so tokens travel in clear text over http:// and ws://. Without a token, anyone who can reach the port can do everything the last column lists.

Service Default bind Token Anyone who passes the check can hylo serve policy 127.0.0.1:8000 --token: Authorization: Bearer <token>, or openpi's Api-Key <token>. /healthz is open; /meta, /hylo and /openpi need the token. get action chunks from the served agent and read its spec hylo serve env, hylo serve agent 127.0.0.1:8765 --token-env NAME reads the token from an environment variable: Authorization: Bearer <token>. /healthz is open. drive the component: step the simulator, or get actions from the agent. The component is fixed when the server starts; clients cannot choose what is loaded. hylo serve workcell 127.0.0.1:8100 --token: Authorization: Bearer <token> on HTTP, ?token=<token> on /events. /healthz is open. start episodes on the robot, send operator events, watch the live stream, and read /status, which includes the configured policy endpoint and its token hylo playground (Studio) 127.0.0.1:8765 --token, or role tokens with --role-token: x-token header or ?token= depends on the role (below)

Only hylo serve env and hylo serve agent read the token from an environment variable. hylo serve policy, hylo serve workcell and hylo playground take it on the command line, so it shows in the process list of that machine.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Keep services on loopback. Reach them through an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 8100:127.0.0.1:8100 robot-host) or a reverse proxy that terminates TLS and authenticates users. Use wss:// and https:// through that proxy.
  2. Set a token on everything that leaves loopback. Use one token per service, so that revoking one does not stop the others. Keep tokens out of repositories.
  3. Give Studio role tokens whenever more than one person can reach it.
  4. Install plugins you trust, and accept configs only from people you would give a shell. A plugin is Python code that runs with your permissions, and Hylo has no allowlist for module:attr. hylo plugins lists what is installed and from which package.
  5. Know what manual approval protects. It controls promotion, not execution: by the time a candidate waits for approval, the campaign has already run its config, including any module:attr its patch names. The protected keys (safety) do not restrict which components a patch names.
  6. Check how third-party checkpoints are loaded. Hylo's own formats are JSON, .npy and .npz. Hylo never unpickles them and refuses object dtypes. A learner or adapter that loads third-party checkpoints follows that library's rules, for example PyTorch's torch.load.

docs.title: Generated code
docs.text:
code.llm, code.program and research submissions use AST validation and a restricted Python namespace. Imports, private attributes and file operations are restricted, and a watchdog interrupts Python execution. The program runs in a thread in the host process: this is not an operating-system jail, memory is not limited, and a call blocked in C code can stop only when it returns. For untrusted programs, use a separately isolated environment with bounded resources. The SafetyShield checks robot actions; it is not host-process isolation.

Campaign approval controls promotion after evaluation. It does not prevent a candidate from executing during evaluation. Sealed program artifacts should be immutable and digest-pinned. Current validation has known gaps: a manifest marked mutable bypasses the digest check, and the code-candidate check does not bind an arbitrary agent configuration to the actual referenced program. Treat configs and candidates as trusted inputs until those checks are tightened; do not describe the current gate as a host-code security boundary.

docs.title: Worlds and MCP
docs.text:
• hylo mcp serves the world tools over stdio to the program that started it: whoever controls that agent can edit stages, run robots and write exports under the stage's output folder. It opens no network port.
  • The Studio's World page starts hylo world chat subprocesses with the configured model; give it a role token when the port is reachable by others.
  • Pretrained policies are never deserialised by a general unpickler: their tensors are read with a reader that knows only tensor rebuilding and refuses any other object, and they run with numpy.
  • Robot models and policy files are fetched from pinned commits and checked file by file against recorded digests; a changed cached file is refused.

docs.title: Studio roles
docs.text:
Studio checks the token on every API call and maps it to a role:

  • With no --token and no --role-token, anyone who can reach the port has every role, including approver.
  • The token given with --token has the approver role.
  • Each --role-token ROLE=TOKEN adds a token for that role.
Role Can viewer read everything, watch workcell streams, and press the e-stop of a workcell (the e-stop is never gated behind a higher role; a plain stop needs the operator role) operator everything a viewer can, plus run live sandbox episodes, start jobs (run, evolve, learn with any --python interpreter, calibrate), start workcell episodes, and send every operator event approver everything an operator can, plus approve a campaign's pending candidate or roll back its active version

Jobs and live sandbox episodes take configs and overrides, so the operator role can run code on the Studio machine. Give it only to people you would give a shell to.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
These are current behaviours to plan around:

  • The workcell compares tokens with a plain string comparison. The policy server and the hylo serve env and hylo serve agent servers use a constant-time comparison.
  • The workcell's /status returns the policy endpoint from its config, token included. Studio shows that status to every role, viewers included. Give the policy token per episode (in the StartEpisode request, or with Studio's --policy NAME=URL#TOKEN) rather than in the workcell config.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Reuse a task implementation with its applicability, version and verification evidence. A skill can supply a program, a sequence of tool calls, a plan or a change to an agent.

docs.title: Reuse paths
docs.text: You want to Start here Develop a program and reuse it in later tasks Program skills Build a library and configure a consuming agent Skill library Reuse tool calls after matching goal failures Recipe skills

docs.title: Representation
docs.text:
A library record connects four things: an implementation, the conditions in which it applies, a version and the evidence supporting its status. Its body can hold a configuration change, subgoal templates, a reference to a sealed program or a sequence of tool calls. This makes a useful result reusable without asking a model to rediscover the same procedure from an earlier conversation.

The consuming component determines what can be applied. A skill agent can adjust steering or recovery rules for an episode; a code agent can call a program; a role campaign can offer a recipe after a matching goal failure. A weights change is evaluated as a campaign candidate. These paths share library concepts, but each needs its own compatible execution mechanism.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Define the task, robot, observations and success conditions.
  2. Develop an implementation and evaluate it beyond its development cases.
  3. Add it to the library with the evidence required by its reuse path.
  4. Retrieve it for matching tasks and revalidate when the conditions change.

Program skills require a campaign promotion gate. Recipe skills require a successful replay without a model; that replay checks task success and does not establish a paired statistical improvement.

docs.title: Evidence and status
docs.text:
A newly proposed skill is retained as a candidate. Passing the applicable gate or replay makes it verified; rejection can refute it, and an inconclusive improvement remains proposed. A promoted program that later fails revalidation can be deprecated. Only verified entries are eligible for application. Failed entries remain available as evidence of what was tried, rather than disappearing and being proposed again without context.

Freezing preserves an implementation. Verification supports its stated scope. Deployment configures an agent on a server and workcell and requires target validation. A verified library entry does not mean that a robot is running it.

docs.title: Retrieval and execution
docs.text:
Matching uses the task's instruction, tags, environment or goal-failure reasons, depending on the skill kind. For example, a role campaign can retrieve a recipe when a new task fails the same checks as the task that produced it. Program skills are ranked by instruction and description similarity; the current retrieval uses word overlap. Matching suggests applicability, so new robots, sensors or task conditions still need validation.

Before a program is offered to a code agent, its source is read back, its digest is compared with the recorded version and its code is checked against the execution restrictions. The model receives callable functions with descriptions and preconditions. This separates selecting a known implementation from generating new task code.

The skill agent applies steering, recovery and plan changes for the current episode and restores the wrapped agent afterwards. Applications and outcomes are recorded so users can inspect which skill influenced a result. During evaluation the library is frozen: reuse can change an episode's behaviour without silently learning a new shared skill from that episode's score.

docs.title: Skill types
docs.text: “Robot skill” names a task capability. A program or recipe skill is a library record referencing an implementation and evidence. A coding-agent skill is a SKILL.md instruction file for a software agent operating Hylo. Policies and controllers can implement robot capabilities, but the library does not wrap every policy in a common skill format. See the supported kinds.

docs.title: Memory and skills
docs.text: Memory supplies earlier observations and experience; skills supply something an agent can apply or execute. A remembered location informs a decision. A retrieved sorting program supplies the behaviour.

docs.title: Store
docs.text:
The store holds runs and artifacts referenced by experiments, campaigns and skill-library records.

Configs name runs and artifacts by id, not by path, so the same config works on every machine. Each machine has one store: a directory tree that maps ids to local paths. It protects entries that other entries still name from deletion, and copies entries between machines.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Installation registers bench/runs as the store, and commands on this page run from bench/:

cd bench
uv run hylo store init runs                # make this directory the store, recorded in the profile
uv run hylo store where                    # the store in use
uv run hylo store ls                       # every run and artifact, by id
uv run hylo store ls --kind artifact --json

--root DIR selects another store for one command. Profiles gives the lookup order.

Workcell output_dir and campaign out_dir are relative to the working directory. Make the directory they write to your store root, or a directory inside it.

docs.title: Ids
docs.text:
Id Names run:<run_id> a run (a directory with evallog.json); run ids end in a random suffix, so they are unique across machines artifact:<name>@<digest> a sealed artifact (a directory with artifact.json): its manifest name and content digest artifact:<name>@<prefix> the same, with a digest prefix of at least 8 hex characters artifact:<name> allowed only while exactly one artifact has that name 
uv run hylo store ref runs/policies/artifacts/flow      # -> artifact:policy.flow@218d7147b2d05110
uv run hylo store show artifact:policy.flow             # entry, local path, what it was built from, referrers

An id that does not resolve says why: not found, ambiguous, or removed (messages).

docs.title: Artifact references
docs.text:
sampler: {type: policy.flow, params: {path: "artifact:policy.flow@218d7147b2d05110"}}
  • An id with a digest pins the artifact's content in the experiment digest. A name-only id does not: if the artifact is replaced, the experiment digest stays the same. Pin with @digest whenever runs must be comparable.
  • Ids become this machine's paths only when a component is built, after the digest is taken. A plugin still receives a path.
  • The run's manifest.json records every id the config used, with the full id and the local path (artifacts:). A name-only id is pinned there, after the fact.

docs.title: Deletion
docs.text:
uv run hylo store rm run:<run_id>
uv run hylo store rm artifact:old-critic@1a2b3c4d --force --reason "superseded"

hylo store rm refuses while another entry refers to the one you delete, and lists what does. These references count:

  • an artifact refers to the runs and artifacts it was built from;
  • a campaign refers to every run and artifact its archive or promotion ledger names.

The store knows only the references in its index. A config file or a script that names an id does not protect it.

--force deletes anyway. Either way a tombstone in <root>/.hylo-store/tombstones.jsonl records what was removed, when, why, and what referred to it. A later lookup of that id says it was removed instead of "not found".

Warning

Do not delete run directories by hand. An artifact's provenance or a campaign's archive may still name them.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text:
uv run hylo store pull robot-host:/home/lab/runs                        # runs recorded on the robot computer
uv run hylo store push gpu-box:/data/runs artifact:policy.flow@218d7147 --with-sources
uv run hylo store push /mnt/backup/runs --dry-run                       # what would be copied
Option Meaning LOCATION PATH or HOST:PATH (ssh and rsync) IDS ... what to copy (default: everything) --with-sources also copy what the selected artifacts were built from --dry-run print the plan --remote-command the hylo command on the other machine (default hylo)

The other side is listed with its own hylo store ls --json, so hylo must be on the remote machine's non-interactive ssh PATH. In a uv workspace it usually is not: pass, for example, --remote-command 'uv run --project /path/to/workspace hylo'.

Sealed artifacts are never copied again or overwritten. If the same path holds a different entry on the other side, that is a conflict, and nothing is copied. Runs and mutable artifacts, such as lesson books, are brought up to date.

Push and pull have been tested between local stores. Transfers over ssh have not been tested.

docs.title: Import runs
docs.text:
An artifact built before manifests existed can be sealed in place, with the runs it was built from:

uv run hylo store adopt runs/memory/my-action-memory --kind action_memory --role behaviour \
    --source run:<run_id>

--source can be repeated. The sources are recorded as you state them. Hylo refuses a gate or held-out source, but it cannot check that your list is complete.

Without any --source, the provenance is recorded as unknown. Such an artifact can still be used in experiments, but a campaign refuses it at stage 0 as a behaviour artifact in a candidate, because a leak of gate or held-out data cannot be ruled out.
