docs.title: Studio
docs.text:
Studio is Hylo's web UI. It shows research sessions, runs, campaigns and artifacts, and it is the control plane for workcells. Start it with hylo playground. It runs the same hylo commands a person would type, with the same checks, and talks to workcells through the workcell API. It never sends actions to a robot.

Use these views to inspect the robot-skill lifecycle: Research shows development, Runs and A/B arena show execution and validation, Self-improvement shows candidate versions, Experience shows skill-library records and artifacts, and Operator handles deployed execution. These remain separate views over the current records.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Build the web UI once first (installation). Until then, Studio answers "frontend not built". Then start Studio from the workspace directory:

uv run hylo playground --repo bench          # http://127.0.0.1:8765
Option Default Meaning --repo DIR . the working directory: Studio lists its examples/configs and examples/evolve, and runs jobs in it (for example a bench checkout) --root DIR runs the runs directory, relative to --repo --workcell NAME=URL[#TOKEN] none a workcell to operate; repeatable --policy NAME=WS_URL[#TOKEN] none a policy server endpoint; repeatable --sessions [LABEL=]DIR none another directory with research sessions or code-agent runs, relative to --repo; repeatable

hylo playground --help lists the rest; tokens are under access.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page What it shows and does Console runs, campaigns and artifacts at a glance, with recent activity Live sandbox one episode of any experiment config, streamed frame by frame Operator station episodes on a workcell with a chosen policy server; reset, verdicts, stop, e-stop Runs & replays every recorded run, per-task success, and episode replay A/B arena two runs compared, paired on task and init state Self-improvement campaigns: cycles, candidates, gate statistics, the promotion ledger; approve or roll back Research research sessions and code-agent runs: every turn's text, code, output and images, submissions, the frozen program, usage and cost Experience skill libraries, lesson books, action memories, and sealed artifacts with provenance and calibration Jobs hylo run, hylo evolve run and hylo calibrate in the background, with their logs World stages and the worlds built from them: a view to orbit, actions and checks by hand, chat sessions with a model

docs.title: Live sandbox
docs.text:
Runs one episode of any experiment config through the episode loop and its safety shield, streamed as it happens. You choose the task and init state from the benchmark's splits, change config overrides, and give the agent a different instruction. The environment's task and success check stay the same. The environment and the agent stay loaded between episodes of the same config.

The sandbox refuses overrides of safety, benchmark, trace, scorers, evolution and schema_version. This list differs from what campaigns protect: it does not include env (safety). Any other override is accepted, including agent.type=module:attr, which runs arbitrary code. That is why the sandbox needs the operator role.

Live episodes are saved under runs/playground/live/<run_id> with the split playground, which learners do not read by default.

For a step-by-step illustration, watch the recorded AI robot-control demo: an English stacking instruction, model tool calls, grasp and place motions, and the task verdict. This is a presentation of a recorded episode; the Live sandbox recording shows how to launch an agent in Studio.

docs.title: Operator station
docs.text: Operates a workcell (--workcell) with a policy server (--policy): start episodes, follow the live stream, confirm resets, give verdicts, stop, e-stop and clear faults. What each event does is in deployment, with a bring-up without hardware.

docs.title: Runs & replays
docs.text: Lists every run under the runs directory with its benchmark, split, agent, success and episodes, filtered by split or text. Opening an episode replays it from its trace: camera frames, executed actions, chunk boundaries, safety interventions, and the success judge's progress estimate along the episode. The judge is set with --judge. By default it is the LIBERO-10 trace judge, if it is in Studio's runs directory.

docs.title: A/B arena
docs.text: Two runs of the same split, paired on task and init state, with the same one-sided exact McNemar test as hylo bench compare (compare two scorecards), plus side-by-side replays of the pairs where one run succeeded and the other failed.

docs.title: Self-improvement
docs.text: Every campaign under the runs directory: its cycles, the candidates with their hypotheses, the gate statistics, vetoes, the promotion ledger and the active version (campaigns). A candidate that passed the gate and waits for approval can be approved here, which runs hylo evolve approve. The active version can be rolled back with a reason, which runs hylo evolve rollback. Both need the approver role.

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
Use this page to inspect strategy development records. Start sessions through the research CLI; this page does not provide an interactive authoring editor.

Lists every research session under the runs directory, and the scene-builder, motion-studio and replay runs under each --sessions directory, with the model, task, best development score, turns, tokens, cost, wall time and why the session stopped. Opening one shows:

  • the timeline: for each turn, the model's text and reasoning, the code it ran, the printed output or error, and the images it was shown; resets, submissions and tool calls in between;
  • a usage panel: prompt tokens (and the cached part) and model latency per turn, the turns that submitted, and the totals;
  • the submissions, each with its outcome, steps and printed output per development case, and its source;
  • the frozen program: its source, digest and provenance;
  • a link to the campaign candidate the program became, found through the candidate's evidence.session; the campaign page links back.

Studio reads the session files directly (log.jsonl or turns.jsonl, summary.json, submissions/, frozen/), so a session that is still running or was interrupted shows what it has so far. It serves files only from inside a session directory, and only images, videos and text.

docs.title: World
docs.text:
Watch the full English demo · 2:10. Recorded AI session replay; waits are shortened.

Lists the stages under runs/world/stages (create one from the page), and for a stage:

  • Scene view: orbit by dragging, zoom with the wheel, choose Perspective, Top or Front, fit the scene, save a snapshot or enter fullscreen. Build world compiles the newest stage revision;
  • Chat: a message starts hylo world chat in the background, or goes to the inbox of a running session. Read model messages and expand grouped tool activity, including failures; scene changes update the view;
  • Scene: search the object collection, filter robots, inspect an object's position and focus the camera on it;
  • Controls: run any world action or goal check on the current generation and inspect the returned result.

Sessions are written to runs/world/sessions/<stage> and can be followed with hylo watch.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text: Starts hylo run, hylo evolve run or hylo calibrate (and hylo learn, through POST /api/jobs) as a local subprocess in --repo, with its log in runs/playground/jobs/<id>.log. Jobs start as soon as you submit them; they are not queued.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Studio binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. Without --token or --role-token, anyone who can reach the port has every role, including approver. Roles, tokens and what each role can do are on the security page.

docs.text:

  • Tool-using agents: what research sessions are.
  • Worlds: what the World page builds and runs.

docs.title: Tool agents
docs.text:
tools.llm lets a chat model operate a robot through typed tools, one checked action at a time. The model can measure freely: find objects, turn pixels into world points, compute, and ask for grasp poses. Every action it takes is a proposal that runs through the kernel and the safety shield, and the next message brings a measured receipt and fresh camera images. The task's own check decides success; the model never sees it.

Use it to try a model on a task without writing a program, to watch how a model approaches a robot problem, and to collect conversations that worked. For a frozen, model-free implementation use code.program; for a model that writes Python against the same tools use code.llm (see Programs).

docs.title: Run an agent
docs.text:
The environment must publish a robot description (mujoco.panda_table, mujoco.aloha_table, mujoco.g1_table, or libero in its tool mode). Complete Installation, configure camera rendering, and make qwen3.5:35b-a3b available at your Ollama endpoint. Run commands from the workspace root. Create runs/configs/ and save this complete configuration as runs/configs/tools-llm-stack.yaml:

schema_version: hylo.experiment/v0.1
name: tools-llm-stack
benchmark: {type: mujoco/manip-v0, params: {tasks: [stack], validation: 3}, split: validation}
env: {type: mujoco.panda_table, params: {cameras: [front, side, wrist], segmentation: true}}
agent:
  type: tools.llm
  params:
    model: {backend: ollama, model: qwen3.5:35b-a3b, vision: true, reasoning_effort: none}
    max_decisions: 20        # actions that moved (or could have moved) the robot
    max_calls: 60            # model calls in the episode
    inbox: runs/steer/inbox.jsonl
trace: {record_privileged: false}

uv run hylo preflight runs/configs/tools-llm-stack.yaml --out runs/tools-llm-stack   # check before running
MUJOCO_GL=osmesa uv run hylo run runs/configs/tools-llm-stack.yaml
uv run hylo watch <run_dir>                                                     # follow it in the terminal

hylo preflight loads the config and its plugins, checks free storage, makes four live calls to the model (a text reply, an image, a tool call with the right arguments, an answer that uses a tool result) and resets the environment once. With --out the results are kept with the run.

Models: any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, vLLM, DeepSeek), the Anthropic API, or a coding-agent CLI. Models without native tool calls get the tools described in the prompt and write calls as fenced blocks. For local reasoning models, reasoning_effort: none keeps replies short.

The same agent started from the Studio's Live sandbox: cameras (RGB, depth, segmentation) and the event log while a local model stacks two blocks, then the replay.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool Kind What it does robot_state read each arm's tool pose, joints, hand opening and whether it holds something look read the camera images with each camera's position, direction and intrinsics locate read objects described in words, measured in 3D; returns target handles and an outlined image pixel_to_world, world_to_pixel read pixels to world points from depth (named points are cross-checked between cameras); points to pixels with occlusion evidence calc read exact arithmetic with numpy and rotation helpers grasp_options, reach_check read grasp poses for a target that fit the open hand; whether a pose is reachable read_artifact, report_issue read reopen an older result the context stored; note an interface problem move_tcp action move the tool point to a pose, on a collision-free path or in a straight line grasp, place action execute a grasp option (approach, close, lift); put the held object at a point or on a target gripper, recover, wait action open or close; back to the previous or home posture; let time pass finish end success with the evidence, give up with a reason, or abort

Rules the agent works under:

  • Read tools can share one reply. An action must be the only call in its reply, and ends the model's turn.
  • Target and grasp handles are tied to the moment they were measured; after the robot moves they are refused as stale and must be measured again.
  • A refused action that moved nothing does not count as a decision. The same action refused three times in a row ends the episode.
  • finish(success) states the model's view only. Episodes are scored by the task's check.

docs.title: Live control
docs.text:
uv run hylo watch runs/<run-dir>                        # the newest episode, followed while it runs
uv run hylo watch runs/<run-dir> --replay --speed 4     # a finished episode on its recorded timing
uv run hylo watch runs/<run-dir> --inbox runs/steer/inbox.jsonl --interactive   # type to steer
uv run hylo watch --say "the target is the small cup" --inbox runs/steer/inbox.jsonl

Each model turn, tool call, receipt and operator message is one line. A message sent to the inbox reaches the model before its next call. Any message marks the episode human_assisted; such episodes do not count as autonomous results and are left out of training exports.

hylo watch --replay on a recorded episode: each model turn, read calls in blue, actions in orange with their receipts, a refused call in red that the model then corrects, and the verdict.

docs.title: Inspect results
docs.text:
Per episode, the trace has the model's turns (agent.tool.turn), every tool result, every action proposal and its receipt, and a summary: model calls, decisions, refusals, tokens, cost, why it stopped, and the outcome the model stated. The prompt is recorded by layer (protocol, evidence rules, boundary, robot description), each with a digest, together with the digest of the tool set.

Inspect the recorded trace example for model turns, proposals, receipts and the episode summary.

uv run hylo seal runs/<run-dir>             # check every hash chain, list every file, make the run read-only
uv run hylo seal --verify runs/<run-dir>    # anything changed, added or removed since sealing
uv run hylo chats runs/<run-dir> --out chats.jsonl   # successful, unsteered conversations as training records

Every trace line carries the hash of the line before it, so a changed, removed or reordered line is found. Sealing is refused when a chain is broken or when a model-visible event contains privileged keys.

docs.title: Task variations
docs.text:
LIBERO tasks can be changed in seven ways, to measure what an agent or a policy relies on. Declare them on the benchmark; each variant is its own task:

benchmark:
  type: libero
  params: {suite: libero_goal, task_indices: [8], perturb: [position, language, task]}   # three variants
  # perturb: [[position, object]]                                                          # one combined variant
env: {type: libero, params: {control: joint_position, tool_obs: true, segmentation: true}}

Perturbation What changes position the object the goal moves trades start positions with another movable object task a different goal in the same scene, with a rewritten instruction, checked by LIBERO's own goal predicate (27 of the 40 tasks of four suites have one) language the instruction is replaced by a paraphrase (three per instruction) object movable objects are recoloured camera the main camera moves about its view axis noise pixel noise and a glare spot on every image robot_init the arm starts from offset joints

Every observation reports what was changed. Perturbations work in both LIBERO modes, for VLA policies as well as tool agents.

docs.title: Control model
docs.text: tools.llm lets a model call typed tools one step at a time. Each action returns a checked receipt before the next decision, and the trace records the prompt, tools, observations and outcome. Use program agents when the model should write a reusable sequence of actions in Python.

docs.title: Use memory
docs.text: Select memory for a decision your agent actually makes. The memory backend and its consuming agent must support the same interface; adding a memory plugin alone does not make an arbitrary model use it.

docs.title: Choose a backend
docs.text: Use the memory types to match your task to a backend and consumer. The example below uses event memory: it records supplied observations and recalls their order without a model.

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
Complete Installation. From the workspace root, run the CPU example:

uv run python harness/examples/memory/06_event_memory.py --quick

Expected output includes 40/40 correct complete-evidence cases. These cases check storage and recall from supplied observations; they do not evaluate visual perception. Event memory shows the minimal Python API.

docs.title: Connect an agent
docs.text:
For spatial memory, start with the composable agent configuration. For event memory, supply an observation extractor and recall queries to the wrapper. For video memory, match the checkpoint's camera, state, controller and runtime requirements before loading the model.

Persistent action banks and skill libraries need development data or promotion evidence first. Follow their building steps before putting a path in an agent configuration; a path alone does not create the artifact.

docs.title: Evaluation boundaries
docs.text: Keep persistent experience sources frozen during evaluation. Episode-local history can update from permitted observations, but must be scoped and reset so another evaluation episode cannot read it. Check the recorded retrievals and compare with the same agent without that memory under matching task conditions.

docs.title: Create a world
docs.text:
Create a small stage, compile it into a MuJoCo world, advance the simulation and check an outcome. This first example uses a falling cube, so it needs no model endpoint, downloaded robot assets or camera renderer.

Complete Installation. Run commands from the workspace root.

docs.title: Build a stage
docs.text:
Create a runs/ directory if needed. Save the following as runs/first_world.py:

from hylo.envs.mujoco.world_tools import Workspace

workspace = Workspace("runs/stages", "first_world")

def call(name, **arguments):
    reply = workspace.surface.call(name, arguments)
    if not reply.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{name}: {reply.error}")
    return reply.result

try:
    stage = call("stage_show")
    if stage["revision"] == 0:
        call("stage_edit", expected_revision=0, ops=[
            {"op": "add", "entity": {
                "id": "table", "shape": {"type": "box", "size": [0.4, 0.4, 0.05]},
                "pose": {"pos": [0, 0, 0.35]}}},
            {"op": "add", "entity": {
                "id": "cube", "shape": {"type": "box", "size": [0.02, 0.02, 0.02]},
                "body": {"dynamic": True, "mass": 0.05}, "pose": {"pos": [0, 0, 0.6]}}},
        ])
    built = call("world_build")
    print("movable:", built["movable"])
    call("advance", seconds=1.0)
    checked = call("check", goal={"op": "contact", "a": "cube", "b": "table"})
    print("cube touches table:", checked["satisfied"])
finally:
    if workspace.world is not None:
        workspace.world.close()

uv run python runs/first_world.py

Expected output includes movable: ['cube'] and cube touches table: True. The stage and its revision history are saved under runs/stages/first_world/. Rerunning rebuilds that saved stage. Use another stage name for a separate example if you have edited this one.

docs.title: Add a robot
docs.text:
Add an entity with a robot pack through stage_edit, then rebuild before acting. Use the pack and action reference to select controls supported by that robot. Camera images and Studio's live scene view require rendering setup.

For an interactive view, build the Studio frontend and run uv run hylo playground --repo . from the workspace root. Open World and select first_world. Rebuild it in Studio: the Python process above has closed its simulation, while the saved stage remains.

docs.title: Model control
docs.text:
Configure a chat backend and camera rendering first. The following uses the default model configuration; hylo world chat --help lists the model options. Run it from the workspace root.

MUJOCO_GL=osmesa uv run hylo world chat "a table with a red cube, a Panda that picks it up, a Go2 walking past" \
    --stage lab --vision --out runs/world-chat/lab --inbox runs/world-chat/lab/inbox.jsonl
uv run hylo watch runs/world-chat/lab
uv run hylo world tools                         # the tool manual

The model reads the stage before editing it, builds, acts and checks; a vision model also gets a view after every action. The session is traced like an episode and can be steered through its inbox.

Coding agents can use the same tools over the Model Context Protocol:

{"command": "uv", "args": ["run", "hylo", "mcp", "--surface", "mujoco.world", "--param", "stage=lab"]}

Models do make mistakes here: forgetting to make an object movable, or weakening a check until it passes. Read the receipts and run the checks yourself before relying on a session's own summary.

docs.title: Role campaigns
docs.text:
hylo roles run CAMPAIGN.yaml works through a set of tasks, each a stage, a request and a goal, split into development and held-out tasks.

  • A worker session solves each development task on a fresh copy of its stage. Every tool call goes into a ledger and counts against the task's budget.
  • A solved task's actions become a recipe skill, keyed by the reasons its goal failed at the start.
  • A verifier replays the recipe on fresh copies without a model. The skill joins the library only if the goal then holds.
  • Held-out tasks run last; they are never used to propose or verify skills. When a task's goal fails with the same reasons, the matching skills are offered to the worker.

docs.text:
Use the World page to inspect and operate the scene.

docs.title: Control a robot
docs.text:
Let a model turn a stacking instruction into robot tool calls, checking each action before continuing. The video shows one successful Panda simulation episode with qwen3.5:35b-a3b; it does not establish an aggregate success rate or hardware performance.

1:45 · English · Recorded episode walkthrough. “Stack the purple block on the green block”: locate both blocks, choose a grasp, pick up the purple block, measure the target again, then place. Front and wrist cameras show the motion alongside the original model's tool calls and measured receipts.

Recording details

The selected qwen3.5:35b-a3b episode has five model calls, two robot actions and 127 control steps, ending in success according to the task's own check. It has no operator messages or safety interventions. This is one recorded simulation episode, not a new aggregate evaluation or a hardware demonstration.

The presentation replays the original actions in MuJoCo at higher camera resolution. All 128 recorded joint and gripper states, including reset, match exactly; the replay reaches the same success verdict. The original trace's 531 hash-chained events verify. Model waits are shortened and robot motions are slowed for readability; selected model text is shown as trace excerpts. The original run took 92.6 seconds. Replay provenance records the source trace hash and verification.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Follow the tool-calling agent guide. A new model run may produce a different result. The recorded conditions and provenance above describe this case.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Give an agent access to earlier observations and experience. Memory can retain object locations, recall event history, supply video context, retrieve successful motions or inform the next proposed change.

docs.title: Memory types
docs.text:
Capability Use Consumer Recall object locations Spatial memory a composable agent or reasoner Recall event order and counts Event memory an agent with an observation extractor Use earlier camera frames Video memory a compatible frozen SimpleMemVLA agent Retrieve successful motions Action memory a flow policy supporting memory steering Learn from previous attempts Lessons the experience proposer

A backend needs a consumer that reads it. Adding a memory plugin alone does not make an arbitrary model use memory. For reusable procedures and agent changes, see Skills.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Use memory starts with a CPU event-recall example, then explains how to connect a consumer. Choose a backend above for its configuration and integration steps.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
An observation is incomplete and temporary: a target leaves view, an instruction refers to an earlier event, or a useful motion was discovered in a previous development run. Memory retains the evidence needed for those different decisions. The query determines the representation: positions and time ranges need structured fields, event order needs a journal, video-conditioned models need frame history, and a motion policy needs action data.

Each memory also needs provenance and a consumer. Remembering a location records where and when it was observed; retrieving a motion identifies the episode it came from. The consuming agent decides how to use that evidence. Storage does not make stale evidence current or turn a perception error into a reliable fact.

docs.title: Spatial and event memory
docs.text:
Spatial memory stores identity, pose, frame, time and scope as fields. This supports queries such as “where was the target?” or “which objects were near this point?” without encoding coordinates only as text. New evidence can invalidate a previous location while retaining the old record, so replay can reconstruct what the agent knew when it acted. A recalled location may still need fresh perception before a grasp.

Event memory records an ordered journal within an episode. Queries retrieve the latest or nth observation, counts, sequences and pending events with evidence references. Answers distinguish known, partial and unknown information. An observed count is only a lower bound without complete coverage; failing to observe an event does not establish that it never happened. An extractor must first turn permitted observations into events.

docs.title: Video history
docs.text: The SimpleMemVLA integration samples chronological camera frames and supplies them, with current observations, to a compatible frozen model. The model uses that context when producing subtasks and action chunks. This path uses an episode buffer and feature cache rather than semantic queries over a shared database. Reset clears the history; a checkpoint must already support video context, and the integration remains experimental.

docs.title: Action priors
docs.text:
Action memory retrieves successful development motions using the policy's observation features. Similarity filters and motion-consistency checks select compatible segments; weighted aggregation produces a motion prior, with a vote for gripper state so open and closed grasps are not simply averaged together.

The prior biases a compatible flow policy's sampling while that policy still responds to the current scene. This allows adaptation to differences between a remembered motion and the present task. Retrieval similarity and agreement control the bias strength; without a usable match the policy samples without a memory prior. Similarity is not proof of suitability, so the same policy with and without memory must be compared on the target task. Recorded LIBERO results do not establish a reliable action-memory gain.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: Lessons retain short strategies and pitfalls for a proposer planning its next change. A reflector proposes small, evidence-citing edits from development episodes; the lesson book validates and logs those operations. The outcomes of candidates that cited a lesson update helpful or harmful counts, and repeatedly harmful lessons retire from retrieval while remaining in the record. This ties retained advice to outcomes and keeps a model from silently rewriting the entire history. Lessons affect behaviour through a model that actually reads them.

docs.title: Memory lifetime
docs.text:
Scope Written Read Episode history from permitted observations during an episode by the agent in that episode Action banks from successful development episodes by a compatible policy, with the bank frozen Lessons from development diagnostics and credited campaign outcomes by a proposer planning its next change

Episode history and persistent experience have different evaluation roles. An agent may need to remember what it saw earlier in the same task. Updating a shared bank from scored episodes would instead let one evaluation task teach the next, making results depend on episode order. Freeze shared banks, skill libraries and lesson books during evaluation, while allowing the protocol's permitted episode history to update and reset normally. Record persistent sources by digest so a result identifies the experience it used.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Scope and reset episode history so another evaluation episode cannot read it. A persistent journal can retain audit evidence without exposing that evidence to later episodes.
  • Freeze shared banks, skill libraries and lesson books during evaluation. Record their digests with the agent.
  • Verify that the consumer uses the retrieved context. Lessons require a model that reads them; action-memory benefit depends on retrieval quality and needs a comparison on the target task.
  • Tool-agent and world-session context stays within its episode or session. Role campaigns reuse experience across tasks through recipe skills.

docs.title: Studio
docs.text: The Experience page shows skill libraries, lesson books and action banks under the runs directory, with their status and evidence.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Use memory: connect a backend to an agent.
  • Memory reference: fields, queries and storage rules.
  • Recorded results: measured benefits and failures.

docs.title: Action memory
docs.text: Action memory lets a frozen flow policy draw on its own past successes. The bank stores segments from episodes that the simulator verified as successful: what the policy saw (as a retrieval key) and the action chunk it produced then. At each decision the agent retrieves similar segments and starts the policy's sampling from them instead of from pure noise. The policy still integrates its own velocity field from the current observation, so memory biases the action; it never replays one.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
First build an action bank from successful development runs and register its artifact id. For the example below, prepare the LIBERO and LeRobot runtimes and checkpoint. This is an agent fragment for an experiment; replace the example artifact id with your bank.

memory.steered wraps a sampler that implements the prior-sampling protocol. For LeRobot flow policies such as SmolVLA, use lerobot.memory_steered, which runs the policy in its own runtime:

agent:
  type: remote
  params:
    ref: lerobot.memory_steered
    runtime: lerobot
    params:
      repo_id: lerobot/smolvla_libero
      steering: {n_samples: 1, seed_noise: true}
      memory: {type: action_bank, params: {path: "artifact:l10-search-v1@40a84dd1afab4a5c"}}
      memory_steer: {k: 10, same_task: true, sim_floor: 0.95, t0_min: 0.1, t0_max: 0.7}

The full LIBERO-10 config is bench/examples/configs/libero10_memory.yaml.

Retrieval settings lists defaults and all tuning options.

Calibrate retrieval and sampling strength on development data. Action memory can reduce success when retrieved motions do not suit the current scene; compare with the same policy without memory before adopting it.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
Build a bank from successful development episodes and load it frozen for evaluation. To incorporate new development experience, save a new artifact. Each decision retrieves similar segments and uses them as a sampling prior while the policy still responds to the current observation.

Close, consistent neighbours give a stronger bias. Distant or disagreeing neighbours give a weaker one; without a usable match, the policy samples as it would without memory. The policy computes retrieval keys in its own forward pass, so retrieval needs no extra model call.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
1. The policy computes a retrieval key inside its own forward pass (for SmolVLA, its pooled visual tokens), so retrieval costs no extra encoder call.
  2. The bank returns the k most similar segments by cosine similarity, from the same task by default, and drops those below sim_floor.
  3. Segments whose motion disagrees with the rest (dynamic time warping over the first steps, more than dtw_mad median absolute deviations from the median) are dropped.
  4. The rest are combined into a prior: a similarity-weighted mean for motion, a weighted vote for the gripper (the nearest segment's gripper when the vote is split).
  5. Confidence, from the similarity and from how much the segments agree, sets where sampling starts: t0 between t0_min (confident, a strong bias) and t0_max (weak). With nothing usable, t0 = 1: exactly the unchanged policy.
The arithmetic

For the kept segments i with similarity s_i and action chunk a_i:

w_i        = softmax(s_i / temperature)
prior      = Σ w_i · a_i                          motion dimensions
vote       = Σ w_i · sign(g_i)                    gripper dimension g
prior_g    = sign(vote) · mean |g_i|              nearest segment's g if |vote| < 0.2
s̄          = clip((Σ w_i · s_i − sim_floor) / (1 − sim_floor), 0, 1)
confidence = s̄ · exp(−dispersion / dispersion_scale)
t0         = t0_max − (t0_max − t0_min) · confidence
x_t0       = (1 − t0) · prior + t0 · noise        then the policy integrates from t0 to 0

dispersion is the mean pairwise DTW distance between the kept segments.

Each decision emits memory.retrieval with the matches, confidence and sampling start time. Inspect these fields when a retrieved prior changes the result.

The chosen chunk's provenance also records t0 and the number of segments kept, and the agent spec records the bank: bank(<digest>,n=<segments>,k=10,floor=0.95,t0=[0.1,0.7]).

docs.title: Build a bank
docs.text:
A bank is a folder with bank.npz (keys, chunks, lengths) and bank.json (schema, digest, and each segment's task, step, progress and source episode); no pickle. It holds at most capacity segments (50,000 by default), oldest first out. Keys are stored L2-normalised as float16, so similarity is a dot product. Loading checks the content against the recorded digest.

For LeRobot policies, build from the runs of development splits, with the policy's own keys:

envs/libero/.venv/bin/python -m hylo.policies.lerobot.memory_build --runs runs/<search runs> \
    --splits search --out runs/memory/l10-search-v1 --repo-id lerobot/smolvla_libero
uv run hylo store ref runs/memory/l10-search-v1        # an artifact id for configs

Only chunks from simulator-verified successful episodes are stored, and replays of identical episodes are stored once. The builder seals the folder as an action_memory artifact and writes build_report.json with nearest-neighbour similarity statistics: set sim_floor from those. The same builder runs as a learner job (lerobot.action_memory) through hylo learn.

For other policies, collect segments from successful episodes and add them to a bank in a script; the MuJoCo memory examples do this (examples/memory/_common.py: segments_from_run), including a bank that each session extends and saves for the next.

docs.title: Noise memory
docs.text: lerobot.noise_steered is a variant that remembers the initial noise that led to successful chunks instead of the chunks themselves, and mixes it with fresh noise over the full flow. Build its bank with memory_build --store noise. Compare it with the base policy under the same evaluation protocol.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The sampler must implement the prior-sampling protocol (sample(..., prior_fn=...) and retrieval_key). LeRobot flow policies do; the reference policy.flow does not on its own.
  • The gripper dimension is always aggregated by vote; there is no option for robots without a gripper.
  • Banks for policies other than LeRobot are built in scripts, not with a command.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Recorded results: measurements, conditions and reproduction commands.
  • Use memory: match a memory to its consuming agent.
  • Memory: lifetime and evaluation boundaries.

docs.title: Event memory
docs.text:
EventMemory stores episode-scoped observations in a SQLite journal and answers exact queries over their recorded order. It supports latest, first, nth, count, sequence, unseen, pending and elapsed-time recall. Each answer carries evidence references and a known, partial or unknown status.

This is a storage and recall component, not a visual detector. An extractor or adapter must turn permitted observations into events. Missing perception cannot become a known fact merely because it was written to memory.

docs.title: Store and recall
docs.text:
from hylo.core.episode_memory import EpisodeScope, MemoryEvent, RecallQuery
from hylo.memory.episode import EventMemory

memory = EventMemory()
memory.reset(EpisodeScope(task_id="example", episode_id="episode-1"))
memory.append([MemoryEvent(
    id="cue-1", step=0, time=0.0, kind="cue", subject="target",
    value="blue", evidence=("observation:0:front",), source="visible-cue-adapter",
)])
answer = memory.recall(RecallQuery(name="target", op="latest", kind="cue", subject="target"))
assert answer.status == "known" and answer.value == "blue"
memory.close()

The cue value above is example input supplied by an adapter. The journal does not infer it from an image. Event IDs must be stable; repeating the same ID and payload is idempotent, while reusing an ID for different evidence is rejected. Events have increasing (step, order) positions and nondecreasing times.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
An observed count is a lower bound unless the caller explicitly declares complete coverage. Negative queries require both coverage and a defined universe. Observation gaps or ambiguous evidence can produce unknown; exceeding the event budget raises an error rather than silently discarding the early events that a later query might require.

Reset selects a task/episode scope. Reopening existing evidence requires resume=True; ordinary reset refuses to reuse a scope that already contains events. Persistent journals can retain audit evidence without making it available to another episode's recall.

docs.title: Agent integration
docs.text: EventMemoryAgent wraps an existing agent with an extractor and recall queries. It makes the recalled context available through the wrapped agent's instruction. The reference SignalExtractor consumes declared, agent-visible state signals; it is not an RGB detector and must not be connected to privileged simulator fields on a visual benchmark.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
CPU tests cover scoped persistence, event ordering, duplicate handling, evidence gaps, bounded recall and agent composition. These establish the storage/recall behavior, not a general visual-memory benchmark benefit.

For contracts and implementation, see the core API, memory API and agents API. Runnable CPU examples live at harness/examples/memory/06_event_memory.py and harness/examples/memory/07_event_memory_occlusion.py in the workspace.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Use memory: choose a consuming agent.
  • Memory interfaces: current contracts and lifecycle rules.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: A lesson is a short note distilled from experience, such as "a narrower grasp slips on flat boxes", that a language model can use when it proposes the next change to an agent. Lessons are kept in a lesson book: a folder with the current lessons (lessons.json) and a log of every change (ops.jsonl).

docs.title: Configure lessons
docs.text:
Add this proposer fragment to a campaign. It requires the language-model backend used by the inner proposer and reflector; the example names a model served through Ollama.

Lessons take effect through the experience proposer, which wraps any proposer of an improvement campaign:

proposer:
  type: experience
  params:
    inner: {type: llm.steering, params: {model: qwen3.5:35b-a3b}}
    lessons: {type: lesson_book, params: {path: runs/lessons/reach}}
    skills: {type: skill_library, params: {path: runs/skills/reach}}
    reflector: {type: llm.reflector, params: {model: qwen3.5:35b-a3b}}
    skill_tags: [mujoco, reach]             # tags given to the skills it derives

Before each round:

  1. The archive so far becomes skills, each with the status its evidence supports (see Skills).
  2. Lessons cited by candidates that have since been decided are credited: +1 for a verified candidate, −1 for a refuted one, once per candidate.
  3. The reflector distils new operations from the parent's development episodes, once per run.
  4. The inner proposer sees the best active lessons for the tasks at hand (up to eight, by net votes) and the index of skills with their status, and lists the lessons each candidate relies on.

The book records the source of each operation, so resuming a campaign does not credit the same outcome twice.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
llm.reflector reads the same development-split material the steering proposer reads (per-episode timelines: grasp steps, still periods, heights, outcome) and proposes operations. It never sees validation, gate or held-out results, so lessons cannot carry information from the splits that decide promotion. Every ADD must cite episodes it was shown; uncited or out-of-scope operations are dropped.

The reflector proposes small edits to a ranked lesson book. Helpful and harmful outcomes update its counts; a lesson retires when its harmful count reaches its helpful count plus two. See the operation rules and lesson fields.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
lessons: {type: lesson_book, params: {path: runs/lessons/reach, frozen: true}}

A frozen book refuses every operation. The Studio's Experience page shows each book's lessons with their counts and its recent operations.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Lessons do nothing without a language model that reads them.
  • The reflector's prompt is written for manipulation timelines; other domains need their own.
  • Near-duplicate detection compares titles only.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Campaigns: run the improvement loop.
  • Memory reference: fields and operation rules.
  • Recorded results: measured scope.

docs.title: Skill library
docs.text: The library stores versioned skills, their applicability, status and evidence. Its records hold data: a configuration change, a subgoal plan, a reference to trained weights or to a sealed program, or a list of tool calls. A skill library is a folder with one JSON file per skill version (<name>@<version>.json). Agents look skills up when a task starts, when a code agent writes its next block, when a proposer plans a round, or when a goal fails.

docs.title: Build a library
docs.text:
You need an existing campaign archive. The commands below run from the workspace root; replace the campaign paths with your own. For a complete example that produces a promoted program before building the library, follow Develop and reuse a program skill.

# steering and weights skills from an improvement campaign's archive
uv run hylo skills runs/campaigns/l10 --out runs/skills/libero10 --tags libero libero_10 --env libero
# program skills from a campaign's promoted code candidates
uv run hylo research skills runs/campaigns/pick --library runs/skills/manip --family pick_place

hylo skills turns every decided archive entry into a skill version with the status its evidence supports, and is safe to run again: entries already in the library are skipped. Candidates that change something other than the steering configuration or the weights are not expressible as skills and are listed as skipped.

The experience proposer runs the same conversion before every round of a campaign, so a library grows while the campaign runs (see Lessons). Role campaigns add recipe skills themselves, after the verifier's replay.

docs.title: Select skills
docs.text:
Only verified skills are applied. Matching uses the task, environment or failure signature, depending on the skill kind. Program retrieval uses instruction similarity. A skill record references its implementation and evidence; programs are checked again before being offered to a code agent.

See the supported kinds, matching rules and status transitions. Refuted skills remain in the library as evidence of unsuccessful candidates. Proposers see their status without the gate's effect sizes or p-values.

docs.title: Apply skills
docs.text: The fragments below belong in an experiment configuration. Prepare the library first and choose an inner agent compatible with the selected skill kinds. The ... in the first fragment must be replaced with that agent's configuration.

docs.title: Skill agent
docs.text:
agent:
  type: skills
  params:
    skills: {type: skill_library, params: {path: runs/skills/libero10, frozen: true}}
    kinds: [steering, recovery, plan]              # the default
    inner:
      type: planner.subgoal
      params: {inner: {type: steered, params: {...}}}

At the start of each episode the library is matched against the task's instruction, tags and environment. The best skill of each kind is applied for that episode only:

  • a steering skill is merged into the nearest steered agent in the wrapped chain;
  • a recovery skill's rules are appended to that agent's rules (at most four rules in total);
  • a plan skill's templates are filled with the trigger's slots and given to the nearest subgoal agent; a plan with a missing slot is not applied.

Everything is undone at the end of the episode. Each application is a skill.applied event, and the episode ends with a summary of the skills used and the outcome, so results can be attributed to the skill.

The agent spec names the library by digest, for example library(<digest>,verified=1,kinds=steering,recovery,plan).

docs.title: Program skills
docs.text:
agent:
  type: code.llm
  params:
    model: {backend: ollama, model: qwen3.5:35b-a3b, vision: true}
    skills: runs/skills/manip        # a path opens the library frozen
    max_skills: 3
    min_skill_similarity: 0.2

The most similar verified program skills are offered to the model as functions, skills.<name>(robot, **kw), with their descriptions and preconditions. Before a skill is offered, its program is read back, its digest compared with the one in the skill, and its source checked by the sandbox; a skill that fails is skipped and reported. See Program skills.

docs.title: Recipe skills
docs.text: In a role campaign, a solved development task becomes a recipe keyed by the reason codes its goal failed with at the start. When a later task fails for the same reasons, the matching recipes, with their steps, are offered to the worker on its retry. Held-out tasks run last with the library frozen. See Worlds.

docs.title: Model export
docs.text: SkillLibrary.export_skill_md(dir) writes one SKILL.md per verified skill (name and description as front matter, trigger, body and evidence below), so a model can scan the index and read a skill only when it needs it. Proposers get an index of all skills with their status but without gate numbers: a proposer that saw effect sizes could fit itself to the gate split.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• hylo skills recognises the steering path of a remote agent (agent.params.params.steering); campaigns that steer a local agent need the conversion functions called from a script, as the memory example does.
  • Weights skills are not applied per episode; reloading a policy is a configuration change for a campaign.
  • Matching instructions to programs uses word overlap, not embeddings.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:

  • Memory reference: kinds, matching and status.
  • Recorded results: measurements and reproduction commands.

docs.title: Spatial memory
docs.text: Spatial memory stores facts about the world with a place and a time: "the red block was at (0.31, −0.12) on the table at t = 4.2 s". An agent writes what it perceives while it can see it, and recalls it once it cannot. The reference backend is sqlite: one SQLite file (or :memory: for a single run), queried by key, kind, time, place and text.

docs.title: Connect an agent
docs.text:
Composable agents pair a reasoner (slow, event-triggered decisions) with a policy (every step). The reasoner gets the memory store, a per-episode working memory with a fixed capacity, and an event emitter.

agent:
  type: composable.object_reach
  params:
    chooser: {type: chooser.rule_color}        # or chooser.llm / chooser.vlm
    memory: {type: sqlite, params: {path: ":memory:"}}   # the default; a file path keeps it across runs

composable.object_reach writes every visible object as a spatial item keyed by episode and object, and when the objects are hidden it recalls them from memory instead. The chooser decides which object the instruction means, from seen or remembered objects alike, so the same code serves both. memory: null turns memory off.

A reasoner of your own uses the same contracts:

from hylo.core.memory import MemoryItem, MemoryKind, MemoryQuery, Pose, TimeSpan

def remember(rctx, obj_id, xy, t):
    item = MemoryItem(kind=MemoryKind.SPATIAL, key=f"{rctx.episode_id}:{obj_id}", content=f"{obj_id} at {xy}",
                      entities=(obj_id,), scope={"episode_id": rctx.episode_id},
                      pose=Pose(frame_id="table", position=(*xy, 0.0)), event_time=TimeSpan(start=t))
    res = rctx.memory.write([item])
    rctx.emit("memory.write", {"op": "write", "events": [list(e) for e in res.events]})

def recall(rctx, near_xy, radius=0.2):
    q = MemoryQuery(kinds=frozenset({MemoryKind.SPATIAL}), scope={"episode_id": rctx.episode_id},
                    near=(Pose(frame_id="table", position=(*near_xy, 0.0)), radius))
    hits = rctx.memory.query(q)
    rctx.emit("memory.retrieval", {"n_hits": len(hits)})
    return hits

Emit the events yourself: they are what makes a decision from memory visible in a replay.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
The reasoner writes observed objects and queries them when perception loses the target. Scope writes and queries to the episode. The same chooser handles visible and remembered objects.

Locations and times are structured fields. A newer keyed fact invalidates the earlier one while preserving history; expire a remembered location when it proves wrong. See the storage rules.

docs.title: Inspect retrieval
docs.text:
Use the trace to check memory.write, memory.retrieval and agent.decision events. A decision's object_source distinguishes seen from remembered objects. The recorded trace shows the switch after targets become hidden.

See Memory reference for item fields, writes and queries.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Text search uses substring matching.
  • Spatial queries require positions in the same frame.
  • Memory does not resolve language: an instruction the chooser misreads is misread with memory too.

docs.text:

  • Use memory: match a memory to its consuming agent.
  • Memory: lifetime and evaluation boundaries.

docs.title: Video memory
docs.text:
SimpleMemVLA is an optional visual-memory agent in Hylo. It keeps sampled episode video and lets a compatible frozen video-conditioned model use that history when producing subtasks and action chunks. Hylo owns the history buffers and sampling; the pinned upstream runtime supplies the neural model and action head. No new training is performed.

This option uses its own streaming history interface. It does not implement the semantic MemoryStore query API, and requires a checkpoint trained to consume video context. Other memory and agent options remain independently selectable.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This is an experimental integration requiring a compatible environment and model runtime. It is not a standalone runnable benchmark config. Before using the agent fragment below:

  1. Prepare the inference dependencies and pinned source described in the adapter README.
  2. Make the local checkpoint and camera/state mappings available in that same runtime.
  3. Match the Panda controller interface below. A full native Hylo kernel-to-RoboMME evaluation remains unverified.

Install the optional hylo-policy-simplememvla workspace adapter in the inference environment. Make the pinned upstream source importable there and supply an existing local checkpoint; the adapter does not download weights or install model dependencies.

agent:
  type: simplememvla
  params:
    checkpoint: /models/simplememvla_robomme
    camera_map: {front: front, wrist: wrist}
    joint_key: joint_pos
    gripper_key: gripper_pos
    execution_steps: 16

The released RoboMME checkpoint expects the Panda joint-position/gripper interface at 20 Hz. State consists of seven arm joints and the first finger position; actions contain seven joint targets and one gripper value. The environment must supply matching units and gripper conventions. The adapter does not translate robot embodiments.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
The released configuration samples 120 front-camera frames across a roughly 60-second window at 2 fps and includes the current wrist image. Sampling follows native frame indices at 20 Hz. The raw buffer retains at most 1,191 front frames and one wrist frame. Fixed short histories repeat the first available frame; checkpoint configurations can instead enable the upstream variable-history rule.

flowchart LR
    observations["RGB at each control step"] --> history["Episode history and frame IDs"]
    history --> sampling["Checkpoint-compatible sampling"]
    sampling --> model["Frozen video-conditioned VLA"]
    instruction["Instruction and current robot state"] --> model
    model --> actions["Subtask and action chunk"]

on_step() records executed control-step observations. Calling act() again on the same step does not duplicate its frame. observe_history(prefix) can supply public demonstration observations after reset and before the first decision; the prefix excludes the current observation. The environment integration must explicitly provide that prefix.

Each session owns its buffers and feature cache. Reset and episode completion clear them. Task IDs, rewards, evaluator success and extra simulator fields are not sent to the model. Older frames leave the rolling window; there is no longer-term video archive or cross-episode retrieval in this implementation.

docs.title: Batching
docs.text:
SimpleMemVLARuntime.infer_batch() shares model weights across independent sessions and preserves row order. Callers assemble batches explicitly. The native agent's act() sends one row; automatic batching across agents is not implemented.

The native agent derives a seed for each decision. Upstream-style shared-stream batching can draw different noise when batch composition changes. Fix the batching and RNG protocol when comparing variants; matching initial scene seeds alone does not ensure matching actions.

Pinned dependencies lists source and checkpoint revisions, attribution and reproduction instructions.

Recorded integration checks cover upstream parity and regression episodes, with their scope and limitations. They do not establish a gain over another memory method.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Use memory: choose another memory or consuming agent.
  • Adapter API: native lifecycle and batching.

docs.title: Reuse a skill
docs.text:
Turn an existing sorting program into a verified skill, then let another agent call it on new layouts. This recorded simulation uses a supplied starter and robot tools, RGB-D cameras and instance segmentation. It demonstrates program development and reuse within one Panda sorting task family.

2:33 · English · Recorded research walkthrough and physics replay. A deliberately limited one-object-per-colour starter becomes a program for sorting multiple objects into matching trays. The video follows the actual source revision, complete-program execution, independent evaluation, skill-library record and later skill call.

Recording details

The model is claude:sonnet. It develops solve(robot) using four development cases; the selected submission passes 4/4. Submission evaluation and subsequent candidate tests execute as code.program, without model calls during execution. This is program development, not model-weight training. The starter and its robot-tool helpers were supplied; this is not a from-scratch result. Two preceding local-model development attempts produced no qualifying candidate; the video follows the selected Claude session.

The recorded candidate passes an independent promotion gate and is then evaluated on held-out scenes. Later agents retrieve and call sort_by_colour@1 in separate validation scenes.

Conditions. One Panda sorting task family, two RGB-D cameras and simulator instance segmentation. The video presents recorded actions with edited timing and higher-resolution replay cameras. The starter and robot-tool helpers were supplied. This does not establish hardware transfer or recognition in real-world images.

Read Developing a program into a reusable skill for the full evaluation, preceding failed attempts, reuse evidence and limitations. Replay provenance identifies the source traces and video checks.

docs.text:
Go2, Go1, A1 and Spot: 0.78 to 1.31 m forward in 4 s, then a turn, all in the same steps. G1 and H1 leg models under pretrained walking policies: 2.2 and 2.0 m in 5 s, then a turn. Crazyflie 2 and Skydio X2 flying three waypoints each. A Panda picks a cube onto a plate; a UR5e with a mounted Robotiq and a TidyBot base move in the same steps.

Motion measurements record distance, turn and posture for the robot-pack demo.

Recorded model edits are re-executed through the World API. The selected sessions retain their original messages and tool failures; the resulting stage matches the recorded source. Two startup attempts without successful scene changes are omitted. This demo shows scene construction and inspection; it does not demonstrate robot task execution. The robot-pack videos show separate recorded examples of robots moving in a world.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
Follow Create a world to build and inspect a scene yourself.

From the workspace root, with the camera renderer configured, run one recorded motion workflow:

uv run python bench/adapters/hylo-env-mujoco/examples/world/showcase.py --out runs/world-showcase quadrupeds

The first run downloads robot assets. Inspect results.json and the generated videos under the output directory. The full results include conditions and other robot families.

docs.title: Worlds
docs.text: A world is a simulation in which agents can act and receive measured feedback. It contains robots, objects, cameras and goals. Use it to develop a task or explore a scene; use a benchmark when you need a fixed comparison.

docs.title: World model
docs.text:
Term Meaning Stage The saved scene description: entities, poses and robot packs, with revision history World The running simulation built from a stage revision Task An instruction and an explicit goal checked against what happened

Changing a stage does not change a running world until it is rebuilt. Actions name the world generation they were planned for, so an action based on an earlier build can be refused. Receipts describe the measured motion; goal checks decide whether the requested result holds.

docs.title: From intent to simulation
docs.text:
A model can choose what a scene should contain and what to try next. Geometry, scene consistency and physical outcomes need explicit checks. Hylo therefore turns an intention into a sequence of validated edits, a compiled simulation and measured actions.

  1. Edit a stage. Small patches add, move or change entities against a known revision. Validation checks names, parents, rotations and mounting relationships before applying the patch. An invalid or outdated patch leaves the stage unchanged; revision history lets an editor restore an earlier scene.
  2. Build a world. Robot packs supply existing models, home postures and supported controls. The compiler combines them with scene geometry and cameras in MuJoCo. A build starts a new world generation and reports fixed and movable entities, available controls and initial overlaps.
  3. Execute an intent. Controllers translate requests such as moving a tool point, walking or flying to a waypoint into simulation-rate commands. This separates the model's decision pace from the robot's control rate and avoids requiring the model to generate joint torques.
  4. Inspect the outcome. Receipts report measured motion and contact or grasp information. Goal checks evaluate predicates on the resulting world and return expected values, measurements and failure reasons.

Patches make changes reviewable and recoverable. Robot packs reuse pinned assets instead of generating a new robot description for every scene. A shared stage gives the Studio, command-line tools and agents the same scene to inspect.

docs.title: Feedback and timing
docs.text:
An action is bound to the world generation it was planned for. Rebuilding or resetting invalidates old actions, so a decision based on an earlier world cannot silently execute in a new one. A repeated action ID does not execute the same action twice. Actions for multiple robots in one call share the same simulation steps.

In interactive world sessions, time advances during actions or an explicit advance request. The world waits while a model decides. This makes inspection and replay practical, but does not measure how that model would behave while a physical robot keeps moving during inference.

For example, a lift command can complete while the block remains too low. The action receipt describes the motion; the task check reports the unmet height and its measured value. Keeping these separate lets an agent correct the attempt without treating an accepted command as task success.

docs.title: Agent integration
docs.text:
A person, a model or a coding agent can edit a stage, build it, act and check outcomes through the same world tools. Robot packs supply models and supported controls. Camera observations can feed an agent's memory; role campaigns can retain replay-verified action recipes as skills.

A successful goal check establishes an outcome in that scene. Comparing improvements across tasks requires a separate evaluation protocol; a world session alone is not that comparison.

For evaluated tasks, define the goal outside the acting agent's session. An agent that can lower its own target can make a check pass without improving the intended outcome. Role campaigns separate task definition, execution and verification, and can replay successful tool sequences before retaining them as recipes. Simulation still depends on the chosen geometry, dynamics, sensors and controllers; those assumptions bound what a result proves.
